bibl.publisher: Longmans, Green and Co.; Hodges, Figgis and Co.

encodingDesc.p: Two supplied OCR witnesses of George W. Mooney (1930), Indiana (INU) and Pennsylvania State (PST). INU is the base; selected clearer PST readings and all witness disagreements are recorded in the accompanying audit. Source wording, including unresolved OCR and editorial differences from Ihm, is retained. This is an OCR draft, not a proofread transcription. Chapter/section references align with Ihm (perseus-lat2). English inner-section boundaries are editorial and have been reviewed against corresponding clauses; printed chapter boundaries are retained. No translation is supplied from Rolfe or Gemini. Commentary section signs are preserved (including OCR $ for §). Domitian 13.3 is aligned by the consulatus septemdecim lemma where the sign is absent. Lemmas use mentioned linked to note type=commentary, following the Sidgwick model. Literal bibl references and explicit glosses are marked without invented reference expansions. Unconfirmed note openings and OCR reading-order issues remain in the review inventory. Introductory material, appendices and index remain available in the complete source-page archives; they are not included in these life-specific reading texts.

revisionDesc.change: Created from two OCR witnesses, retaining and documenting unresolved readings.

p.note: : a cognomen derived from his mother Flavia Domitilla, who died before his father Vespasian became emperor; cf. Vesp. 3. Similarly Vespasian derived his cognomen from his mother Vespasia Polla.
: on Oct. 24, 51 A.D., his father being consul for the last two months of that year (Vesp. 4, 2). His birthday is mentioned C.I.L. x 444, ίχ. Κ. Novembr. natal. Domitiani Aug. n(ostri).

: Servius Tullius divided the city within his walls into 4 regiones: the Suburan, the Esquiline, the Viminal or Colline, and the Palatine (Varro L.L. v 41 sqq.; Dion. Hal. iv 14). Augustus was born regione Palati (Aug. 5). The city, within and without the Servian walls, was divided by Augustus in 7 B.C. into 14 regiones and 265 vici or parishes (Aug. 30; Plin. N.H. iii 66). The names of these regiones are unknown; they may have been distinguished merely by numbers. At the beginning of the 4th cent. the names of the 14 regiones were: I Porta Capena, II Coelimontium, III Isis et Serapis, Iv Templum Pacis, v Esquiliae, VI Alta Semita, VII Via Lata, VIII Forum Romanum, Ix Circus Flaminius, x Palatium, XI Circus Maximus, XII Piscina Publica, XIII Aventinus, XIV Transtiberim. The "Alta Semita," from which the sexta regio took its name, ran all along the back of the Quirinal, on the line of the mod. Strada di Porta Pia.

: this "Pomegranate street" was on the line of the mod. Via delle Quatro Fontane; see Jordan-Huelsen Topogr. Rom i 3, 426, with the plan (no. vii) of the Quirinal. It probably got its name from a tree that grew there; cf. Mart. i 117, 6, where the poet mentions his lodgings on the Quirinal in the street of the Pear-tree (ad Pirum). Augustus was born in the street of the Ox-Heads (ad Capita Bubula), which led from the valley of the Colosseum up the slope of the Palatine (Aug. 5). A house could be designated in the same way; e.g. the villa of Livia was known as ad Gallinas (Galb. 1); so too a vicus; e.g. that at the Porta Collina was called ad tres Fortunas from three temples of Fortune there. The pomegranate (malum Punicum) was introduced into Italy from the north of Africa; cf. Plin. N.H. xiii 112, Africa circa Carthaginem Punicum malum cognomine sibi vindicat; aliqui granatum appellant: Colum. xii 42, mala granata (i.e. with many seeds, grana), quae Punica vocantur: Mart. xiii 42, 43. ..
: cf. Mart. ix 20, 1, Haec, quae tota patet tegiturque et marmore et auro, | infantis domini (i.e. Domitian) conscia terra fuit.

: see c. 5. Besides this temple on the Quirinal, Domitian also built temples to Divus Titus and Divus Vespasianus between the Clivus Capitolinus and the Capitol. These temples are much praised by Martial; e.g. ix 1, 8, Manebit altum Flaviae decus gentis | cum sole et astris cumque luce Romana. | Invicta quidquid condidit manus, caeli est: ix 34, Iuppiter Idaei risit mendacia busti | dum videt Augusti Flavia templa poli; cf. Stat. S. v 1, 240, aeternae modo qui sacraria genti | condidit inque alio posuit sua sidera caelo. In the dedication to Vespasian of his Argonautica Valerius Flaccus (i 15) says of Domitian: Ille tibi cultusque deum delubraque genti | instituet, cum iam genitor lucebis ab omni | parte poli. Domitian intended the templum gentis Flaviae to be a tomb for members of his house. The ashes of Vespasian were brought thither from the Mausoleum Augusti (see on Vesp. 23, 4), and there too were placed the ashes of Titus and his daughter Julia (see Dom. 17, 3), and finally those of Domitian himself. This temple was in existence in the 4th cent., but no traces of it remain (Jordan-Huelsen, p. 426).
: Macrob. Sat. vii 7, 4, secundum iura publica duodecimus annus in femina et quartus decimus in puero definit pubertatis aetatem.
: defined by Varro (ap. Censor. 14) as from 15 to 30 yrs. of age; by Isidorus (Orig. xi 2, 4) as from 14 to 28.
: cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, Domitianus maculosae adulescentiae.

: this use of gerere for agere is very rare; cf. Sulpic. ap. Cic. Fam. iv. 5, ut cum aliquo adulescente primario coniuncta aetatem gereret: Petron. Satyr. 63, vitam Chiam gessi: Val. Flacc. vi 693, semivir impubemque gerens sterilemque iuventam: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 44, annos gerens proxime quadraginta. Casaubon would read egisse. In Vesp. 24, annum agens aetatis sexagesimum, there is a variant gerens.

: during Domitian's riper boyhood and early youth his father Vespasian, after his proconsulship in Africa, was in very straitened circumstances and was compelled to mortgage all his property (see Vesp. 4, 3). Even in the families of the poorer classes it was usual to have the salinum and patera of silver, as these were used in sacrifices to the household gods. From the middle of the 3rd cent. B.C. the use of silver in wealthy houses became more and more widespread, not merely for ordinary table service (argentum escarium, potorium) but also for display on the abacus. The argentea vasa in a big house are referred to in Plaut. Aul. 341, hic autem apud nos magna turba ac familia est, | supellex, aurum, vestis, vasa argentea. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 318 sq.

: Burman, Oudendorp, and others prefer constet, the conjecture of Lipsius, connecting it with ut in the preceding sentence, on the ground that an example of Domitian's infamia is required as well as of his inopia. With constat, the example of infamia is given in the form of a separate statement, independent of the ut clause. Wolf's reasonable objection to constet is that it attributes to Suet. such a clumsy expression as “Fertur aetatem gessisse tanta infamia, ut satis constet,” when he could easily have written “Clodiusque conservarit, etc."
: not mentioned elsewhere.

: Nero's poetical productions included lyrics, tragic monodies, an epic entitled "Troica," poems (probably elegiac) on amatory subjects (cf. Mart. ix 26, 9, Nero lascivum iuvenis cum a tibi lusit opus: Plin. Ep. v 3), and lampoons, of which the “Luscio” would be one, others being referred to in Suet. Ner. 24, quamvis id ipsum in rege Mithridate carmine quodam suo reprehendisset: Tac. A. xv 49, Quintianus mollitia corporis infamis et Nerone probroso carmine diffamatus. "Luscio," which does not occur elsewhere, is presumably connected with luscus (“one-eyed''), and Casaubon suggested that there may be a reference to the "Luscio” in Pers. i 128, lusco qui possit dicere "lusce," as that Satire of Persius is (in his opinion) full of attacks on Nero and his poems. Juvenal is probably hitting at Nero's pretensions as a satirist in iv 106, improbior saturam scribente cinaedo. The originality of Nero's poetry is denied by Tacitus (A. xiv 16), and defended by Suetonius (Ner. 52) on the ground that he had seen the rough drafts and corrections in Nero's own handwriting. See Friedl., Sitteng. ii¹º 218 sq.; Ribbeck, Gesch. röm. Dichtung iii 44 sqq.
: see on Tit. 3, 2.

: Marcus Cocceius Nerva, emperor from 96 to 98 A.D. He was consul with Vespasian in 71, and with Domitian in 90. There does not seem to be any evidence in support of the charge against him mentioned here.

div.p: § 2. confugit in Capitolium: he was not with Flavius Sabinus (elder brother of Vespasian, Vesp. 1, 3) when he occupied the Capitol against the Vitellians (Vitell. 15, 3), but under cover of darkness Sabinus succeeded in bringing in Domitian along with his own children; cf. Tac. H. iii 69, Sabinus arcem Capitolii insedit Vitellianus miles socordi custodia clausos circumdedit; eoque concubia nocte suos liberos Sabinus et Domitianum fratris filium in Capitolium accivit. Martial (ix 101, 13) speaks flatteringly of Domitian as having played a leading part in the conflict: Adseruit possessa malis Palatia regnis, | prima suo gessit pro Iove bella puer; cf. Stat. Th. i 21, Defensa prius vix pubescentibus annis | bella Iovis: id. Silv. i 1, 79: Sil. Ital. Pun. iii 609, Nec te terruerint Tarpeii culminis ignes, etc.

p.note: : i.e. part of the miles urbanus (the 4 city cohorts) and the vigiles who had flocked to the house of Sabinus (who was praefectus urbis); Tac. iii 69, primores senatus plerique equestris ordinis omnisque miles urbanus et vigiles domum Flavii Sabini complevere. It was thus a medley of senators, knights, and soldiers who occupied the Capitol along with Sabinus.
: for the burning of the temple of Jupiter Opt. Max. on the Capitol see Vitell. 15, 3.

: Tac. iii 74, Domitianus prima inruptione apud aedituum occultatus. When his father Vespasian was established as emperor, Domitian pulled down the chamber of the aedituus and built a small shrine to Jupiter Conservator, with an altar on which his own adventures were represented in marble. At a later period he built a temple on the Capitol to Jupiter Custos (Dom. 5). Piso, the adopted son of Galba (Galb. 17), had previously found temporary shelter from the soldiers of Otho in the chamber of an aedituus of the temple of Vesta (Tac. i 43). The aedituus or temple-guardian" (also called aeditumus, Varr. R.R. i 2; aedituens Lucr. vi 1273; Gr. ἱεροφύλαξ) dwelt either in the temple or close to it. Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 214 sqq., divides aeditui into aeditui magistri who had charge of the buildings, treasures, records, etc., and aeditui ministri who kept the temple clean, showed visitors round, etc.

: at the ingenious suggestion of a freedman, according to Tac. iii 74: sollertia liberti lineo amictu turbae sacricolarum inmixtus ignoratusque. A similar disguise was used by the proscribed aedile Volusius in 43 B.C.; cf. App. Bell. Civ. iv 47, Οὐολούσιος δὲ ἀγορανομῶν προεγράφη, καὶ φίλον ὀργιαστὴν τῆς Ἴσιδος ἔχων ᾔτησε τὴν στολήν, καὶ τὰς ὀθόνας ἐνέδυ τὰς ποδήρεις καὶ τὴν τοῦ κυνὸς κεφαλὴν ἐπέθετο καὶ διῆλθεν οὕτως ὀργιάζων αὐτῷ σχήματι ἐς Πομπήιον: Val. Max. vii 3, 8. The Isiaci, priests and worshippers of Isis, wore linen garments (ὀθόναι); cf. Oth. 12, 1, traditur (Otho) sacra Isidis saepe in lintea religiosaque veste propalam celebrasse. The epithet liniger is often applied to the goddess and her devotees (Ov. Am. ii 2, 25; Met. i 747, etc.: Juv. vi 533: Mart. xii 29, 19). The Isiac worship was introduced at Rome about the time of Sulla, and survived repeated attempts of the government to suppress it. Augustus would only tolerate it outside the city walls. In 19 A.D. Tiberius, in consequence of a flagrant scandal, ordered the priests of Isis to be crucified and her image to be thrown into the Tiber. Now, in 69 A.D., we find an Iseum or temple of Isis on the Capitol, though in 58 B.C. and three times shortly afterwards her temple there was wrecked by the consuls. The first state temple to Isis was built in the Campus Martius; the date is uncertain, but it is first mentioned in connexion with the triumph of Vespasian and Titus in 71 A.D. See Wissowa, Religion der Römer2 351 sqq.

: Tacitus calls them sacricolae. The word sacrificulus: "sacrificer'" (only here in Suet.) may be used in the same contemptuous sense as it bears at times in Livy where it is joined with vates in describing the false priests and soothsayers who brought in foreign superstitious rites at Rome (especially in periods of national danger), in opposition to the regular priests and augurs of the Roman state religion; see Weissenborn. on Liv. xxv 1, 8, sacrificuli ac vates ceperant hominum mentes: xxxix 16, 8, quotiens hoc patrum avorumque aetate negotium est magistratibus datum, uti sacra externa fieri vetarent, sacrificulos vatesque foro circo urbe prohiberent.

: vanae, the reading of some of the later MSS., is generally adopted in the old editions; also by Roth and Preud'homme, but not by Ihm. variae may mean "shifting" "fickle," or "complex” "many-sided" as Turnebus explained it: "varia esse potuit illa religio, variusque cultus et caerimonia, variique cultores, unde et facilior Domitiano latebra." See also Alexander (op. cit., 21 sqq.). Iac. Gronovius ingeniously suggested Phariae (i.e. Egyptian), but all the examples quoted of the use of that epithet are from poetry.
: Tacitus differs in saying (iii 74) that it was close to the Velabrum (on the near side of the river) that he found refuge in the house of Cornelius Primus, a client of his father.
: his cousin Sabinus, son of Flavius Sabinus (Dio lxiv 17). For the sociative abl. without the normal cum (Kühner-Stegmann, i 407) cf. Aug. 8, paucissimis comitibus subsecutus.

div.p: § 3. Caesar consalutatus: Tac. iii 86, Domitianum, postquam nihil hostile metuebatur, ad duces partium progressum et Caesarem consalutatum miles frequens, utque erat in armis, in paternos penates deduxit: Dio lxvi 1, Καίσαρες ὅ τε Τίτος καὶ ὁ Δομιτιανὸς ἐπεδείχθησαν. Claudius was the first to assume the cognomen “Caesar" as an imperial title (see on Galb. 1), and this was continued by each successive dynasty, Vitellius alone refusing to be thus styled (Vitell. 8, 2). The title “Caesar'" was borne not merely by the founders of these dynasties, but also by their agnate descendants, and was distinctively used of the sons and grandsons of the reigning emperor. When Hadrian made his adoptive son Verus assume the name of Caesar, he gave to "Caesar" the limited meaning of the prospective "Augustus" or emperor, and “Caesar" continued to be used as the title of the designated successor to the throne. See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 770 sq.

p.note: : Tac. iv 3, ipsi (Vespasiano) consulatus cum Tito filio, praetura Domitiano et consulare imperium decernuntur. Domitian succeeded Frontinus as praetor: iv 39, et mox eiurante ("resigning") Frontino Domitianus praeturam cepit. He was given the consulare imperium (Suetonius loosely says cons. potestas) in the absence from Rome of the two consuls, his father in Egypt and his brother in Palestine. It was quite unprecedented for a praetor urbanus to receive the consulare imperium; see Mommsen, ii³ 650, on the combination of the consulare imperium with the praetorship and propraetorship.

: “in name only," discharging none of the judicial duties appertaining to the office; cf. Dom. 13, 3, consulatus .. paene titulo tenus gessit: Iul. 76, 2, tertium et quartum consulatum titulo tenus gessit contentus dictaturae potestate: Claud. 25, 1, instituit imaginariae militiae genus quo absentes et titulo tenus fungerentur. Similar phrases are verbo tenus (Cic. Liv. Tac.), nomine tenus (Tac.), ore tenus (e.g. Tac. A. xv 45, Graeca doctrina ore tenus exercitus).

: presumably the praetor peregrinus, who ranked next to the praetor urbanus in the exercise of urbana iurisdictio. The name of the praetor peregrinus in 70 A.D. is unknown. Baumg.-Crusius and Bremi say that it was Mucianus, but he was consul suffectus (for the second time) in that year.

: cf. Tac. H. iv 2, nomen sedemque (i.e. the palace) Caesaris Domitianus acceperat, nondum ad curas intentus, sed stupris et adulteriis filium principis agebat (i.e. played the part of emperor's son): Tac. Agr. 7, iuvene admodum (18 yrs. old) Domitiano et ex paterna fortuna tantum licentiam usurpante.

: cf. Calig. 37, 3, ne singula enumerem: Claud. 29, 1, ne singillatim minora quoque enumerem: Galb. 3, 1, elogia universi generis exequi longum est: Liv. xxvii 27, multos circa unam rem ambitus fecerim, si . omnia exequi velim.

: contrectare, to stroke or caress, was used in the further sense of violare (Plaut., Tac., etc.; contrectatio, Cic.); so adtrectare, e.g. Ner. 26, 2, a quodam laticlavio, cuius uxorem adtrectaverat, prope ad necem caesus. Here M has contract- (so Ihm and Preud 'homme), but contrect- in Calig. 42; Claud. 35, 2; Ner. 34, 4.

: daughter of Domitius Corbulo, the famous general of Claudius and Nero. On the arrival of Vespasian from Egypt, Domitian kept her among his mistresses on his estate near the Alban Mount and afterwards married her; cf. Dio lxvi 3, ὁ δὲ Δομιτιανὸς ... τῷ ἔρωτι τῆς Δομιτίας τῆς Κορβούλωνος θυγατρὸς προσέχων ἐτύγχανε· ταύτην γὰρ Λουκίου Λαμίου Αἰλιανοῦ (Αἰμιλιανοῦ codd.) τοῦ ταύτης ἀνδρὸς ἀποσπάσας τότε μὲν ἐν ταῖς ἐρωμέναις ἐποιήσατο, ὕστερον δὲ καὶ ἔγημεν. Her subsequent history is narrated in Dom. 3, 1. See also Tit. 10, 2.

: his full name was L. Aelius Plautius Lamia Aelianus (C.I.L. vi 2059; iii p. 854). In 80 A.D., under Titus, he was consul suffectus. He was put to death by Domitian for a jesting reference to the emperor's abduction of his wife; see c. 10, 2. The Lamiae were the oldest and most illustrious family of the gens Aelia; cf. Hor. C. iii 17, Aeli vetusto nobilis ab Lamo, etc.; Juv. iv 154, Sed periit (Domitianus) postquam cerdonibus esse timendus | coeperat .. Hoc nocuit Lamiarum caede madenti; vi 385, quaedam de numero Lamiarum ac nominis Appi.

: Dio lxvi 2, πολλοῖς ἀρχάς (governorships) τε καὶ ἐπιτροπείας (procuratorships) αὐτὸς (i.e. Mucianus) καὶ ὁ Δομιτιανὸς ἔδοσαν, καὶ ἐπάρχους (prefects) ἄλλους ἐπ᾿ ἄλλοις καὶ ὑπάτους (consuls) ἀπέδειξαν. Tacitus (H. iv 39) describes the reckless conduct of Domitian at Rome before the arrival of Vespasian: vis penes Mucianum erat; nisi quod pleraque Domitianus, instigantibus amicis aut propria libidine (“caprice'”), audebat.

: Dio (l.c.) says that Vespasian wrote to thank Domitian for not having dismissed him: πάντα αὐτοὶ (i.e. Mucianus and Dom.) ὡς αὐταρχοῦντες ἐποίουν, ὥστε τὸν Οὐεσπασιανὸν ἐπιστεῖλαί ποτε τῷ Δομιτιανῷ ὅτι “ χάριν ἔχω σοι, τέκνον, ὅτι με ἐᾷς ἄρχειν καὶ οὐδέπω με καταλέλυκας.” Reports had reached Vespasian in Egypt of Domitian's presumptuous behaviour: Tac. iv 51, Vespasianus in Italiam resque urbis intentus adversam de Domitiano famam accipit, tamquam terminos aetatis et concessa filio egrederetur. •

: in 69 A.D. the Batavian auxiliaries of the Rhine legions under Civilis had revolted, and on the death of Vitellius, Classicus, prefect of an ala of the Treveri, in concert with Civilis, proclaimed an independent "Imperium Galliarum," to which the Roman legions in Germany swore allegiance. The government of Vespasian sent 7 legions under Cerealis against Classicus and Civilis, and shortly after, when exaggerated reports of the rebels' successes reached Rome, Mucianus and Domitian set out for the war: simul Domitianus Mucianusque accingebantur, dispari animo, ille spe ac iuventa properus, hic moras nectens queis flagrantem (Domitianum) retineret, ne ferocia aetatis et pravis inpulsoribus, si exercitum invasisset, paci belloque male consuleret (Tac. Η. iv 68). When near the Alps, they heard of the defeat of the Treveri by Cerealis, and Mucianus seized the opportunity to advise Domitian that the subjugation of an already defeated foe was a task unworthy of him, and that he should merely display from Lugdunum (Lyons) the might and prestige of imperial power (ib. 85). Domitian saw through the artifice (ib. 86), but apparently went no farther than Lugdunum. Josephus, the panegyrist of the Flavian emperors, attributes the surrender of the Treveri and Batavi to the news of Domitian's approach (Bell. Iud. vii 85 sqq.); cf. Mart. ii 2, 4: vii 7, 3: Sil. Ital. iii '607, At tu transcendes, Germanice, facta tuorum, | iam puer auricomo praeformidate Batavo. Germanias: Germania Superior and Germania Inferior; see on Vitell. 7, 1. ..

: Tacitus (H. iv 86) says that Domitian, when at Lugdunum, secretly sent envoys to Cerealis asking him if he would hand over the army and the command to him if he came to the Rhine. Cerealis eluded the "boyish" request by judicious temporizing, and it was left uncertain whether Domitian's idea was to wage war against his father or to provide himself with resources against his brother: qua cogitatione bellum adversus patrem agitaverit an opes viresque adversus fratrem, in incerto fuit; nam Cerealis salubri temperamento elusit ut vana pueriliter cupientem. The ambitious nature of the youthful Domitian is mentioned in Dio lxvi 3, οὐδὲν γὰρ μικρὸν ἐπενόει.
: born in 51, he was 18 years old at this time.

: that he might be under his father's supervision Dio and be made to realize that he was subject to the patria potestas. (lxvi 9, quoted on c. 3, 1) says that for some time before Vespasian 's return Domitian had been living at his Alban villa, and that a guilty conscience made him so apprehensive of his father's arrival that he even simulated madness, to create an impression that he was not responsible for his conduct. Vespasian, when emperor, dwelt mainly in the Horti Sallustiani (between the Quirinal and Pincian hills) and seldom lived in the Palace (Dio lxvi 10). sellam: i.e. a sella gestatoria or sedan-chair, the occupants of which sat upright, as opposed to the lectica or litter in which they were borne reclining or half-reclining. Dio, lx 2, says that Claudius was the first emperor to use the sella gestatoria, and that after him emperors and ex-consuls continued to use it down to Dio's day (flor. 180 A.D.); whereas Augustus and Tiberius had been carried in lecticae, such as were used by women (and children). See also on Oth. 6, 3, muliebri sella.
: see on Galb. 10, 2.
: for this joint triumph of Vespasian and Titus see Vesp. 8, 1; Tit. 6, 1.

: cf. Zonar. xi 17, τῶν δ' Ἱεροσολύμων ἁλόντων ὁ Τίτος εἰς τὴν Ἰταλίαν ἐπανελθὼν τὰ ἐπινίκια αὐτός τε καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἐφ᾽ ἅρματος ἔπεμψαν, συνέπεμψε δέ σφισιν αὐτὰ καὶ ὁ Δομετιανὸς ὑπατεύων (consul) ἐπὶ κέλητος : Joseph. Bell. Iud. vii 152, μεθ' & Οὐεσπασιανὸς ἤλαυνε πρῶτος, καὶ Τίτος εἵπετο, Δομετιανὸς δὲ παρίππευεν, αὐτός τε διαπρεπῶς κεκοσμημένος καὶ τὸν ἵππον παρέχων θέας ἄξιον. At the triumph of Augustus in 29 B.c. for his victory at Actium, Tiberius (aged 13) rode on the left trace-horse of the emperor's chariot, while Octavia's son Marcellus (aged 14) rode the one on the right (Suet. Tib. 6). The white horse of Domitian was in keeping with the white horses which drew Vespasian and Titus. White chariot-horses, recalling the white steeds of Jupiter and the Sun (Liv. v 23), were used by Camillus in his triumph in 396 B.C.; later by Julius Caesar (Dio xliii 14) and by the emperors (Suet. Ner. 25, Plin. Pan. 22, etc.).

: this is Ihm's certain correction for quis ex or qui sex or in sex of the MSS. Burman had already conjectured quin ex sex, and Bentley suggested quin ex consulatibus or eque sex or quinis ex; but quin et is the regular combination in Suet., e.g. Tit. 8, 1; 8,2; Vesp. 12; Oth. 12, 1. That ex and not in is the prep. required is shown by Dom. 13, 3, ex quibus (consulatibus) septem medios continuavit; Claud. 14, ex quibus (consulatibus) duos primos iunctim gessit; Calig. 17, 1, ex omnibus (consulatibus) duos novissimos coniunxit. The six consulships referred to are those which Domitian held before Vespasian's death; he was altogether 17 times consul, see c. 13, 3.

: he was consul ordinarius in 73 A.D., his colleague being M. Valerius Messalinus; he was consul suffectus in 71, 75, 76, 77, 79. The consuls elected at the beginning of the year gave their names to the year and were known as ordinarii; those appointed later in the year were called suffecti, but their names too were recorded in the Fasti. From the time of Augustus the consuls elected on Jan. 1 did not usually hold office throughout the year, but resigned after some months and were succeeded by suffecti (Dio xlviii 35). In the second half of Augustus' reign 6 months was the usual tenure; so too under Nero (Suet. Ner. 15, consulatum in senos plerumque menses dedit); but the tenure mainly depended on the caprice of the emperor, as in the case of Tiberius. In the year of confusion 69 A.D. there were 15 consuls. From the time of Vespasian 4 months or 2 months became the normal tenure. When the emperors themselves assumed the consulship, they generally held it for an even shorter period than private persons, sometimes for a few months, sometimes only for a few days (Dom. 13, 3). See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 82 sqq.

: Titus was colleague of the emperor Vespasian in seven consulships 70, 72, 74-77, 79 A.D. Before the consular election in 73 he withdrew in favour of Domitian, and presumably it was in consequence of his action that Vespasian also decided not to hold the office in that year (for a list of Vespasian's consulships see on Vesp. 8, 1). By his withdrawal Titus gave another example of the brotherly affection (pietas) which he always showed towards Domitian in spite of his hostile attitude (see on Tit. 9, 3). Domitian held his first consulship in 71, when he was consul suffectus from March 1 to June 30, the ordinarii for the year being Vespasian and M. Cocceius Nerva. In the same year he appears on coins as consul designatus iterum, i.e. designated again as consul suffectus for 72, Vespasian and Titus being designated as ordinarii. Apparently at the spring comitia in 72 Titus allowed Domitian to be designated in his place as consul ordinarius for 73, and Domitian, waiving his claim to be consul suffectus in 72, continued to be consul designatus throughout that year, and then became consul ordinarius on Jan. 1, 73. See Gsell, Essai sur le régne de l'empereur Domitien p. 19; Weynand, in Pauly-Wissowa vi 2548.

div.p: § 2. simulavit et ipse modestiam: not only did his father humble him (Dio lxvi 10, ὁ Οὐεσπασιανὸς ἐκείνου ἐταπείνου τὸ φρόνημα), but he himself affected a retiring modesty; cf. Tac. H. iv 86, Domitianus sperni a senioribus iuventam suam cernens, modica quoque et usurpata antea munia imperii omittebat, simplicitatis ac modestiae imagine in altitudinem conditus ("wrapping himself in a profound reserve," C. and B.) studiumque litterarum et amorem carminum simulans, quo velaret animum et fratris aemulationi subduceretur, cuius disparem mitioremque naturam contra interpretabatur.

p.note: : Domitian seems to have essayed epic poetry, his themes being (a) the fight for the Capitol between the Flavians and Vitellians in Dec. 69; cf. Mart. v 5, 7, ad Capitolini caelestia carmina 2L belli | grande cothurnati pone Maronis opus: (b) the Jewish War; cf. Val. Flacc. i 7 (addressing Vespasian), versam proles tua pandet Idumen | (namque potest), Solymo nigrantem pulvere fratrem. The astronomical Aratea sometimes attributed to him is by Germanicus, son of Drusus. Quintilian (x 1, 91) speaks in extravagantly fulsome terms of Domitian 's poetic gifts: Hos nominavimus (as epic poets) quia Germanicum Aug. (i.e. Domitian) ab institutis studiis deflexit cura terrarum, parumque diis visum est esse eum maximum poetarum. Quid tamen his ipsis eius operibus in quae donato imperio iuvenis secesserat sublimius, doctius, omnibus denique numeris praestantius? Quis enim caneret bella melius quam qui sic gerit? Quem praesidentes studiis deae propius audirent? etc. So too Pliny (N.H. praef. 5) praises Titus as a poet who could emulate his brother: Quantus in poetica es! O magna fecunditas animi! quemadmodum fratrem quoque imiteris excogitasti. Silius Italicus (iii 619) says of Domitian: Quin et Romuleos superabit voce nepotes | quis erit eloquio partum decus: huic sua Musae | sacra ferent, etc.

: see c. 20. recitavit publice: a practice indulged in even by emperors. Claudius gave constant recitals of his prose works through a professional reader (Claud. 41, assidue recitavit per lectorem). Nero recited his poems himself, not only at home but in the theatre; this caused such delight that a festival of thanksgiving was voted and the poems, inscribed in letters of gold, were dedicated to Jupiter Capitolinus (Ner. 10). On the subject of recitationes, which were such a feature (and such an infliction) of social life under the Empire, see Friedl. Sitteng. ii¹º 225 sqq.
: see on Tit. 5, 3.
: see on Vesp. 6, 4.

: a great nomad race, divided into various branches, dwelling in the steppes north of the Caspian and from the Tanais (Don) to the Caucasus. Pompey in the war against Mithridates came in contact with the "duros aeterni Martis Alanos” (Luc. viii 223; cf. Amm. Marc. xxiii 5). Nero shortly before his death was preparing an expedition against them (Тас. Н. і 6). Their devastating incursion into Media and Armenia in the time of Vespasian is described in Joseph. Bell. Iud. vii 244 sqq. Vespasian took measures to guard the Caucasus passes against them, and a Roman garrison was stationed beyond the Armenian frontier in the Iberian fortress Harmozika near Tiflis (see Mommsen, Prov. Rom. Emp. ii 64). Later, under Hadrian, the Alani renewed their inroads (Dio lxix 15), and it was then that the historian Arrian, prefect of Cappadocia, wrote his "Εκταξις κατ' 'Αλανῶν on the tactics to be used against them.

: discutere (lit. 'to pull to pieces'") was used in the sense of irritum facere "to bring to nought," "to render null and void"; cf. Cic. Q. Fr. ii 10 (12), de Commageno, quod rem totam discusseram, mirifice mihi blanditur Appius: Liv. xxxiv 56, eam rem litterae Ti. Sempronii discusserunt: xxxix 10, obsecrare ut eam rem quocumque modo discuteret. Dio, lxvi 15, says that Vespasian declined to meddle in a conflict between the Parthians and Alans which did not concern him: τοῖς δὲ Πάρθοις πολεμωθεῖσι πρός τινας, καὶ τῆς παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ συμμαχίας δεηθεῖσιν οὐκ ἐβοήθησεν, εἰπὼν ὅτι οὐ προσήκει αὐτῷ τὰ ἀλλότρια πολυπράγμονεῖν. Imhof (T. Flav. Domitianus, p. 33) thinks that a more genuine reason for Vespasian 's refusal was his unwillingness to send Domitian at the head of an army to the East. Vologaesus had cause to feel hurt by Vespasian's refusal, for he had laid Vesp. under an obligation by his offer to provide him with 40,000 Parthian bowmen to aid him against Vitellius (Vesp. 6, 4).

: Tiridates, king of Armenia, and Pacorus, king of Media, whose kingdoms had been overrun and ravaged by the Alani, were both brothers of Vologaesus. The solicitations of Domitian would be addressed principally to the king of Armenia, as his was a vassal kingdom in alliance with Rome.

div.p: § 3. patre defuncto: Vespasian died on June 23, 79 A.D. (Vesp. 24).

p.note: : for the indirect question with cunctari cf. c. 17, 1, cunctantibus conspiratis, quando et quomodo aggrederentur: Claud. 21, 6, diu cunctatus an omnes igni ferroque absumeret: Plin. Ep. vi 16, 11, cunctatus paulum an retro flecteret: Stat. Th. xi 595, cunctatur nescia virgo, | quid paret. First in Sall. Cat. 52, de parricidis quid statuatis, cunctamini?

: i.e. double the largess which his brother Titus offered them to ensure their support. The elevation to power of a new emperor was preceded or followed by a donativum to the soldiers. Augustus left by will a donativum of 1000 sesterces for each praetorian, 500 for each soldier of the urban cohorts, and 300 for each legionary; the total amount thus distributed by his heir and successor Tiberius being nearly 72,000,000 sesterces. Tiberius, in turn, bequeathed a donativum of the same amount, which Caligula on his accession doubled. Claudius on receiving the imperium bought the loyalty of the praetorians by a largess of 15,000 sesterces to each, and gave the same sum each year on the anniversary of his accession. Nero paid the same price. Galba estranged the army by refusing a “donativum grandius solito" which had been promised (see Galb. 16, 1). Vitellius, lacking money, gave the soldiers every licence in lieu thereof (Tac. H. ii 94). Vespasian paid each man merely 100 sesterces, and was none the less well served (Dio lxv 22, Tac. H. ii 82). The amounts paid by Titus and Domitian are not specified. Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus, and M. Aurelius paid 20,000 sesterces. See Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 140; Daremberg-Saglio, ii 385.

: Domitian's expectation that he would be left particeps imperii with Titus was not fulfilled, but Titus from the very beginning of his reign was ready to proclaim him as his consors and successor (Tit. 9, 3, where see note). Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vi 32) says that Domitian poisoned Titus, not because he objected to sharing the throne with his brother, but to sharing it with one who was both gentle and good: οὐ τὸ ξὺν ἀδελφῷ ἄρχειν δεινὸν ἡγούμενος, ἀλλὰ τὸ ξὺν πράῳ τε καὶ χρηστῷ.
: the allegation being that this was done by Titus, who possessed the qualifications of a master forger, if he chose to use them; see Tit. 3, 2.

: cf. Tit. 9, 3, fratrem insidiari sibi non desinentem, sed paene ex professo sollicitantem exercitus, etc.: Dio lxvi 26, (ὁ Τίτος) μετήλλαξεν (obiit) .. ὡς μὲν ἡ φήμη λέγει πρὸς τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ ἀναλωθείς, ὅτι καὶ πρότερον ἐπεβεβούλευτο ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ. 2L2

: for the conflicting accounts of the death of Titus and the charges made against Domitian, either of poisoning him or of accelerating his death when he was ill, see on Tit. 11. Dio (l.c.) says that while Titus was still breathing, Domitian rode post-haste to Rome, entered the praetorian camp, received the title and authority of emperor, and gave the soldiers the same donativum as Titus had done. For pro see on Vitell. 3, 2, pro afflicto lamentata est.

: cf. Dio lxvii 2, αὐτός τε γὰρ καὶ φιλεῖν τὸν ἀδελφὸν καὶ πενθεῖν προσεποιεῖτο, καὶ τούς τε ἐπαίνους τοὺς ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ μετὰ δακρύων ἔλεξε, καὶ ἐς τοὺς ἥρωας αὐτὸν σπουδῇ ἐσέγραψε, πάντα τὰ ἐναντιώτατα ὧν ἠβούλετο σκηπτόμενος: Eutrop. vii 22, (Titus) inter divos relatus est. Pliny, Paneg. 11 (quoted on Vesp. 23 ad fin.), asserts that Titus deified Vespasian, and Domitian deified Titus, merely in order that they might be thought, the one a son, the other a brother of a god. Domitian built in the Campus Martius an elaborate Porticus Divorum containing two aedes for the worship of the deified Vespasian and Titus, hoping doubtless that there would be a third aedes in his own honour when he was consecrated (Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom i 3, 565). Domitian, however, was not deified.

: these orationes were those known as orationes principis ad senatum. The proposals (relationes) which the emperor brought before the senate, though in form they kept up the fiction that the emperor himself was speaking, were usually read to the senate by one of the quaestores Caesaris (see on Tit. 6, 1). For the use of obliquus "indirect" cf. Tac. A. xiv 11, temporum Claudianorum obliqua insectatione: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, causidicorum obliqua dicta (= 'figurae,” Vesp. 13): Amm. Marc. xv 5, 4, Silvano rogante obliquis verbis; so too the adv., e.g. Tac. A. v 2, consulem oblique perstringens.
: addressed to the people; see on Tit. 8, 1. An example of an edict of Domitian which reflected on Titus was that in which he forbade the making of eunuchs; see on Dom. 7, 1.
: cf. Ner. 22, 1, inter initia imperii; so inter initia without gen., e.g. Dom. 9, 1, inter initia ab omni caede abhorrebat. This use of inter initia for initio is post-Aug. (Kühner-Stegmann, i 551).

: it is very doubtful whether horarum for aliquot horarum is defensible. horarium is the reading in the Ed. Rom. ii (1470) and the Ed. Venet. (1471). The adj. horarius (= unius horae), with which Wolf compares momentarius and temporarius, does not occur in any other author, and is not given in any of the MSS.; a subst. horarium (= horologium, an instrument for measuring time) is found in Censorinus. Most probably some numeral has fallen out before horarum (or after it, according to Casaubon, who proposed horarum iii). Voss conjectured lararium, which is very improbable. The same difficulty arises in Ner. 37, 2, mori iussis non amplius quam horarum spatium dabat, where G has iii horarum, and some of the late MSS. duarum horarum; Beroaldus read horarium. For secretum see on Oth. 3, 1; cf. Tac. Agr. 39, (Domitianus) secreto suo satiatus, "after taking his fill of his usual seclusion" (Furneaux-Anderson). The inaccessible solitude in which Domitian spent so much time brooding during the years of his despotic cruelty at Rome is mentioned in Plin. Pan. 48, non adire quisquam, non alloqui, audebat, tenebras semper secretumque captantem; nec unquam ex solitudine sua prodeuntem, nisi ut solitudinem faceret.
: see on c. 21, nihil aliud quam deambulabat.

: Dio (lxvi 9) says that Domitian did this in his Alban villa at the time when he was pretending to be half-witted, through fear of Vespasian's wrath on his return to Italy, and that he kept up the practice when he became emperor: ὑπὸ γὰρ τοῦ συνειδότος ὧν TE ἐφρόνει καὶ ὧν ἐπεποιήκει οὔτε ἐθάρσει, καὶ προσέτι καὶ μωρίαν ἔστιν ὅτε προσεποιεῖτο. ἐν γοῦν τῷ ᾿Αλβανῷ χωρίῳ τὰ πλεῖστα διάγων ἄλλα τε πολλὰ καὶ γελοῖα ἔπραττε, καὶ τὰς μυίας γραφείοις κατεκέντει. τοῦτο γὰρ εἰ καὶ ἀνάξιον τοῦ τῆς ἱστορίας ὄγκου ἐστίν, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι γε ἱκανῶς τὸν τρόπον αὐτοῦ ἐνδείκνυται, ἀναγκαίως ἔγραψα· καὶ μάλισθ' ὅτι καὶ μοναρχήσας ὁμοίως αὐτὸ ἐποίει, Aurelius Victor (Caes. 11, 5) assigns it to the period of Domitian's reign when he was enervated by his excesses: dehinc atrox caedibus bonorum segnisque, ridicule, remotis procul omnibus, muscarum agmina persequebatur, postquam ad libidinem minus virium erat.

: the stilus (γραφίς, γραφεῖον, graphium), which was used for writing on wax-covered tablets, was made of bone, ivory, or metal and was sharpened to a very fine point, the upper end being generally circular and flat for the purpose of smoothing the wax and deleting what had been written. It could be used as a weapon; e.g. Julius Caesar, when he was attacked by the conspirators, stabbed Casca through the arm with a graphium or stilus (Suet. Iul. 82). Vibio Crispo Q. Vibius Crispus was consul (suffectus) under Nero, and a second and third time under Vespasian or Domitian; proconsul of Africa under Vespasian. As a pleader he accumulated a vast fortune (300,000,000 sesterces, according to Tac. Dial. 8; cf. Mart. iv 54, 7, divitior Crispo). Tacitus (H. ii 10) describes him as “pecunia potentia ingenio. inter claros magis quam inter bonos.” His eloquence is praised by Quintilian, x 1, 119, Vibius Crispus compositus (“finished'') et iucundus et delectationi natus. He was one of Vespasian's chief friends; cf. Tac. Dial. 8, (Marcellus Eprius et Crispus Vibius) per multos iam annos potentissimi sunt civitatis ac, donec libuit, principes fori, nunc principes in Caesaris (i.e. Vespasian) amicitia agunt feruntque cuncta. Juvenal (iv 81 sqq.) mentions him as a councillor of Domitian and says that he owed his long life of 80 years to his unfailing astuteness in swimming with the stream (numquam direxit bracchia contra | torrentem). One of his best known mots was on the banquets of Vitellius (see note on Vitell. 13, 1). Quintilian (v 13, 48: viii 5, 15) gives other examples of his wit.

: Dio lxvi 9, ὅθεν οὐκ ἀχαρίτως τις εἶπε πρὸς τὸν ἐρωτῶντα “ τί πράττει Δομιτιανός;” ὅτι “ ἰδιάζει τε, καὶ οὐδὲ μυῖα αὐτῷ παρακάθηται.” So in [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, 8, Hinc percontanti cuidam, quisquamne in palatio esset, responsum “Ne musca quidem"; in Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, 5 the reply is given as "Ne musca quidem, nisi forte apud palaestram.” A proverbial method of describing a deserted place was to say that not even a fly was there; cf. Plaut. Truc. 281, Quas tu mulieres | mihi narras? ubi musca nulla femina est in aedibus (i.e. not even a female fly). Otto, Sprichw. p. 235.
: in 73 A.D.; see on c. 2, 1.

: filium sustulerat, susceperat; see on Vesp. 3. The name of the boy is unknown; for the view that it was "Vespasianus" see on "Vespasianum," Dom. 15, 1. He probably died in the first few years of his father's reign. From the fact that on the coins where the boy appears as "Divus Caesar” Domitian does not bear the title "Germanicus," which he assumed in 83 after his victory over the Chatti (c. 6, 1), it has been inferred that the son died before that year (Gsell, op. cit. 53, n. 4; Stein, in Pauly-Wissowa v 1514). His deification is referred to in Stat. S. i 1, 97: Sil. Ital. iii 629. Martial (iv 3), describing Domitian sitting through a fall of snow at the games in 88, represents the snow-shower as a prank of the deified boy: Quis siccis (“frozen”) lascivit aquis et ab aethere ludit? Suspicor has pueri Caesaris esse nives. For the coins of his mother Domitia on which the youthful “Divus Caesar" figures see Eckhel, vi 401: Cohen, i² 535.

: a reading suggested by Madvig (Adv. Crit. ii 581), which I have adopted faute de mieux, though there is no evidence that Domitian had any children except the one son. Roth had already conjectured consalutavit, concluding that this is given in a dismembered form in M, where the reading is alteroque anno consulatu filium *** vit Augustam (some letters being erased before vit, while a later hand has written on the margin deest aliquid). The other MSS. have either consulatus (-tu in R) filium et Augustam (Gr) or consalutaverat ut Augustam (X). The latter is the vulgate before Roth's ed.; but Domitian cannot have saluted Domitia as "Augusta" in 74, seven years before he was emperor. This chronological difficulty may be removed by reading ex qua in septimo (for secundo, i.e. IN VII for IN II) suo consulatu filium tulerat, alteroque anno consalutaverat Augustam. Suetonius would thus put the son's birth in 80; and say correctly that Domitian saluted Domitia as "Augusta" in 81 when he became emperor. For the omission of the relative pronoun (quam) in the second clause see the examples in Kühner-Stegmann, ii p. 324. In the texts of Roth and Preud'homme a lacuna is marked between tulerat and alteroque anno consalutavit Augustam; in that of Ihm between anno and consalutavit Augustam. Numerous corrections have been proposed; e.g. alteroque anno a consulatu filiam, Augustam eandem ... repudiavit (Lipsius): in octavo suo consulatu... alteroque anno ab hoc consulatu filiam, Augustam eandem repudiavit (Graevius): alteroque anno suo consalutaverat Augustam, etc. (Ernesti, who deletes suo after secundo and explains anno suo as "year of his reign''): filiam tulerat alteroque anno filium, ac consalutaverat Augustam (Oudendorp): alterumque imperii altero anno, consalutavit Augustam (Mommsen): alteroque anno principatus [or quam imperium adeptus est] amisit (Ihm): filiam tulerat alteroque anno principatus filium, eodem illo anno consalutavit Augustam (Alexander). ..

: this compound, which generally denotes the mutual greetings of a number of friends or the acclamations of a multitude (e.g. Dom. 1, 3: Tit, 5, 2), is rarely used of individuals; cf. Tac. H. i 57, is .. imperatorem Vitellium consalutavit: Petron. Satyr. 7, 131: Apul. Met. viii 31.

: Domitia must have received this title about the time of Domitian's accession (Sept. 13, 81), for she is so styled in the Acta Arvalia of Oct. 1, 81 (C.I.L. vi 2060, Henzen p. cxi); cf. Euseb.-Hieron. Chron. p. 160 Schoene, under the year 2097 (Oct. 1, 80-Sept. 30, 81): Domitiani uxor Augusta appellata. The title of "Augusta" was first conferred by Augustus in his will on his wife Livia (Tac. A. i 8). Caligula offered it to his grandmother Antonia, wife of Drusus, mother of Germanicus and Claudius (Calig. 15); she refused it during her lifetime, and Claudius conferred it on her after her death (Claud. 11). Agrippina, wife of Claudius and mother of Nero, was styled "Augusta" (Tac. A. xii 26), as were Poppaea, wife of Nero, and her daughter Claudia (A. xv 23). Vitellius honoured his mother with the title (id. H. ii 89). Julia, daughter of Titus, appears as "Augusta" on the coins of her father (see on Tit. 4, 2). For the various inscriptions and coins where Domitia bears this title see Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii 26. From Domitian's time the wife of the emperor is regularly called "Augusta." Cf. Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 821.

: a famous pantomimus, born in Egypt, who was the darling of the licentious Roman matrons, and was so influential at the court of Domitian that appointment to posts of state depended on his patronage. The alleged banishment of Juvenal to Egypt is said (Schol. Juv. i 1, vii 92) to have been due to his attack on Paris in Sat. vii 86 sqq. (cf. vi 82 sqq.). Dio (lxvii 3) states that Domitian caused Paris to be murdered in the public street for intriguing with Domitia, and also put to death some of his admirers who scattered flowers and perfumes on the spot where he fell. Suetonius (c. 10 infr.) says that Dom. put to death a pupil of Paris, who resembled his master in form and skill. Martial (xi 13) has a well-known epitaph on Paris: Urbis deliciae salesque Nili, | ars et gratia, lusus et voluptas, | Romani decus et dolor theatri | atque omnes Veneres Cupidinesque | hoc sunt condita, quo Paris, sepulcro.
: see on Vesp. 22, quasi amore suo deperiret.

: according to Dio (lxvii 3), Domitian had thoughts of putting Domitia to death, but he spared her on the intercession of Ursus (i.e. Flavius Ursus, to whom Statius addresses Silv. ii 6). She was banished from court probably between the end of 82 and 84 A.D.; see Stein in Pauly-Wissowa, v 1515.

: Dio (l.c.) mentions this demand of the people as a fact: εἶτα δεηθέντος τοῦ δήμου κατηλλάγη τῇ Δομιτίᾳ. Quasi (like ut, velut, sicut, tanquam, nec aliter quam, haud secus quam, perinde atque). was used, especially in post-class. writers, with participial clauses in a subjective sense to express an ostensible reason, a pretended motive, an imaginary condition, etc. (Kühner-Stegmann, i 790 sq.).

: Domitia, though taken back by Domitian, lived in constant dread of his vengeance, and she was privy to the plot which brought about his death; see c. 14, 1. It is uncertain whether she bore any more children to him; but Martial (vi 3, in 90 A.D.) refers to the expected birth of an imperial offspring. Domitia outlived Domitian by many years, and probably died not long before 140 A.D. (Stein, l.c.).

div.p: § 2. circa administrationem: cf. Iul. 45, 2, circa corporis curam morosior: Tib. 69, circa deos ac religiones neglegentior: Ner. 51, circa cultum habitumque adeo pudendus. This use of circa in the sense of de or quod attinet ad is not found in class. Lat. (Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 253). For other meanings of circa in Suet. see on Oth. 11, 2.

p.note: : cf. Tac. H. i 10, Mucianus malis bonisque artibus mixtus: id. A. vi 51, (Tiberius) inter bona malaque mixtus incolumi matre. It is probable that quoque is a corruption due to the following quoque, and that the correct reading is mixturaque (Lipsius). Bentley suggested mixtura prope aequabili; Ernesti reads mixtura aequabili. =

: super is difficult: the context clearly requires Rolfe's rendering “contrary to" (so Stahr wider seine angeborene Natur''), but there does not seem to be any parallel to this; if, as most do, we take super praeter (cf. Oth. 5, 1), then the statement that Domitian's natural tendencies to rapacity and cruelty were increased by need and fear contradicts what Suetonius says in c. 9 about his natural mildness and freedom from avarice, his later rapacity and cruelty being described in c. 10 and c. 12. It is possible that natura should be read, and super taken in the sense of de (cf. Iul. 5: 20, 1: Tib. 13, 2), the meaning being "as far as one can guess about his natural disposition, it was need that made him rapacious and fear that made him cruel.”
: the Flavian amphitheatre (Colosseum); see Vesp. 9, 1: Tit. 7, 3.

: the Circus Maximus in the valley between the Aventine and Palatine hills. It was improved by Julius Caesar to hold 150,000 spectators. As the upper tiers of seats and the galleries were of wood, it suffered repeatedly from fires. Augustus restored it with added splendour after a destructive fire in 31 B.c. It was partly burned down in 36 A.D. and Claudius restored and enlarged it to accommodate 250,000. Nero had it rebuilt within four years after the great fire at Rome in 64 A.D. which broke out in the Circus (Tac. 4. xv 38). In Domitian's reign the Circus was once more damaged by fire (see Dom. 5).

: racing-chariots were usually bigae and quadrigae, sometimes trigae, and exceptional instances of six-horsed chariots (seiuges, seiugae) are mentioned. Connected with the chariotraces were the races between the riders of two horses, who leaped from one to the other during the race (desultores); cf. Iul. 39, 2, circensibus quadrigas bigasque et equos desultorios agitaverunt nobilissimi iuvenes: Dion. Hal. vii 73, πρῶτος ὁ τῶν τεθρίππων τε καὶ συνωρίδων καὶ τῶν ἀζεύκτων ἵππων ἐγίγνετο δρόμος. See Friedlaender in Marquardt Staatsv. iii² 524. ...

: these conflicts between divisions of troops, foot or cavalry, were a development of the armaturae or military evolutions, either on horseback (arm. equestris) or on foot (arm. pedestris), and the mock-fights carried out by the young citizens in the Circus from the days of the Republic (cf. Liv. xliv 9). Distinct from the armatura equestris was the Ludus Troiae or manoeuvres executed on horseback by the young nobles (Iul. 39, Aug. 43, Calig. 18, Claud. 21; cf. Verg. Aen. v 596 sqq.). Julius Caesar in his triumphal games included a battle between two opposing armies, with 500 foot-soldiers, 20 elephants, and 30 horsemen on each side (Iul. 39).
: see on Galb. 6, 1, commissione ludorum Floralium.
: see on Vesp. 5, 5.

: no details of this naval spectacle are given by any writer. Nero, in 57 or 58 A.D., flooded the arena of the amphitheatre which he built in the Campus Martius, and exhibited a naval battle between the Athenians and Persians, the water containing fish and sea-monsters of all kinds (Ner. 12); he gave a similar spectacle in 64 (Dio lxii 15). In 80 A.D. Titus used the flooded arena of the new Flavian amphitheatre for a battle between the Corcyraeans and Corinthians (Dio lxvi 25; see on Tit. 7, 3).
: see on Vesp. 12. A sea-fight in the amphitheatre was not the only unusual spectacle he gave, for he also gave venationes, etc., by artificial light, and held contests between women as well as men.

: spectacles in which wild animals were killed by other animals or by men. They were introduced at Rome by M. Fulvius Nobilior at his triumphal games in 186 B.C. They became more and more elaborate, and under the Empire a wonderful variety of animals was provided: lions, tigers, bears, panthers, leopards, elephants, hippopotami, rhinoceroses, crocodiles, etc. At first they formed part of the Ludi Circenses. Julius Caesar built a wooden amphitheatre for the venationes (θέατρον κυνηγετικόν, Dio xliii 22; Dio uses the same phrase for the amphitheatre of Statilius Taurus, and for that of Titus). They continued, however, to be given in the Circus as well as in the amphitheatre. The men who fought against the beasts (bestiarii) were condemned criminals or prisoners of war or hirelings who were trained in a special school for the purpose (ludus bestiariorum). See Friedl., Sitteng. ii10 77 sqq.

: cf. Cic. Quint. Fr. iii 7, 2, ad lychnuchum ligneolum scribere; so ad lumina "by torch light" (Calig. 45, 1, etc.), ad lunam (Aen. iv 513), ad lucernam (Flor. iv 2, 71). The lychnuchus (λυχνοῦχος) was a lampholder or candelabrum; for the varieties see Marquardt, Privatl.2 711. Julius Caesar at his triumph "ascendit Capitolium ad lumina, quadraginta elephantis dextra sinistraque lychnuchos gestantibus” (Iul. 37, 2). Statius (Silv. i 6, 85 sqq.) describes the illumination of the amphitheatre at one of Domitian's entertainments: Vixdum caerula nox subibat orbem, | descendit media nitens harena | densas flammeus orbis inter umbras | vincens Gnosiacae facem coronae (i.e. Ariadne's crown). | Conlucet polus ignibus nihilque | obscurae patitur licere nocti. Vollmer (ad loc.) points out that as the amphitheatre was open to the sky the lights must have been hung from a huge post in the centre of the arena. nec modo, sed et see on Tit. 8, 3.

: in Nero's reign women of high family took part in the gladiatorial combats and the venationes; cf. Tac. A. xv 32, feminarum illustrium senatorumque plures per harenam foedati: Juv. i 22, cum Mevia Tuscum | figat aprum et nuda teneat venabula mamma (where see Mayor). Titus, at the dedication of the new amphitheatre, had some of the 9000 beasts in the venatio (Tit. 7, 3) slain by women of low rank (γυναῖκες, οὐ μέντοι ἐπιφανεῖς, Dio lxvi 25). The participation by women in the contests of the arena under Domitian is also mentioned by Dio, lxvii 8, ἔστιν ὅτε καὶ νάνους (“dwarfs'") καὶ γυναῖκας συνέβαλλε (committebat); cf. Stat. S. i 6, 53, stat sexus rudis insciusque ferri | et pugnas capit improbus viriles; Mart. Spect. 6, etc. In 200 A.D. Septimius Severus forbade women to enter the arena (Dio lxxv 16).

: Claudius in 47 A.D. had imposed on the quaestors the duty of furnishing gladiatorial shows at their own expense. Suetonius (Claud. 24) says he put this burden on the "college of quaestors" in lieu of paving the streets: Collegio quaestorum pro stratura viarum gladiatorium munus iniunxit (for street-paving as a charge borne by quaestors see Hirschfeld, Kais. Verwaltungsb. p. 261). Claudius was acting on a resolution moved by a servile senator Dolabella: Tac. A. xi 22, P. Dolabella censuit spectaculum gladiatorum per omnes annos celebrandum pecunia eorum qui quaesturam adipiscerentur. The burden fell on quaestores designati as we see from Tac. A. xiii 5, where its abolition under Nero in 54 A.D. is mentioned: ne designatis quaestoribus edendi gladiatores necessitas esset. It was reimposed by Domitian, and continued to the end of the Empire. =
: iamdudum, iamdiu, πάλαι. This use of olim is peculiar to writers of the Silver age.

: Seneca (Ep. 7, 4) distinguishes ordinaria paria (par = pair of gladiators) from postulaticia paria, the latter being kept in reserve by the munerarius and only produced in response to the insistent calls of the spectators (Summers ad loc.). Such demands of the spectators are often mentioned; e.g. Claud. 21, 5, cum Palumbum (a gladiator) postulantibus daturum se promisit, etc.: Mart. Spect. 20, Cum peteret pars haec Myrinum, pars illa Triumphum, | promisit pariter Caesar utraque manu. | Non potuit melius litem finire iocosam. | O dulce invicti principis ingenium! (Friedlaender says that Myrinus and Triumphus were bestiarii, as in the case of gladiators the spectators would clamour for a special pair.)

: a ludus gladiatorius, or training-school for gladiators, belonging to the emperor Caligula is mentioned in Plin. N.H. xi 245. Later there were four imperial schools at Rome: (1) the ludus matutinus for the training of bestiarii (this probably existed in the time of Claudius); (2) the ludus magnus; (3) the ludus Gallicus; (4) the ludus Dacicus. It is generally held that the last three were established by Domitian as dependencies of the Colosseum; the Gallicus and Dacicus deriving their names from the nationality of the gladiators trained there. See Daremberg-Saglio, ii 1580. When ludus is used without specification, as here and in c. 17, it probably means the ludus magnus (Hirschfeld, op. cit. 290). Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 1071) thinks that after the building of the Colosseum private individuals were forbidden to maintain troupes of gladiators at Rome as they had been in the habit of doing. Imperial gladiatorial schools were also to be found in other parts of Italy (e.g. Capua and Praeneste) and in the provinces.

: more splendidly accoutred than the ordinary gladiators supplied by the lanista to the munerarius (see on Vitell. 12). Pertinax sold as part of the belongings of Commodus “arma gladiatoria gemmis auroque composita" and also "torques (necklets) gladiatorias” (Capitol. Pert. 8). On the rich and artistic equipment of gladiators see Friedl. Sitteng. ii10 60. The adj. aulicus (αὐλικός, = ad aulam, i.e. domum regiam, pertinens) is also used by Suet. in Ner. 45, 1, aulicis luctatoribus; Oth. 2, 2, aulicam libertinam. The word occurs only once earlier as a subst., "courtier," in Nepos Dat. 5, 2, invidiam aulicorum excepit; so in Suet. Calig. 19, 3, causam ab interioribus aulicis (“"most confidential courtiers'') proditam. For apparatus (sumptuousness, magnificence) cf. Vitell. 10, 1: Claud. 17, 2, triumphavit maximo apparatu: Cic. Tusc. v 9, maximo ludorum apparatu; Cic. Off. ii 55, ludorum venationumque apparatu pecunias profundunt.

div.p: § 2. coccinatus: this rare form (= coccino indutus) occurs in Mart. i 96, 6; ν 35, 2. Suetonius also uses the subst. coccum for scarlet (threads or strands); Ner. 30, 3, purpura coccoque funibus nexis. The dye was got from a worm, the cochineal kermes (coccus ilicis); Pliny (N.H. ix 141) wrongly describes it as a vegetable product (granum). See Marquardt, Privatl.2 506.

p.note: : "with a small and monstrously misshapen head"; or "with a prodigiously small head" (Thomson-Forester). portentosus is often used of monstrous growths, freaks of nature; e.g. Cic. Div. ii 28, 60, si quando aliqua portentosa aut ex pecude aut ex homine nata dicuntur; so too prodigiosus, e.g. Quintil. ii. 5, 11, distortis et quocunque modo prodigiosis corporibus. Dwarfs and physical monstrosities of every kind enjoyed extraordinary favour both at Court and among the wealthy classes at Rome under the Empire. Augustus was exceptional in his loathing for them; cf. Aug. 83, pumilos (‘dwarfs'') atque distortos et omnes generis eiusdem, ut ludibria naturae malique ominis abhorrebat. Mayor on Juv. viii 32 has collected a number of passages on this subject; cf. Friedl. Sitteng. ii¹º 372. Ernesti needlessly proposed to alter parvo to pravo.
: here (as in Iul. 6, 2; 52, 1: Aug. 35, 3: Tib. 4, 3) Suetonius puts cum before the relative, an order of words found at times in Cic. and constantly in Nepos and Livy (Kühner-Stegmann, i 585).

p.mentioned: auditus est dum ex eo quaerit
p.note: : a remarkable constr. instead of the normal cum ex eo quaereret. At a dinner given by Tiberius, a dwarf who was standing by among the jesters suddenly asked Tiberius why Paconius, who was charged with treason, remained so long alive; the emperor rebuked him for his pertness, but a few days later wrote to the senate to expedite the execution of Paconius (Tib. 61).
: = constitutione praesidum provinciarum (Baumg.-Cr.). See on ‘‘ordinavit,” Vesp. 23, 2.
: see on “praefectus Aegypti,” Vesp. 6, 3.

: Marcus Iunius Mettius Rufus is frequently mentioned in papyri as prefect of Egypt. These references (including Pap. Hamb. i 2 p. 125 sq., Pap. Oxyrh. i 72, 10, ii 237 col. viii 43, ii 247, Рар. Strassb. 22, 25, Pap. Amherst. 68 col. ii p. 81) are tabulated in chronological order by Janssen (ad loc.), who shows that Rufus was already prefect (ἡγεμών) in Aug. 89, and that he was still in office in 94; his successor Petronius Secundus is mentioned as prefect in March 95 (Dessau, Inscr. Lat. 8759 d.). See also Mommsen, Eph. Epigr. vii p. 427; Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii p. 374.

: Dio lxvii 8, ἐν καινῷ τινι χωρίῳ ναυμαχίαν ἐπετέλεσε. The "new place" of which Dio speaks is distinguished from the vetus naumachia of Augustus used also by Titus (see on Tit. 7, 3). The new basin which Domitian constructed was probably in the Vatican valley. The title regio Naumachiae for the quarter extending from St. Peter's to the Castle of St. Angelo (Mausoleum Hadriani) survived all through the Middle Ages; see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom i 3, 661. Domitian's basin was destroyed in a short time and the stone was used for other purposes (Dom. 5).

: "regular," "full-sized.” Suetonius is fond of the use of iustus in the sense of “qualis quis ex iure esse debet vel ex recepta consuetudine esse solet” (Baumg.-Cr.); e.g. Vesp. 3, habuit paene iustae uxoris loco: Galb. 12, 2, iustos milites fecerat: Vitell. 15, 1, iustae militiae commoda: Galb. 21, statura fuit iusta: Claud. 17, 1, iusti triumphi decus.

: Dio (l.c.) says that not only did nearly all of the combatants in the naval fight die, but also many of the spectators. When a violent storm with torrential rain came on, Domitian allowed no one to leave, and though he changed his own robe, nobody else was allowed to do so; in consequence, numbers fell sick and died. To console the populace, Domitian gave a public banquet lasting all night long.

div.p: § 3. fecit ludos Saeculares: in 88 A.D. Tacitus, who was one of the Quindecimviri sacris faciundis who had charge of the Ludi Saeculares, when mentioning (A. xi 11) the previous celebration under Claudius in 47, refrains from describing them, as he says he had already given a description of those of Domitian (in one of the books of the Historiae now lost). Other references to Domitian's celebration are in Mart. iv 1, 7, Hic (i.e. Domitian) colat ingenti redeuntia saecula lustro, | et quae Romuleus sacra Tarentos habet; x 63,3; Stat. Silv. i 4, 17; iv 1, 37 (Janus addresses Domitian), mecum altera saecula condes | et tibi longaevi revocabitur ara Tarenti. In these passages Tarentos (-um) is the name of a volcanic fissure in the Campus Martius where there was an ara Ditis patris et Proserpinae and the Ludi Saeculares were performed; hence, under the Republic, they were called the Ludi Tarentini. The festival lasted three days and three nights. The ceremonies are described in Zosimus ii 5 (quoted in full by Wickham in his Introd. to the Carmen Saeculare of Horace, an ode sung to Apollo in the celebration by Augustus in 17 в.с.). In 1887 the subterranean ara Tarenti was discovered, and in 1890 fragmentary tables of marble with inscriptions commemorating the Ludi Saeculares of Augustus and Septimius Severus were found in the bed of the Tiber (Mommsen, Eph. Epigr. viii 225 sqq.; Daremberg-Saglio, iv 990 sqq.).

p.note: : the chronology of the Ludi Saeculares (Tarentini) is very obscure and depends mainly on statements in the De die natali of Censorinus (238 A.D.). Dio (liv 18) says that the celebration by Augustus was the fifth, and Censorinus (17, 8) mentions four earlier in 449, 348, 249, 149 (146) в.с. The saeculum was reckoned as 100 or 110 years, the latter estimate being connected with the Greek belief that a new cycle, a παλιγγενεσία, began after four periods of 110 years. The Quindecimviri adopted the period of 110 years, and when Augustus (who was chief Quindecimvir) wished to celebrate the games in 17 B.C., the Quindecimviri invented records of previous celebrations in 456, 346, 236, 126 в.с. Claudius held the Ludi in 47 A.D., the 800th year from the foundation of Rome, and said that Augustus had been premature: Claud. 21, Fecit et saeculares, quasi anticipatos ab Augusto nec legitimo tempori reservatos, quamvis ipse (Claudius) in historiis suis prodat, intermissos eos Augustum multo post diligentissime annorum ratione subducta in ordinem redegisse. At this celebration the summons of the herald to behold games: "quos nec spectasset quisquam nec spectaturus esset'" caused much amusement, as many were still alive who had seen them under Augustus. Domitian, though professing to follow the calculation of Augustus and the period of 110 years, was six years in advance in holding them in 88 A.D. Subsequent celebrations were (1) by Antoninus Pius in 147, the 900th year from the foundation of Rome; (2) by Septimius Severus in 204, after two intervals of 110 years from the Ludi of Augustus in 17 в.с.; (3) by the emperor Philippus in 247, the 1000th year of Rome. Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 385 sqq. See

: the chariot race (missus, ἆθλον, ἅμιλλα) was usually seven laps (curricula, spatia) round the metae at either end of the arena, the finishing-point being a chalk line (creta, calx). The total distance traversed was about 9 kilometres, and Friedlaender (in Marquardt, Staatsv.. iii² 515) calculates that the number of races per hour would average 3. Dio (lix 7) says that in races held by Caligula in 37 A.D. there were 20 on the first day and 24 on the second, whereas 12 was the biggest number previously. From the time of Claudius and Nero the usual number seems to have been 24, though there are instances of 30, 36, 40, and 48. It is almost incredible that Domitian could have got through 100 missus in one day, even by reducing the number of laps. Dio (lxxii 16) mentions that Commodus got through 30 in 2 hours; but, as Friedl. says, the missus must have been much shortened or held in a smaller circus. In our passage Friedl. would read diebus for die, but in the Ludi Saeculares of Augustus the Circenses only occupied one day. In fixing the number of races at 100 Domitian was probably influenced by the number of years in the saeculum.

div.p: § 4. quinquennale certamen: Nero, eager for glory as a poet, singer, and player on the cithara, introduced Greek agones (ἀγῶνες, certamina) or artistic competitions at Rome in 60 A.D.; cf. Ner. 12, 3, instituit et quinquennale certamen primus omnium Romae more Graeco triplex, musicum (singing, instrumental music, poetry, oratory) gymnicum equestre, quod appellavit Neronia. Apparently this was discontinued at Nero's death, and in 86 A.D. Domitian, to celebrate his restoration of the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, founded a similar agon Capitolinus. The prizes were oaken wreaths; cf. Mart. iv 54, 1, O cui Tarpeias licuit contingere quercus, etc.: Juv. vi 387, an Capitolinam deberet Pollio quercum | sperare? The contest in Gr. and Lat. declamation was soon abandoned; that in Gr. and Lat. poetry became widely famed, and a poet's chief ambition was to be crowned by the emperor's hand. Statius often (e.g. S. v 3, 225 sqq.) laments his want of success with his Thebais.

p.note: : this reading of Stephanus for coronatorum is supported by Ner. 22, 2, palmarum numerum ampliare, and is accepted by nearly all subsequent editors. Ihm retains coronatorum, but it seems very doubtful Latin.

: et means "as well as in poetry." Both prosa (= proversa "straightforward") oratio and prosa by itself are used by Quintil. and other post-class. writers; Cic. has oratio soluta, opp. to vincula numerorum. The praise of Jupiter Capitolinus was a stock theme in the contests in eloquence at the agon Capitolinus (Quintil. iii 7, 4, laudes Capitolini Iovis, perpetua sacri certaminis materia). Suetonius mentions that Palfurius Sura had once received the prize (Dom. 13, 1).

: the citharoedus sang to the accompaniment of his cithara; the psilocitharista (-es) played without singing; the chorocitharista played an accompaniment to a chorus (cf. choraules). The form χοροκιθαριστής is not found in Greek, but χοροκιθαρεύς occurs in inscriptions (C.I.G. 2758 F, 2759); ψιλοκιθαριστής is not found outside inscriptions, but we have such expressions as ψιλὴ κιθάρισις καὶ αὔλησις (Plat. Legg. 669 E), and ψιλή μουσική, instrumental music, opposed to ἡ μετὰ μελῳδίας, accompanied by song (Aristot. Pol. viii 5, 11). Suetonius is the only Lat. author cited as using chorocitharista and psilocitharista, but citharoedus (κιθαρῳδός) is found frequently.
: see c. 5.

: cf. Dio lxvii 8, ἐποίησε δὲ καὶ θέαν (spectaculum) πολυτελῆ, ἐν ᾗ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδὲν ἐς ἱστορίαν ἐπίσημον παρελάβομεν, πλὴν ὅτι καὶ παρθένοι τῷ δρομικῷ ἠγωνίσαντο. This innovation of Domitian's was soon discontinued. He may have been copying the Spartans (cf. Xen. de rep. Lac. 1, 4; Eur. Androm. 595 sqq.; Propert. iii 14) or the famous races between girls at the festival in honour of Hera at Olympia which are described in Pausan. v 16, 2.

: the pallium and crepidae were the distinctive Greek dress, as opp. to the Roman toga and calcei; cf. Tib. 13, 1, redegit se, deposito patrio habitu, ad pallium et crepidas. Caligula, besides the military boot (caliga) from which he got his name, also wore cothurni and crepidae (Calig. 52). Latin comedies with Greek themes and dresses were called fabulae palliatae, while fábulae crepidatae denoted Latin tragedies of a like kind. purpurea toga Graecanica: Mommsen (Staatsr. i3 417 n.) explains this as the vestis Graecula (C.I.L. vi 8552), the Greek festal attire which the Roman emperors wore during their stay in Greek cities (e.g. Claudius in Naples, Dio 1x 6, ἐν μὲν ταῖς τῆς μουσικῆς θεωρίαις ἱμάτιον καὶ κρηπίδας, ἐν δὲ τῷ γυμνικῷ ἀγῶνι πορφυρίδα καὶ στέφανον χρυσοῦν ἐλάμβαve: Hadrian in Athens, Dio lxix 16); also on festal occasions at Rome (e.g. Nero on his triumphal entry into Rome after his victory at the Olympic games, Ner. 25, in veste purpurea distinctaque stellis aureis chlamyde: Commodus in the Roman theatre, Dio lxxii 17). The ἀγωνοθέται, or presidents at the Greek games, wore a purple robe (πορφυρίς) and a golden crown, and so Domitian as ἀγωνοθέτης at his agon Capitolinus conformed to the Greek usage. Suetonius uses Graecanicus = "in the Greek fashion" (Varr. L.L., Plin. N.H., etc.) only here; elsewhere always Graecus.
: an illustration of a similar crown with three medallions inset is given in Daremberg-Saglio, i 1525, fig. 1986. temples of Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva were all on the Capitol. The

: they not only sat beside him but also acted as assessors or judges of the contests along with him; cf. C.I.L. ix 2860, coronatus est inter poetas Latinos omnibus sententiis iudicum. In Herodian i 9, 2 the emperor Commodus at the Capitoline contests is described as θεατὴς καὶ ἀθλοθέτης σὺν τοῖς λοιποῖς ἱερεῦσιν.

: the flamen Dialis attached to Jupiter (Diespiter) was one of the three flamines maiores (the other two were the Martialis and Quirinalis). The office, which lasted for life, was of great dignity but involved many disabilities. The Dialis had a seat in the senate, was preceded by a lictor, etc., but he was forbidden e.g. to mount on horseback, to be absent from Rome, or to swear an oath (sometimes, to enable him to hold a magistracy, his colleague took the oath for him; Liv. xxxi 50). Candidates for the office were few, and it was in abeyance from 87 to 11 B.C. when Augustus restored it (Aug. 31, 4). See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 328 sqq. The flamen Dialis sat beside Domitian at these contests, as the emperor was the earthly representative of Jove.

: the Flaviales were the priests who had charge of the worship of the deified Flavian emperors, Vespasian and Titus. Such worship began with the appointment of the Augustales (sodales, sacerdotes, 25 in number) by Tiberius in honour of Augustus and the Julian gens (see on Galb. 8, 1). Besides the title Flaviales we also find in inscriptions Flaviales Titiales, Titiales Flaviales, or simply Titiales; Titus, as the most popular of the Flavian emperors, giving his name to the priesthood of the gens. Other similar collegia were the Claudiales, Hadrianales, Antoniniani (Ant. Pius), Aureliani (M. Aurelius), and lastly Alexandriani (Alexander Severus).
: see on Vitell. 7, 1.

: the estate and villa, which may have originally belonged to Pompey, at the foot of the Mons Albanus in Latium was a favourite resort of the earlier emperors and was developed by Domitian into a walled area including a palatial residence, baths, theatre, amphitheatre, camp for the praetorians, etc. It became the notorious arx Albana of which Tacitus (Agr. 45) and Juvenal (iv 145) speak with such bitterness. Dio mentions the "Albanum" of Domitian and says (lxvii 1): τοῦτο τὸ χωρίον ὑπὸ τὸ ὄρος τὸ ᾿Αλβανόν, ἀφ᾽ οὗπερ οὕτως ὠνομάσθη, ὂν ὥσπερ τινα ἀκρόπολιν ἐξείλετο.

: the more usual form is Quinquatrus (pl.), originally a festival of Mars on the 19th of March (five days after the Ides, whence the name according to Varr. L.L. vi 14), but when the temple of Minerva on the Aventine was dedicated on that day, the festival ceased to be purely military and was celebrated by various arts and trades in honour of their patroness Minerva. From 168 B.C. it lasted from the 19th to the 23rd of March and the name came to be misunderstood as the "five-day" festival (cf. Ov. Fast. iii 809-834). It was a holiday time in schools (Juv. x 115, with Mayor's note). Augustus on one occasion spent every day of the Quinquatrus at the gaming-table (Aug. 71, 3); Nero, when trying to compass the death of his mother Agrippina, invited her to Baiae to celebrate the Quinquatrus with him (Ner. 34, 2; Oth. 3, 1, n.).

: cf. Dio lxvii 1, θεῶν μὲν γὰρ τὴν ᾿Αθηνῶν ἐς τὰ μάλιστα ἤγαλλε, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τὰ Παναθήναια (= Quinquatria) μεγάλως ἑώρταζε, καὶ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀγῶνας καὶ ποιητῶν καὶ λογογράφων, μονομάχων (gladiatorum) τε κατ' ἔτος, ὡς εἰπεῖν, ἐν τῷ ᾿Αλβανῷ ἐποίει. Domitian worshipped Minerva with superstitious veneration (superstitiose colebat, c. 15, 3); he regarded himself as her especial favourite, and is said to have even claimed to be her son (Philostr. vit. Apollon. vii 24). Quintilian (x 1, 91) speaks of her as the familiare numen of Domitian; cf. Mart. viii 1, 4, Pallas Caesariana; ix 3, 10: Stat. S. i 1, 5; iv 1, 22. He erected temples to her at Rome including that in the Forum Transitorium (begun by Dom. and completed by Nerva, see Dom. 5), and that to Minerva Chalcidica in the Campus Martius. Her image appears on many of his coins. He gave the title of Prima Minervia to a new legion enrolled by him.

: used of the directorship of a cult, the presidency of a religious body, as in Calig. 22, 3 (of Caligula's own worship), magisteria sacerdotii ditissimus quisque, et ambitione et licitatione maxima, vicibus comparabant; cf. Capitolin. M. Anton. Philos. 4, fuit in eo sacerdotio (i.e. the Salii) et praesul et vates et magister et multos inauguravit atque exauguravit nemine praeeunte quod ipse carmina cuncta didicisset.

: Juvenal (iv 99) mentions these as held at the arx Albana of Domitian: profuit ergo nihil misero quod comminus ursos | figebat Numidas, Albana nudus harena | venator. Suetonius refers to them again in c. 19.

: it was at this Alban festival that Statius three times won the golden olive-crown, though he was unsuccessful at the agon Capitolinus; cf. Silv. iv 2, 63 (describing a banquet with Domitian), qua mihi felices epulas mensaeque dedisti | sacra tuae, talis longo post tempore venit | lux mihi, Troianae qualis sub collibus Albae, | cum modo Germanas ācies, modo Daca sonantem | proelia Palladio tua me manus induit auro. Martial mentions the golden olive-crown: iv 1, 5, hic (i.e. Domitian) colat Albano Tritonida (= Minervam) multus in auro: ix 23, 1, O cui virgineo (= Palladio) flavescere contigit auro, etc.: ix 24, 5, non solam tribuit Pallas tibi, Care, coronam. See on Vesp. 19, 1, coronas aureas.

div.p: §5. congiarium: see on Vesp. 18.

p.note: : this was the normal amount given in the 1st cent. A.D. by various emperors: Tiberius, Caligula (twice), Claudius, Vespasian, Nerva. Augustus gave five congiaria, one being 300 sesterces; cf. Aug. 41, 2, congiaria populo frequenter dedit, sed diversae fere summae: modo quadringenos, modo trecenos, nonnunquam ducenos quinquagenosque The total amount nummos. Nero gave 400 sesterces (Ner. 10, 1). distributed at each of the three congiaria of Domitian was 60,000,000 sesterces (Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 138).

: the first two congiaria may have been given at the triumphs over the Chatti and Dacians in 83 and 89; see c. 6, 1. The third was given in 93 to celebrate the victory over the Sarmatians; cf. Mart. viii 15, Dum nova Pannonici numeratur gloria belli, | omnis et ad reducem dum litat ara Iovem, | dat populus, dat gratus eques, dat tura senatus, | et ditant Latias tertia dona tribus.

: this presumably is the same banquet as that mentioned in c. 13, 1, in amphitheatro epuli die. Janssen would identify it with that given by Domitian in the amphitheatre on the Kalends of December, which is so vividly described in Stat. Silv. i 6, and also with those mentioned in Dio lxvii 4, τοῖς τε θεωμένοις συχνὰ διὰ τῶν σφαιρίων (= tesserarum) ἐδίδου, καί ποτε καὶ ἐδείπνισεν αὐτοὺς κατὰ χώραν καθημένους: Mart. v 49, 8, Hic error tibi profuit Decembri, | tum, cum prandia misit Imperator, | cum panariolis tribus redisti: viii 50, 7, Vescitur omnis eques tecum populusque patresque, | et capit ambrosias cum duce Roma dapes. Friedlaender explains Mart. v 49 as referring to the banquet (prob. in 88) described by Statius, but thinks that in viii 50 Martial refers to another banquet (prob. in Jan. 93) given by Dom. after his victory over the Sarmatians. Vollmer (on Stat. l.c.) reasonably regards it as purely arbitrary to identify the banquet described by Statius with any of those mentioned elsewhere. Janssen seems to overlook the chronological difficulty of identifying the banquet described by Statius as given on Dec. 1 with that mentioned by Suetonius as given at the Septimontium on Dec. 11 (or the following days); another difficulty in this identification is noticed on c. 13, 1.

: this is a correction by Iac. Gronovius of sacrorum quidem. Some of the "codices deteriores" have sacro quidem (read by Roth and Preud'homme) and sacrorum quidem die (read by Sabellicus and most of the early editors). Among the emendations which have been proposed are:-Sept. sacro quondam (Torrentius and Bentley): Sept. sacro senatui quidem (Politian, followed by Baumg.-Cr.) : Sept. sacro primoque die (Oudendorp): Sept. sacro, primo quidem die (Ernesti). All readings except that of Gronovius involve putting a fuil stop after epulum and treating the following sentence as an independent statement. Ihm regards the correction of Gronovius as probable, and it is defended by Alexander (op. cit. 27 sqq.) and read by Janssen and Rolfe. The Septimontium or Septimontiale sacrum was celebrated on Dec. 11. The seven montes were the three divisions of the Palatine, viz. Palatium, Cermalus, Velia; the three of the Esquiline, viz. Mons Oppius, Mons Cispius, and the Fagutal; and the Subura (on this and the correction "Sucusa" see Platner-Ashby, Topogr. Dict. Rome). Originally the festival ranked among sacra popularia or publica, but with the extension of Rome it was considered as one of the feriae privatae celebrated by the montani, and not by the pagani who inhabited what was at first the farm-land round Rome. On the day of the Septimontium there was a sacrifice (palatuar) on the Palatine by the flamen Palatualis, and no vehicles drawn by beasts of burden were allowed in the old city (Plut. Quaest. Rom. 69). See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 190; Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 113. In Domitian's time apparently the Septimontium must have lasted for more than one day, part of the celebration consisting of gladiatorial displays as in the case of the Quinquatria, etc.

: cf. Calig. 18, 2, panaria cum obsonio viritim divisit: Stat. S. i 6, 27 (describing the imperial servants distributing the food in the amphitheatre), Ecce autem caveas subit per omnes | insignis specie, decora cultu | plebes altera non minor sedente. | Hi panaria candidasque mappas | subvectant epulasque lautiores, | illi marcida vina largiuntur, etc. panarium (panis), lit. "bread-basket," is used in Plin. Ep. i 6, 3 for a "luncheonbasket"; Martial (v 49, 10) has the diminutive panariola for the small baskets (sportellae) of food provided for the people by Domitian.
: like sportula (see on c. 7, 1), sportella was a dim. from sporta (σπυρίς, σπείρω) a plaited basket; it occurs also in Cic. Fam. ix 20, Petron. Satyr. 40.

: obsonium (ὀψώνιον) denoted any cooked food eaten in addition to bread, but more especially fish (Marquardt, Privatl.2 432); it often 2 м implies "dainties," e.g. Vitell. 10, 12, inter profusissimos obsoniorum apparatus: Iul. 43, 2, legem praecipue sumptuariam exercuit dispositis circa macellum custodibus, qui obsonia contra vetitum proposita retinerent.
