: cf. Stat. S. i 6, 42, Una vescitur omnis ordo mensa, | parvi, femina, plebs, eques, senatus: | libertas reverentiam remisit. Et tu quin etiam (quis hoc vacare, | quis promittere possit hoc deorum?) | nobiscum socias dapes inisti. | Iam se, quisquis is est, inops beatus | convivam ducis esse gloriatur. For the pleonasm cf. Liv. vi 12, 10, primum initium certaminis: iii 54, 9, prima initia inchoastis libertatis.
: adverbial acc., see on Tit. 7, 3.
: cf. Calig. 18, 2, sparsit missilia variarum

: Ner. 11, 2, sparsa et populo missilia omnium rerum per omnes dies: singula cotidie milia avium cuiusque generis, multiplex penus, tesserae frumentariae, vestis, aurum, argentum, gemmae, margaritae, tabulae pictae, mancipia, iumenta, atque etiam mansuetae ferae, novissime naves, insulae ("apartment houses''), agri. Sometimes the gifts themselves, at other times tesserae entitling the recipients to gifts or amusements, were scattered among the people. The first sparsio missilium that can be dated was that of Agrippa in 33 B.C., when he rained tesserae upon the heads of the people in the theatre and provided vast quantities of wares of all kinds to be scrambled for (Dio xlix 43). Statius (S. i 6, 66) mentions Domitian's dives sparsio at the feast in the amphitheatre.

: = sedes populi in theatro (amphitheatro); so equestria (sc. loca or sedilia) in Calig. 26, 4. This substantival use seems peculiar to Suetonius; cf. Claud. 25, 4, where the German envoys, having been shown to the seats of the common people in the theatre (in popularia deducti), insisted on sitting with the senate in the orchestra, where the Parthian and Armenian envoys were sitting. For the position of the popularia in the amphitheatre see below on cuneos.

: such tokens, billets, or tallies were used for various purposes; e.g. the tesseraę frumentariae (Aug. 40, 2; Ner. 11, 2) and tesserae nummariae (Aug. 41, 2) for which the poorer classes could get corn or money. Dio (lxi 18, lxvi 25) describes those distributed by Nero and Titus at their sparsiones as small wooden balls inscribed with what they could be exchanged for. The shape and material of the tesserae scattered on such occasions varied; see Daremberg-Saglio, iii 1936, for illustrations of those in the form of fish, animals, etc., with a number marked on them. Sometimes they were shaped like coins and were called nomismata; cf. Mart. viii 78, 9, nunc veniunt subitis lasciva nomismata nimbis, | nunc dat spectatas tessera larga feras.

: "wedges" or "blocks" of seats. In the amphitheatre the senators occupied seats on the podium or terrace on the top of the wall surrounding the arena. Each of the rising divisions of seats (gradus) above the podium was called a maenianum; the equites sat in the 14 rows of the first maenianum; in the second were the popularia or seats of the populus; in the third were wooden benches for the pullati or lower classes. The lines of seats in the maeniana were divided into blocks (cunei) by short flights of stairs, to facilitate access. The podium was separated from the seats of the equites by a wall (balteus) and a passage or promenade (praecinctio), and each maenianum was separated from that above it in the same way.
: = publice promisit; cf. Galb. 16, 1.

: Eutrop. vii 23, Romae quoque multa opera fecit: in his Capitolium, et Forum transitorium, Odeum, Divorum porticus, Iseum, Serapeum, ac stadium: Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, 4, multaque opera inchoata per patrem, vel fratris studio, atque in primis Capitolium absolvit: Epit. 11, 3, Romae multa aedificia vel coepta vel a fundamentis construxit: Oros. vii 10, 2, plurimas urbis aedes destructis populi Romani rebus exstruxit. Martial (ix 3) declares that Olympus would be bankrupt if the gods tried to pay their debt to Domitian for his magnificent temples; Jove could not even pay a paltry composition. According to Plutarch (Poplic. 15) building was merely a disease with Domitian, and the line of Epicharmus on the ἄσωτος or spendthrift “ Οὐ φιλάνθρωπος τύ γ᾽ ἐσσ᾽· ἔχεις νόσον· χαίρεις διδούς." might be applied to Domitian in some such way as this: “ Οὐκ εὐσεβὴς οὐδὲ φιλότιμος τύ γ᾽ ἐσσί· ἔχεις νόσον· χαίρεις οἰκοδομῶν, ὥσπερ ὁ Μίδας ἐκεῖνος ἅπαντά σοι χρυσᾶ καὶ λίθινα βουλόμενος γίνεσθαι.”
: in 80 A.D., under Titus; see Tit. 8, 3.

: the early history of the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus is given on Vitell. 15, 33; for its form and splendour as restored by Domitian see Jordan Topogr. Rom i 2, 86 sqq. and the illustrations in Daremberg-Saglio i 903 sqq. The doors were plated with gold, and it was roofed with gilt tiles. Plutarch (l.c.) says that the gilding alone cost more than 12,000 talents (about £2,400,000), and he adds the interesting detail that the columns of Pentelic marble were excellently proportioned when he saw them at Athens, but that when they were cut and polished anew at Rome their beauty was impaired by their appearing too slender for their height.

: Plut. (l.c.), ἅμα τῷ τελευτῆσαι Οὐεσπασιανόν, ἐνεπρήσθη τὸ Καπιτώλιον. ὁ δὲ τέταρτος οὗτος νεὼς ὑπὸ Δομιτιανοῦ καὶ συνετελέσθη καὶ καθιερώθη. After the temple had been burned down in 69 A.D. (see Vitell. 15, 3) it was restored by Vespasian (Vesp. 8, 5), and Plut. says that Vespasian was luckier than Sulla who died before his temple to Jupiter Capitolinus was dedicated, whereas Vespasian died before his was destroyed, as it was by fire immediately after his death. From the Acta Arvalia (C.I.L. vi 2059, Newton 159) we learn that on Dec. 7, 80 A.D. the Fratres Arvales (who had to meet in the adjoining temple of Ops since that of Jupiter Capitolinus had been burned) offered their vows for the restoration and dedication of the temple by Titus: M. Tittio Frugi, T. Vinicio Iuliano cos., vii Idus Decembr., in Capitolio in aedem Opis sacerdotes convenerunt ad vota nuncupando ad restitutionem et dedicationem Capitoli ab Imp. T. Caesare Vespasiano Aug.

: in marked contrast to his father Vespasian, who inscribed on the buildings which he restored merely the names of the original builders and not his own; Dio lxvi 10 (Zonar. xi 17), τὰ τεμένη καὶ τὰ δημόσια ἔργα τὰ πεπονηκότα ἀνελάμβανε, καὶ τὰ ἤδη ἐφθαρμένα ἐπανεσκεύαζε, καὶ συντελουμένοις αὐτοῖς οὐ τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ἐπέγραφεν ὄνομα, ἀλλὰ τὸ τῶν πρώτως δομησαμένων.

: as a thankoffering for his escape from the Capitol when it was stormed by the Vitellians he built in Vespasian's reign a : 2 м 2 small shrine (sacellum) to Jupiter Conservator on the site of the dwelling of the aedituus who had sheltered him (see on c. 1, 2), and when he became emperor he also consecrated a vast temple to Jupiter Custos, with an effigy of himself in the arms (or on the lap) of the god; Tac. H. iii 74, mox imperium adeptus Iovi Custodi templum ingens seque in sinu dei sacravit. There are coins of Domitian (from 84 A.D. on) inscribed Iovi Conservatori, and others (from 86 on) inscribed Iovi Custodi (Eckhel, vi 379, 393; Cohen, i² 430, 432).

: Vespasian's Temple of Peace (Vesp. 9, 1) and the area surrounding it lay to the S.E. of the Forum Augusti, separated from it by the street known as the Argiletum, which ran from the Subura to the Forum Romanum. This portion of the Argiletum was converted by Domitian into a “forum” called (a) forum Nervae, as it was completed and dedicated by Nerva in 98; (b) forum Transitorium (or Pervium), on account of the highway which ran through it; (c) forum Palladium, from the temple of Minerva built in it; cf. Mart. i 2, 8, Limina post Pacis Palladiumque forum.
: on the site of the house where he was born; see on c. 1, 1.

: Domitian constructed a stadium for foot-races and other athletic contests to the W. of the Thermae of Nero in the Campus Martius, near the Pantheon. It held 15,000 spectators, and must have been finished before 86 A.D. if it is the stadium mentioned in c. 4, 4. After the burning of the Colosseum in the reign of Macrinus (217-18 A.D.) the stadium was used for some years for the shows of the amphitheatre (Dio lxxviii 25). It was restored by Alexander Severus (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 24). In the middle of the 4th cent. Ammianus (xvi 10, 14) mentions it and the Odeum among the “decora urbis aeternae.” For its subsequent history and remains see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom i 3, 592 sqq. Julius Caesar had erected a temporary stadium for athletic contests at his triumph: Iul. 39, 3, stadio ad tempus exstructo regione Marti Campi; so too Augustus: Aug. 43, 1, (edidit) athletas quoque exstructis in campo Martio sedilibus ligneis. The stadium connected with the gymnasium of Nero (Ner. 12, 3) which was destroyed by lightning in 62 was probably on the same site as that of Domitian.

: this Odium (1) or Odeum (ē) was also in the Campus Martius between the stadium and the trigarium. It was a roofed theatre for musical performances, and held an audience of 5000. The name was borrowed from the Gr. ᾠδεῖον which denoted a building for the same purpose, such as that of Pericles at Athens. Dio (lxix 4) mentions among the works of Trajan an ᾠδεῖον which seems to have been a restoration of that of Domitian.
: for this new basin or lake for the representation of sea-fights see on c. 4, 2, Edidit navales pugnas effosso iuxta Tiberim lacu.
: see on c. 4, 1. ..

: the date of this fire is unknown, and it is not mentioned by any other author. Burn (Rome and the Campagna c. xii) assumes that it occurred in Domitian's reign and that Domitian rebuilt the whole Circus with stone taken from his Naumachia. More probably it was Trajan who used the stone when he restored the Circus with great magnificence; cf. Plin. Pan. 51, Immensum latus Circi templorum pulchritudinem provocat: digna populo victore gentium sedes, nec minus ipsa visenda quam quae ex illa spectabuntur, etc.: Dio lxviii 7, οὕτως γάρ που καὶ μεγαλόφρων καὶ μεγαλογνώμων ἔφυ ὥστε τῷ ἱπποδρόμῳ ἐπιγράψαι ὅτι ἐξαρκοῦντα αὐτὸν τῷ τῶν Ῥωμαίων δήμῳ ἐποίησεν, ἐπειδὴ διαφθαρέντα πῃ καὶ μείζω καὶ περικαλλέστερον ἐξειργάσατο.

: a tribe dwelling about the Taunus mts., their territory corresponding to the mod. Hesse and part of Bavaria. They had been defeated by Drusus in 11 B.с., by Germanicus in 14 A.D., and again in the reign of Claudius (50 A.D.). The occasion of Domitian's expedition against them in 83 is uncertain (see Vollmer, Introd. to Stat. Silv., p. 44). There are vague expressions in Frontin. Strateg. i 1, 8, cum Germanos qui in armis erant vellet opprimere: Stat. S. i 4, 89, Rhenumque rebellem. Dio (lxvii 5) says the object was to aid the Cherusci, a tribe friendly to Rome, whose king had been driven out by the Chatti. Domitian marched north, nominally to hold a census of the two Gauls. Frontinus (ex-governor of Britain, who served in this campaign) says that he adopted this pretext lest news of his coming should stir the Germans to a bigger rising (Strateg. i 1, 8). Frontinus also praises the generalship of Domitian, e.g. his accustoming his cavalry to fight on foot when the Chatti took to the forests, and his establishing 120 miles of limites (ii 3, 23; ii, 7; i 3, 10). No great victory is recorded, and the war seems to have ended by the granting of a treaty to the Chatti (Stat. S. iii 3, 168, victis parcentia foedera Chattis). Domitian celebrated a triumph, assumed the title "Germanicus," let the consulship for 10 successive years be decreed to him, took the censorship for life, and wore the toga triumphalis as often as he entered the senate (Dio lxvii 4). His achievement, though lauded by Statius (S. i 1, 27, etc.) and Martial (i 4, 3; ii 2, 3; ix 1, 3), is belittled and ridiculed by hostile writers; e.g. Tac. Germ. 37, Germani triumphati magis quam victi sunt; Tac. Agr. 39; Plin. Pan. 16. (lxvii 4) says that he never even saw the foe: ἐκστρατεύσας εἰς τὴν Γερμανίαν, καὶ μηδ᾽ ἑορακώς που πόλεμον, ἐπανῆκε. Modern historians connect Domitian's campaign with a new plan of frontier defence, the "Limes Germanicus," a rampart of earth guarded at intervals by forts protecting the Roman possessions in the neighbourhood of the Rhine. This was begun by Vespasian, and Domitian annexed the territory of the Taunus mts. to the province of Upper Germany and continued the line of defence between the Moenus (Main) and the Nicer (Neckar), so as to connect the Moenus and the Rhine. See Bury, Stud. Rom. Emp. 403 sqq.; Mommsen, Prov. Rom. Emp. i 150 sqq.; Weynand, in Pauly-Wissowa vi 2556 sqq.; Gsell, op. cit. 193 sqq. The most recent account of the Roman frontier fortifications will be found in Henderson's Five Roman Emperors, cc. v and vi. .. Dio

: the Sarmatae or Sauromatae dwelt from the Vistula to the Don, in Poland and Russia. Domitian's punitive expedition against them lasted 8 months from May 92 to Jan. 93 (Gsell, p. 226). It is not mentioned by any historian except Eutropius (vii 23, 4) who, as usual, follows Suetonius: Expeditiones quattuor habuit, unum adversum Sarmatas, alterum adversum Cattos, duas adversum Dacos. De Dacis Cattisque duplicem triumphum egit, de Sarmatis solam lauream usurpavit. Multas tamen calamitates isdem bellis passus est; nam in Sarmatia legio eius cum duce interfecta est, et a Dacis Oppius Sabinus consularis et Cornelius Fuscus praefectus praetorio cum magnis exercitibus occisi sunt. Martial frequently refers to this Sarmatian expedition; e.g. in vii 1 and 2 he mentions a lorica, or cuirass, made of boars' hoofs (probably Sarmatian workmanship, see Friedl.), which was taken from a temple of Minerva at Rome and sent out to be worn by the emperor; in vii 80 he says that peace has been established: Quatenus Odrysios iam pax Romana triones | temperat et tetricae conticuere tubae, etc. Statius also lauds Domitian's victory (S. iii 3, 167 sqq.; iv 3, 153; 7, 49).

: this legion was probably v Alaudae (Parker, Rom. Leg. p. 110; see on Vesp. 8, 2); it has also been identified with xxi Rapax, which is not mentioned after the time of Domitian (Schilling, De leg. Rom. i Minervia et xxx Ulpia, p. 24).

: the chronology and history of Domitian's two campaigns against the Dacians, whose territory included Roumania, are obscure (see Vollmer, 48 sqq.; Brandis, in Pauly-Wissowa iv 2248; Henderson, op. cit. 160 sqq.). Under their king Decebalus (or Diurpaneus) the Dacians invaded Moesia in the winter of 85 and defeated and slew Oppius Sabinus, the Roman legatus there. After the death of Sabinus the emperor took the field and marched to the Danube, but entrusted the conduct of the war to Cornelius Fuscus, the praetorian prefect. Fuscus drove the Dacians out of Moesia, and it was then, apparently, that Domitian returned to Rome and celebrated a triumph (see on c. 13, 3; cf. Stat. S. iii 3, 118, сит prima truces amentia Dacos | impulit et magno gens est damnata triumpho). Fuscus next threw a bridge of boats across the Danube and penetrated into Dacia, but he met with a disastrous defeat and was himself slain. His successor Julianus again invaded Dacia and gained a great victory at Tapae in 89. About this time Domitian, after the suppression of the revolt of L. Antonius in Upper Germany, had marched from the Rhine to Pannonia to punish the Marcomani and Quadi for not sending the aid promised to Fuscus against the Dacians; but he was defeated by them with the aid of the adjoining Sarmatian Iazyges, and so was ready to grant terms of peace when Decebalus sent envoys to Pannonia. Domitian placed a diadem on the head of Diegis, brother of Decebalus, who was the leader of the embassy, as a token that Dacia's king was now a vassal of Rome. After his return to Rome in '89 Domitian celebrated a magnificent triumph (see below). The title "Dacicus," which is only used by Martial in the dedicatory letter to Bk. viii, is a mere piece of flattery and not an official title (Friedl. ad loc.).
: he was consul ordinarius in the early months of 84 A.D. along with the emperor Domitian, who was consul then for the tenth time (C.I.L. xiv 245, Dessau 6126).

: appointed procurator of Pannonia by Galba in 69 (Тас. Н. ii 86). He warmly supported the cause of Vespasian, and next to Antonius Primus had most influence at the councils of Vespasian 's generals (H. iii 4). He was made commander of the fleet at Ravenna (H. iii 12), and was voted the insignia praetoria by the senate in Dec. 69 after the victory of the Flavians (H. iv 4). Juvenal (iv 111) mentions him as one of the consilium hastily summoned to the arx Albana by Domitian: Et qui vulturibus servabat viscera Dacis | Fuscus, marmorea meditatus proelia villa. Martial (vi 76) refers to his position as praetorian prefect charged with Domitian's safety, and talks of his victorious shade haunting a vassal grove in vanquished Dacia: Ille sacri lateris custos Martisque togati, | credita cui summi castra fuere ducis, | hic situs est Fuscus. Licet hoc, Fortuna, fateri: | non timet hostiles iam lapis iste minas; | grande iugum domita Dacus cervice recepit | et famulum victrix possidet umbra nemus. For an appreciation of his military ability see Davies, J.R.S. x 19; Henderson, op. cit. 162.
: see on Tit. 4, 2.

: varia = vario eventu; cf. Tac. H. v 10, legatum varia proelia ac saepius adversa excepere. For the disasters to Domitian's armies cf. Eutrop. vii 23, 4 (quoted above on “Sarmatas"): Tac. Agr. 41, tot exercitus in Moesia Daciaque et Germania et Pannonia temeritate aut per ignaviam ducum amissi, tot militares viri cum totis cohortibus expugnati et capti: Oros. vii 10, 3, Bellum adversum Germanos et Dacos per legatos gessit pari reipublicae pernicie, cum et in urbe ipse senatum populumque laniaret et foris male circumactum exercitum adsidua hostes caede conficerent. Nam quanta fuerint Diurpanei, Dacorum regis, cum Fusco duce proelia, quantaeque Romanorum clades, longo textu evolverem, nisi Cornelius Tacitus, qui hanc historiam diligentissime contexuit, de reticendo interfectorum numero et Sallustium Crispum et alios auctores quam plurimos sanxisse et se ipsum idem potissimum elegisse dixisset. Domitianus tamen pravissima elatus iactantia sub nomine superatorum hostium de exstinctis legionibus triumphavit. The defeats of Sabinus and Fuscus are also mentioned in Iordan. Get. xiii 76. Dio (lxvii 6) says that Domitian claimed the credit of all the successes, none of which was due to him, and blamed others for reverses incurred in consequence of orders issued by him. ..

: usually explained as meaning that in 89 Domitian celebrated at the same time a double triumph over the Chatti who had supported L. Antonius in his revolt (see § 2) and over the Dacians, this being the triumph dated between Oct. 1, 89 and Sept. 30, 90 by Euseb.- Hieron., p. 161 Schoene, Domitianus de Dacis et Germanis triumphavit. Brandis, however, seems right in taking the words to mean that Domitian twice celebrated a triumph over each of the two: over the Chatti in 83 and 89, and over the Dacians in 86 and 89. Suetonius often uses duplex in the sense of duo; e.g. Vesp. 4, 2, d. sacerdotium: Ner. 1, 2, d. censura: Aug. 16, 1, d. naufragium: Aug. 13, 1, bellum duplici proelio transegit, quorum priore vix.. evaserat. On this view, which is strongly supported by Janssen, the complete number of Domitian's triumphs is given here; the two earlier ones (in 83 and 86) are referred to in c. 13, 3, post duos triumphos transnominavit, where see notes. A colossal equestrian statue of Domitian was set up in the Forum on his triumphal return in 89 (Stat. S. i 1). The triumphal games were under the direction of L. Arruntius Stella (S. i 2, 180), and the cost of the celebration was met by an exaction of aurum coronarium from the provinces. Dio (lxvii 7) derides the triumphal procession with its "spoils" supplied from the emperor's palace, and asserts that the "peace" granted to the Dacians was in reality a humiliating agreement on Domitian's part to pay a vast sum to Decebalus and to furnish him with Roman artificers for civil and military purposes. Similarly Pliny (Pan. 17) contrasts the sham victories of Domitian with the solid successes of Trajan in his Dacian wars.

: cf. Ner. 13, 2, where Nero deposits a laurel wreath in the Capitol (laurea in Capitolium lata) after Tiridates, king of Armenia, appeared at Rome as a suppliant and had his diadem restored by the emperor. It was part of the ceremony of a regular (iustus) triumph that the triumphing general, when the procession reached the temple of Capitoline Jove, should deposit in the lap of the god the laurel branch which he bore in his hand and the laurel wreaths with which the fasces were crowned; cf. Sil. Ital. xv 120, laurumque superbam | in gremio Iovis excisis deponere Poenis. Furthermore, a laurel wreath was placed in the lap of the god when news of a victory reached Rome; cf. Plin. N.H. xv 30, laurus.. in gremio Iovis Opt. Max. deponitur quoties laetitiam nova victoria attulit. Sometimes the wreath was sent from the scene of the victory; cf. Plin. Pan. 8, allata erat ex Pannonia laurea hanc imperator Nerva in gremio Iovis collocarat. The poets refer to Domitian's waiving his claim to a formal triumph over the Sarmatae; e.g. Mart. viii 15, 5, hos quoque secretos ("suppressed'') memoravit Roma triumphos, | nec minor ista tuae laurea pacis erat; ix 101, 19, Saepe recusatos parcus duxisse triumphos | victor Hyperboreo nomen ab orbe tulit: Stat. S. iii 3, 171, quae (clementia) modo Marcomanos post horrida bella vagosque | Sauromatas Latio non est dignata triumpho: iv 1, 39, mille tropaea feres, tantum permitte (i.e. "only accept'") triumphos: | restat Bactra novis, restat Babylona tributis | frenari, nondum in gremio Iovis Indica laurus.

div.p: § 2. bellum civile: this revolt of L. Antonius is described by Statius as "civile nefas” (S. i 1, 80); in inscriptions it is called “bellum Germanicum” (e.g. C.I.L. vi 1347, Dessau 1006).

p.note: : L. Antonius Saturninus was military commander in Upper Germany, and at the end of 88 A.D., acting in concert with some of the senate, he induced the two legions (xiv Gemina Martia Victrix and xxi Rapax) in winter-quarters at Moguntiacum (Mainz) to proclaim him Imperator. He provided himself with funds by seizing the savings of the legionaries (see c. 7, 3). He was relying on the support of the Germans beyond the Rhine, who had earlier taken part in the revolt of Civilis, especially the Chatti and their allies the Usipi. L. Appius Maximus Norbanus, who in all probability was military commander in Lower Germany (see Henderson, op. cit. 111), promptly advanced against him and defeated him in Jan. 89. Domitian had summoned Trajan to march from Spain over the Pyrenees and Alps (Plin. Pan. 14), and had himself left Rome to quell the rising before he heard of the victory of Norbanus, and after the news he continued his march to the Rhine. The officers of the disaffected legions were executed and many senators were put to death by Domitian. Cf. Dio lxvii 11 (where Norbanus is praised for burning the captured correspondence of Saturninus, to save his fellow conspirators): [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, 9, his eius (Domitiani) saevitiis, ac maxime iniuria verborum, qua scortum vocari dolebat, accensus Antonius, curans Germaniam superiorem, imperium corripuit. Quo per Norbanum Appium acie strato, Domitianus longe taetrior, in omne hominum genus, etiam in suos, ferarum more grassabatur. Martial (iv 11) says that Antonius Saturninus wished to emulate M. Antonius the triumvir: Dum nimium vano tumefactus nomine gaudes, | et Saturninum te, miser, esse pudet, | impia Parrhasia movisti bella sub ursa, | qualia qui Phariae coniugis arma tulit, etc. Martial also praises the loyalty of Norbanus, ix 84, Cum tua sacrilegos contra, Norbane, furores | staret pro domino Caesare sancta fides, etc.
: see on Vitell. 7, 1.
: ''thawed," a poetical word; cf. Luc. i 219, madidis Euri resolutae flatibus Alpes: Ov. Trist. iii 10, 13, nix iacet, et iactam ne sol pluviaeque resolvant, | indurat Boreas perpetuamque facit.

: "inasmuch as," "since." Suet. uses siquidem (εἴ γε) twenty times and always with the indic. The causal signification is found at times in Cic. (Kühner-Stegmann, ii 427) and prevails, almost exclusively, in post-Aug. writers. Trachmann (op. cit. p. 39) assumes that in our passage siquidem expresses a doubt: “Suetonius iis, quae addita 'siquidem' particula adiecit, illud praesagium tanquam ex vano haustum in dubium vocare videtur; but Suetonius is too firm a believer in presages of every kind to throw any doubt on their reality.

: the regular word for an eagle's screams; cf. Liv. i, 34, S, aquila cum magno clangore volitans: Cic. carm. frg. 32, 14 (Baehrens), Iovis satelles (i.e. aquila) clangorem fundit vastum: Plin. N.H. x 6, melanaëtos sola aquila sine clangore.

: Plutarch (Aem. Paul. 25), describing the inexplicable way in which the report of the victory of Paulus over Perseus at Pydna (168 B.C.) suddenly spread at Rome, gives earlier instances of such strange happenings: (1) the defeat of the Crotoniats by the Locrians at the Sagras in Bruttium (6 cent. B.C.) known to the Greeks at Olympia on the same day; (2) the defeat of the Persian fleet by the Greeks at Mycale in Lydia (479 B.с.) known to the Plataeans on the same day; (3) the defeat of the Tarquins at Lake Regillus in Latium by the Romans (496 в.с.) announced at Rome by two mysterious horsemen said to be Castor and Pollux. He adds that all these stories are confirmed by what happened in his own day with regard to the report at Rome of this defeat of L. Antonius: Ὅτε γὰρ ᾿Αντώνιος ἀπέστη Δομετιανοῦ καὶ πολὺς πόλεμος ἀπὸ Γερμανίας προσεδοκᾶτο, τῆς ῾Ρώμης ταραττομένης ἄφνω καὶ αὐτομάτως ὁ δῆμος ἐξ αὑτοῦ φήμην ἀνέδωκε νίκης, καὶ τὴν ῾Ρώμην ἐπέδραμε λόγος αὐτόν τε τὸν ᾿Αντώνιον ἀνῃρῆσθαι καὶ τοῦ σὺν αὐτῷ στρατεύματος ἡττημένου μηδὲν μέρος λελεῖφθαι. Τοσαύτην δὲ λαμπρότητα καὶ ῥύμην ἡ πίστις ἔσχεν, ὥστε καὶ θῦσαι τῶν ἐν τέλει πολλούς. Ζητουμένου δὲ τοῦ πρώτου φράσαντος, ὡς οὐδεὶς ἦν, ἀλλ᾽ ὁ λόγος εἰς ἄλλον · ἐξ ἄλλου διωκόμενος ἀνέφευγε, καὶ τέλος καταδὺς ὥσπερ εἰς πέλαγος ἀχανὲς τὸν ἄπειρον ὄχλον ἐφάνη μηδεμίαν ἀρχὴν ἔχων βέβαιον, αὕτη μὲν ἡ φήμη ταχὺ τῆς -πόλεως ἐξερρύη, πορευομένῳ δὲ τῷ Δομετιανῷ μετὰ δυνάμεως ἐπὶ τὸν πόλεμον ἤδη καθ' ·ὁδὸν ἀγγελία καὶ γράμματα φράζοντα τὴν νίκην ἀπήντησεν. Ἡ δ᾽ αὐτοῦ τοῦ ·κατορθώματος (victoriae) ἡμέρα καὶ τῆς φήμης ἐγίνετο, ἐπὶ πλέον ἢ δισμυρίους σταδίους τῶν τόπων διεστώτων. Ταῦτα μὲν οὐδεὶς ἀγνοεῖ τῶν καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς.
: Dio (lxvii 11) says that Domitian sent the heads of Antonius and those executed as his accomplices to be exposed on the Rostra at Rome. multa in.. habui sane, non
: for this constr. cf. Cic. Legg. iii 5, 12, nihil modo multum, quod putarem novandum in legibus.

: under the early Empire clients, instead of being asked occasionally to a regular dinner (recta cena, see on Vesp. 19, 1) by their patronus, received from him a portion of food (sportula) as a daily reward for their attentions. These doles were carried away in a small basket (sportula, see on sportellae, c. 4, 5); hence the same name was given to the dole itself. Patrons soon found it more convenient to give in lieu of food a small sum of money (usually 100 quadrantes, less than a shilling). Nero, from motives of economy, substituted sportulae for publicae cenae (Ner. 16, 2, adhibitus sumptibus modus; publicae cenae ad sportulas redactae). A publica cena was not a dinner given at state expense, but one provided either by a magistrate, or by the emperor, or even by a private person in a public place (in publico), e.g. the Forum, to which the people or part of the people were invited. Domitian restored the publicae cenae and abolished the publicae sportulae, and, presumably, every patron had to furnish a recta cena for his clients; but the change was disliked by both patrons and clients, and the suppression of the money sportula did not last more than three or four years. Martial only mentions it in Bk. iii (published 87/88 A.D.); in his later Books the money sportula has been restored. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 207 sqq.

: restored by Beroaldus for grecum. The chariot-drivers (aurigae, agitatores) of each factio formed a grex under the control of the dominus factionis: cf. Ner. 22, 2, spectaculum multiplicatis missibus ("races") in serum protrahebatur, ne dominis quidem iam factionum dignantibus nisi ad totius diei cursum greges ducere (i.e. they refused to bring out their drivers at all unless there was to be a full day's racing).

: companies of contractors who entered into an agreement with the giver of the games (munerarius, editor spectaculorum) to provide the chariots, horses, drivers, and all other requisites. Each factio had its own distinctive colour which was worn by its charioteers and displayed on its chariots. Everyone at Rome, from the emperor down, became a violent partizan of one of the different colours.

: Dio lxvii 4, τοῖς δὲ ἁρματηλάταις δύο γένη ἕτερα, τὸ μὲν χρυσοῦν, τὸ δὲ πορφυροῦν ὀνομάσας, προσκατέστησε. These two new colours soon completely disappeared. The "Purple" is once mentioned in Mart. xiv 55 (84/85 A.D.), Proficies nihil hoc, caedas licet usque, flagello, si tibi purpureo de grege currit equus (this contemptuous reference shows that the "Purple” found no favour with Domitian, though introduced by him). The only other mention of the "Purple" is in C.I.L. vi 10062 (Dessau 5282): D. m. Epaphroditus agitator f(actionis) r(ussatae); vicit clxxviii et ad purpureum liber (i.e. manumissus) vic. viii. Some identify ‘pannus chelidonius'' in C.I.L. vi 10046 (Dessau 5313) with “pannus purpureus,” but the reading is uncertain; see Friedl. in Marquardt Staatsv. iii² 518.

: pannus (a cloth, garment, or rag) was used specially for the coloured tunic of the charioteer in the races; cf. Pliny, Ep. ix 6, Quo magis miror tot milia virorum tam pueriliter identidem cupere currentes equos, insistentes curribus homines videre. Si tamen aut velocitate equorum aut hominum arte traherentur, esset ratio non nulla: nunc favent panno, pannum amant, et si in ipso cursu medioque certamine hic color illuc, ille huc transferatur, studium favorque transibit, et repente agitatores illos, equos illos, quos procul noscitant, quorum clamitant nomina, relinquent: Juv. xi 198, Totam hodie Romam circus capit, et fragor aurem | percutit, eventum ('success'') viridis quo colligo ("infer”) panni.

: White (albus), Red (russatus, russeus), Green (viridis or prasinus, from πράσον a leek), Blue (venetus, see Vitell. 7, 1); cf. Sidon. carm. xxiii 323, micant colores | albus vel venetus virens rubensque. White and Red were the original colours; Tertull. Spect. 9, ab initio duo soli fuerunt, albus et russeus. Pliny (N.H. vii 186) quotes from the acta a notice of the death of one Felix, a driver of the Red factio, on whose pyre one of his admirers cast himself; this was in the 1st cent. B.C. The prasina factio is first mentioned in the reign of Tiberius (C.I.L. vi 33950) and of Caligula (Suet. Calig. 55; Dio lix 14): the veneta first in the time of Nero and Vitellius (C.I.L. vi 10055; Suet. Vitell. 7, 1; Dio lxv 5). Caligula, Nero, Domitian, L. Verus, Commodus, Elagabalus favoured the "Green"; Vitellius and Caracalla the “Blue.'”

: cf. Plin. Pan. 46, Obtinuit aliquis (i.e. Domitian) ut spectaculum pantomimorum populus Romanus tolli pateretur... Rogatus es tu (i.e. Trajan) quod cogebat alius (i.e. Dom.), coepitque esse beneficium, quod necessitas fuerat. Neque enim a te minore concentu ut tolleres pantomimos, quam a patre tuo (i.e. Nerva) ut restitueret exactum est. Utrumque recte: nam et restitui oportebat quos sustulerat malus princeps et tolli restitutos. Under the Empire the word histrio ("actor'") came to be used specially of a pantomimus or dancer. Such histriones enjoyed extraordinary favour; cf. Tac. Dial. 29, Iam vero propria et peculiaria huius urbis vitia paene in utero matris concipi mihi videntur, histrionalis favor et gladiatorum equorumque studia. Besides public performances in the theatres, the emperors and wealthy families kept histriones for their private entertainment (cf. Aug. 74). The licence in which they indulged gave rise to abuses which the emperors made spasmodic efforts to check. Augustus, though he limited or abolished the ius virgarum in histriones of the praetors (Aug. 45, Tac. A. i 77), punished severely their misconduct in private life or on the stage. Tiberius banished all histriones from Italy (Tac. A. iv 14, cf. Suet. Tib. 37), but Caligula restored them (Dio lix 2). In 56 Nero again expelled the pantomimi, but they reappear before 60. Titus refused to countenance his favourite pages who were the leading pantomimi of the day (Tit. 7, 2). Nerva, at the request of the people, removed Domitian's ban. Trajan reimposed it, but withdrew it after his Dacian triumph in 107. Hadrian allowed the imperial dancers (aulici histriones) to appear on the public stage (Spart. Hadr. 19). See Friedl., Sitteng. ii10 125 sqq.

: in 82 A.D.; cf. Philostr. vit. Apollon, vi 42, Δομετιανοῦ δὲ βασιλέως ὑπὸ τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον εὐνούχους τὸ μὴ ποιεῖν νομοθετήσαντος. Dio (lxvii 2) says that he did this as a slur on Titus: καίπερ καὶ αὐτὸς ᾿Εαρίνου τινὸς εὐνούχου ἐρῶν, ὅμως, ἐπειδὴ καὶ ὁ Τίτος ἰσχυρῶς περὶ τοὺς ἐκτομίας ἐσπουδάκει, ἀπηγόρευσεν ἐπὶ ἐκείνου ὕβρει μηδένα ἔτι ἐν τῇ τῶν ῾Ῥωμαίων ἀρχῇ ἐκτέμνεσθαι. The reform is praised by Statius (S. iv 3, 13 sqq.) and by Martial (ii 60, vi 2, etc.). Ammianus (xviii 4, 5) mentions it as a redeeming feature of Domitian's reign: Horum et similium taedio iuvat veterem laudare Domitianum, qui, licet patris fratrisque dissimilis memoriam nominis sui inexpiabili detestatione perfudit, tamen receptissima inclaruit lege qua minaciter interdixerat ne intra terminos iuris dictionis Romanae castraret quisquam puerum. Nerva renewed this law, and Hadrian made offenders against it liable to the penalties of the Lex Cornelia de sicariis.
: see on Vesp. 4, 3; cf. Mart. ix 6, 4 (referring to this law of Domitian): Non puer avari sectus arte mangonis | virilitatis damna maeret ereptae.

: presumably lest the dealers, if they were allowed to ask exorbitant prices for their remaining stock, might be tempted to break the law (Baumg.-Cr.). For the prices of eunuchs (varying from about £20 to £4000) see Marquardt, Privatl.2 174.

div.p: § 2. ad: temporal, on the occasion of"; cf. Calig. 51, 1, ad minima tonitrua et fulgura conivere solebat. See App. i. § 12.

p.note: : very frequently used by Suet. in the sense of aliquando; cf. c. 14, 1: 18, 2: Oth. 3, 2: Vesp. 5, 4: 25: Tit. 8, 1.
: between Oct. 91 and Sept. 92 (Euseb.).

: = novas vites sereret, “plant new vines." The only other instance cited of the use of this verb is in the Christian writer Paulinus Nolanus, carm. 21, 659, vitam novellantes Deo, where it is used in a metaphorical sense of a new devotion or consecration. We find the adj. novella used as an epithet of vitis in Verg. E. iii 11, atque mala vites incidere falce novellas (cf. Varr. R.R. i 31, 1, novellae vineae); the subst. novelletum, “a vine-nursery," occurs in Dig. xxv 1, 6. ut in provinciis vina succiderentur: Philostratus (vit. Soph. i 6) refers to this legislation of Domitian about vines in Asia, and says it was due to the idea that wine leads to sedition: ἐδόκει τῷ βασιλεῖ μὴ εἶναι τῇ ᾿Ασίᾳ ἀμπέλους, ἐπειδὴ ἐν οἴνῳ στασιάζειν ἔδοξαν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐξαιρεῖσθαι μὲν τὰς ἤδη πεφυτευμένας, ἄλλας δὲ μὴ φυτεύειν ἔτι. Again (vit. Apollon. vi 42) he describes how Apollonius encouraged the Ionians to send an embassy to Domitian to urge the repeal of this measure on the ground that the emperor, though he had provided against men being made sterile, was rendering the earth sterile (τῶν μὲν ἀνθρώπων φειδόμενος, τὴν δὲ γὴν εὐνουχίζων). The Ionians sent the sophist Scopelianus, who met with such success that not merely was permission to plant vines granted, but a fine was imposed on those who did not plant them.

: for nec (= neque vero, neque tamen) cf. Oth. 1, 1, senator est factus nec praeturae gradum excessit. We may assume that the petitions of the vine-growers influenced the emperor, but Suetonius (c. 14, 2) states that it was the boding import of some Greek verses circulated against him which more than anything else led him to revoke his order. Statius (S. iv 3, 11) says: qui (i.e. Domitian) castae Cereri diu negata | reddit iugera sobriasque terras; and Vollmer (ad loc.) infers that the prohibition of vine-growing must still have had some force in 95 A.D., the year in which this poem of Statius was written. Rostovtzeff (Soc. and Econ. Hist. Rom. Emp. p. 189) says that it was apparently enforced in Africa, to a certain extent in the Danube provinces, in the north and centre of Gaul, and in part of Spain. On the subject of vineculture in the provinces and the restrictions imposed on it in the interest of the Italian growers see Marquardt, Privatl.2 p. 446; Mommsen, Prου. Rom. Emp. i 108. As early as 129 B.C. the planting of the vine and olive was forbidden in the provinces beyond the Alps (Cic. de rep. iii 9, 16) and this restriction was not completely removed till the reign of Probus (276-282 A.D.); cf. Vopisc. Prob. 18, Gallis omnibus et Hispanis ac Britannis hic permisit ut vites haberent vinumque conficerent.

: important positions in the imperial household such as ab epistulis, a libellis, a rationibus, a patrimonio, which were held exclusively by freedmen down to Nero's time. Otho made an innovation by appointing as his secretary (ab epistulis) the orator Secundus (Plut. Oth. 9). Vitellius transferred such offices to equites: Tac. H. і 58, Vitellius ministeria principatus per libertos agi solita in equites Romanos disponit. An instance of an eques under Vitellius holding posts previously held by liberti is Propertianus who is described in C.I.L. xi 5028 (Dessau 1447) as "pro(curator) imp(eratoris) a patrim(onio) et heredit (atibus) et a libell(is)." See Hirschfeld, Kais. Verwaltungsb. p. 112, n. 4. Domitian, as Suetonius says here, divided the posts between liberti and equites. An eques so appointed was Cn. Octavius Titinius Capito (friend of the younger Pliny, cf. Ep. i 17, etc.) who was “procurator) ab epistulis et a patrimonio (sc. Domitiani),” ‘‘iterum ab epistulis divi Nervae,” and “ab epistulis tertio imp. Traiani” (C.I.L. vi 798, Dessau 1448). Hadrian, who established a Civil Service at Rome, excluded liberti and confined these offices to equites; cf. Spart. Hadr. 22, ab epistulis et a libellis primus equites Romanos habuit (“primus'' is inaccurate, as Mommsen points out, Staatsr. ii³ 838, n. 2). Domitian in his administration limited in every way the authority of the senate (cf. Plin. Pan. 62), and gave increased power to the equites and liberti. He appointed as commander in his Dacian campaign (c. 6, 1) Cornelius Fuscus who was praefectus praetorio (an equestrian post, see on Tit. 6, 1). An equestrian procurator of Asia was commissioned to govern the province in place of the proconsul who had died (C.I.L. v 875). He included equites as well as senators in his consilium (C.I.L. ix 5420), and so a senator, tried before the imperial consilium, might have equites and not merely his peers as judges. The favour shown by Domitian to freedmen (cf. Tac. H. i 76, Agr. 41; Plin. Pan. 42, 49, 88) was a reaction from the repressive policy of Titus and Vespasian, and a reversion to the privileges given to them by Vitellius, Otho, Galba, Nero, Claudius, and Caligula.

div.p: § 3. geminari castra prohibuit: geminare is used here not in the sense of duplicare but of coniungere; cf. Hor. A.P. 13, serpentes avibus geminentur: Stat. S. i 2, 240, dat Iuno verenda | vincula et insigni geminat Concordia taeda. When several legions were united in the one camp, the consciousness of their strength often led to mutiny. On the death of Augustus three legions in Pannonia, which were quartered in the same summer-camp (aestiva), revolted (Tac. A. i 16), and at the same time four legions similarly concentrated in Lower Germany conspired to make Germanicus emperor (A. i 39).

p.note: : each camp had its shrine, usually in the principia (Oth. 1, 2, n.), in which the ensigns were placed and the imagines of the emperors were worshipped. This shrine formed an inviolable sanctuary.. In a vault beneath it were deposited the savings of the legionaries which were kept and administered by the ensign-bearers (signiferi). When the soldiers received a donativum on the occasion of any special success, etc., half of it must be deposited under the protection of the ensigns; cf. Veget. ii 20, Illud vero ab antiquis divinitus institutum est, ut ex donativo, quod milites consequuntur, dimidia pars sequestraretur apud signa, et ibidem ipsis militibus servaretur, ne per luxum aut inanium rerum comparationem a contubernalibus posset absumi. Miles deinde, qui sumptus suos scit apud signa depositos, de deserendo nihil cogitat, magis diligit signa, pro illis in acie fortius dimicat, more humani ingenii, ut pro illis habeat maximam curam, in quibus suam videt positam esse substantiam. Vegetius says that each cohort had a sack (follis) in which these sums were placed under the charge of the signifer. The evidence of Latin papyri containing military accounts establishes the fact that the sum credited to a soldier's depositaccount from such irregular donativa was augmented by additions from his regular pay; the expenses for food, clothing, etc. are deducted from his stipendium and any surplus is added to his deposit. See Grenfell, Hunt, and Hogarth, Fayûm Towns and their Papyri pp. 252 sqq.; Reinach, in Daremberg-Saglio iv 1324 sqq.; Parker, Rom. Legions, 217 sqq.
: see c. 6, 2.

: i.e. the winter-quarters of the 14th and 21st legions at Moguntiacum (Mainz). The other two legions under the command of L. Antonius in Upper Germany were the 8th (Augusta), encamped at Argentoratum (Strassburg), and the 11th (Claudia), encamped at Vindonissa (Windisch). There does not seem to be any authority for assuming that they took part in the revolt.

: in 83 A.D., to celebrate his victory over the Chatti; cf. Zonaras xi 19, καὶ τοῖς στρατιώταις ἐπηύξησε τὴν μισθοφοράν, τάχα διὰ τὴν νίκην· πέντε γὰρ καὶ ἑβδομήκοντα δραχμὰς (= denarios) ἑκάστου λαμβάνοντος ἑκατὸν ἐκέλευσε δίδοσθαι. From the time of Julius Caesar payments were made to the soldiers every four months, each payment being called a stipendium, so that the soldiers got three stipendia each year. Caesar also raised the pay for the foot-soldier to 225 denarii a year, so that each stipendium was 75 denarii. The number of stipendia remained the same under Domitian (as Zon. implies), but he raised each of the three stipendia to 100 denarii, or a total amount of 300 denarii a year; this addition to the earlier pay being equivalent to paying a fourth stipendium of 75 denarii. See Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 96.
: = 75 denarii; see on Galb. 20, 2.

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, 2, ius aequissime dixit; cf. Iul. 43, 1, ius laboriosissime ac severissime dixit: Aug. 33, 1, ipse ius dixit assidue et in noctem nonnunquam, si parum corpore valeret, lectica pro tribunali collocata, vel etiam domi cubans: ib. 72, 2, Tibur, ubi etiam in porticibus Herculis templi persaepe ius dixit. For the civil and criminal jurisdiction of the emperors in virtue of their imperium see Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 958 sqq.; Willems, Le Droit Publique Romain 458 sqq.; Greenidge, Roman Public Life 381 sqq. plerumque "Ius ..

: in the early editions the punctuation was .dixit. Plerumque rescidit''; the punctuation in the text is that proposed by Burman and adopted by Oudendorp, Ernesti, and the modern editors; Oudendorp suggested another punctuation “pro tribunali. Extra ordinem.. rescidit," and Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 981, n. 1) approves of this, thinking that there is a distinction made between Domitian's own jurisdiction and the extraordinary supervision which he exercised over the iudices, partly by admonition and partly by quashing their decisions.

: et means in addition to his sittings in his palace and his arx Albana. Criminal cases, as a rule, were heard by the emperor in his own house; when he sat in the Forum he nearly invariably heard civil cases (Mommsen, op. cit. ii³ 965, n. 4; 983, n. 3). Dio frequently mentions the emperors sitting as judges in the Forum; e.g. lvii 7 (of Tiberius), ἐπεποίητο βῆμα ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἐφ᾽ οὗ προκαθίζων ἐχρημάτιζε : lx 4 (of Claudius), τὸ μὲν πλεῖστον ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἄλλοθι ἐπὶ βήματος ἐδίκαζε : lxvi 10 (of Vespasian), ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ πολλάκις ἐδίκαζεν : lxix 7 (of Hadrian), ἐδίκαζε τότε μὲν ἐν τῷ Παλατίῳ, τότε δὲ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ τῷ τε Πανθείῳ καὶ ἄλλοθι πολλαχόθι, ἀπὸ βήματος, ὥστε δημοσιεύεσθαι τὰ γιγνόμενα.
: see on Vesp. 7, 2. Magistrates administering justice in the Forum (Tit. 4, 2) at the place called the Comitium (Dom. 8, 4) sat on a sella curulis placed on a platform (tribunal, βῆμα). ..

: Domitian may have followed the example of Claudius in sitting on days usually exempt from legal business: Claud. 14, Ius laboriosissime dixit, etiam suis suorumque diebus sollemnibus (i.e. anniversaries in his family), nonnumquam festis quoque antiquitus et religiosis. Nec semper praescripta legum secutus, etc.; but the Princeps always judged extra ordinem, by cognitio (Tit. 7, 1, n.), the case being decided either by himself alone or with the assistance of counsellors chosen at his own discretion, down to the time of the definite organisation of the consilium principis under Hadrian. Bentley proposed to insert et before extra ordinem.
: verdicts prompted by interested motives, by a desire to curry favour; cf. Cic. Cluent. 38, 108, quo in reo qui absolvit ambitiosus existimatur: Ulp. Dig. iv 43, ambitiosa decreta.
: see on Vesp. 10.
: see on Vesp. 3.

: “ unsubstantial,” “unfounded,” "superficial," lit. "sprinkled on the surface and not sinking deep"; cf. Sen. Ep. 23, 4, haec, quibus delectatur vulgus, tenuem habent et perfusoriam voluptatem hoc, de quo loquor, solidum est, et quod plus pateat introrsus. So too the adv. perfusorie means “vaguely,” “indefinitely"; Ulp. Dig. xliii 24, 5, debebit .. neque quidem perfusorie, aut obscure, dicere aut denuntiare. In Cic. Rosc. Amer. 29, 80 there is the phrase aliquem iudicio perfundere, which Forcellini interprets: iudicii vexationem, ceu aquam, offundere, in ius vocare, et afficere molestia sistendi se ante iudicem, parandae defensionis, et causae dicendae; eadem ratione “aspergere alicui molestiam'' dixit Cic. Q. Fr. ii 10. Halm conjectured pervertere; Trojel pessundare. From that use of perfundere Ernesti (followed by Baumg.-Cr.) explains perfusoria assertio here as "ea qua dominus (slave-owner) iustus adducitur per calumniam litis . . in periculum servi amittendi.”

: ‘assertio” tam a servitute in libertatem, quam a libertate in servitutem trahi significat (Priscian iii 365, 9). The word is post-Aug. See on Vesp. 3, ingenuam pronuntiatam, patre asserente. Dio (lxvii 13) mentions that Domitian, as censor, restored to his former owner a slave who had been illegally declared freeborn and had risen to be a centurion: Κλαύδιον Πακᾶτον τῷ δεσπότη καίπερ ἑκατονταρχηκότα ἀπέδωκεν, ὅτι ἠλέγχθη δοῦλος ὤν.
: = corruptos "bribed," a Ciceronian word.

: in civil proceedings where the final decision lay with an individual, either as judge (iudex) or arbitrator (arbiter), he brought in a consilium of counsellors or assessors (consiliarii, assessores, cf. Galb. 14, 2) to assist him in arriving at a decision; cf. Cic. Quinct. 2, 10; Q. Rosc. 4, 12; Verr. ii 29, 71; Plin. Εp. v 1; Val. Max. viii 2, 2; Gell. N.A. xii 13, 2: xiv 2,9. See Mommsen, Staatsr. i³ 314.

div.p: § 2. tribunis: the emperor directed the tribunes to bring the indictment for repetundae before the senate, probably because a private accuser could not bring a charge against a magistrate who was in office (Mommsen, ii³ 121). The usual procedure in a cognitio senatus was for the accuser to lodge his complaint with the consuls, and if the case was admitted by them, the matter came before the senate, which formed the high court of criminal judicature under the Empire; cf. Tac. A. ii 28, adit consules, cognitionem senatus poscit: xiii 14, postulatus apud consules a patre interfectae.

p.note: : αἰσχροκερδῆ; cf. Cic. Fam. xiii 36, quosdam sordidos homines qui Caesaris beneficia vendebant: Plin. Ep. iii 9, 2, proconsulatum .. non minus violenter quam sordide gesserat. So sordes is used for low avarice, despicable extortion on the part of a magistrate; e.g. Plin. Ep. ii 12, 4, damnatus sordium: Ven. Sat. Dig. xlviii 11, 6, utque urbani magistratus ab omni sorde se abstineant, neve plus doni muneris in anno accipiant quam quod sit aureorum centum.

: see on Oth. 2, 2. iudices a senatu petendi: in cases of repetundae or peculatus heard before the senate, if the accused was convicted the senate did not itself fix the amount to be refunded (litis aestimatio), but appointed senatorial iudices or reciperatores (usually 3 or 5) for the purpose. Sometimes the case was referred directly to such special commissioners; cf. Tac. A. i 74, de pecuniis repetundis ad reciperatores itum est: Plin. Ep. ii 11, 2, Marius Priscus omissa defensione iudices petiit; iv 9, 16; vi 29, 10. provinciarum praesidibus: see on Vesp. 6, 4.

: for modestia see on Tit. 4, 1. Schiller (Gesch. röm. Kaiserz. i 533) says that Domitian took as his model Tiberius, whose memoirs were his constant reading (Dom. 20), and that with the possible exception of Tiberius no emperor kept his magistrates at home and abroad under stricter discipline. Domitian's careful choice of his officials is praised by Statius, S. v 1, 79: vidit, qui cuncta suorum | novit et inspectis ambit latus omne ministris. His repression of the plundering practised by provincial governors is eulogised by Silius Italicus, Pun. xiv 685: At ni cura viri, qui nunc dedit otia mundo, | effrenum arceret populandi cuncta furorem, | nudassent avidae terrasque fretumque rapinae. Baebius Massa, governor of Hispania Baetica, was prosecuted by Pliny in 93 A.D. on the complaint of the provincials and was convicted of extortion (Plin. Ep. iii 4, vii 33). This is the only known case of provincial accusation during his reign. In later times Domitian was cited as an example of the truth that a bad emperor with good amici is less injurious than a good emperor with bad amici, Trajan being instanced as a good emperor who incurred odium by entrusting the State to unprincipled men (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 65). Among those designated to the consulship by Domitian were Nerva, Trajan, Verginius Rufus, Agricola, and the grandfather of Antoninus Pius (Duruy, op. cit. iv 697 n.). Pliny was quaestor in 90, tribune in 92, praetor in 93; Tacitus was praetor in 88 (H. i 1, dignitatem nostram a Domitiano longius provectam non abnuerim).

: Tib. 33, si qua in publicis moribus desidia aut mala consuetudine labarent, corrigenda suscepit. After his victory over the Chatti in 83 A.D. (c. 6, 1) Domitian took the censorship for life, a unique event in the history of that office; cf. Dio lxvii 4, τιμητὴς δὲ διὰ βίου πρῶτος δὴ καὶ μόνος καὶ ἰδιωτῶν καὶ αὐτοκρατόρων ἐχειροτονήθη. Martial (vi 4, 1) salutes him as "censor maxime, principumque princeps"; cf. Quintilian (iv prooem. 2), Cum vero mihi Domitianus Augustus sororis suae nepotum delegaverit curam, non satis honorem iudiciorum caelestium intelligam, nisi ex hoc oneris quoque magnitudinem metiar. Quis enim mihi aut mores excolendi sit modus, ut eos non immerito probaverit sanctissimus censor? etc. His censorship is also referred to in Juv. iv 11, Sed nunc de factis levioribus, et tamen alter | si fecisset idem, caderet sub iudice morum; in ii 29 sqq. Juvenal bitterly contrasts Domitian's moral ordinances as censor with his scandalously immoral conduct in relation to his niece Julia (see c. 22).

: = inter equites; cf. Claud. 25, 4, in senatu (i.e. among the senators in the orchestra) sedentes. The seats of the knights in the theatre are called by Suet. equestria (c. 4, 5 n.); cf. Calig. 26, 4, describing how Caligula, to foment discord between the plebs and the equites, used to have the tickets for gifts scattered about in the theatre before the appointed time, in order that the rabble might occupy the equestria and a quarrel might ensue when the equites claimed their reserved seats. By the lex Roscia theatralis (67 B.c.) the equites were assigned the 14 rows of seats in the theatre immediately behind the senators' seats in the orchestra. Augustus allowed equites who had been impoverished by the civil wars to sit in the 14 rows, provided that they themselves once had, or their parents had had, the census equester of 400,000 sesterces (Aug. 40, 1). Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 534. Any unqualified person occupying the seats of the equites was liable to a penalty (poena theatralis) and summary ejection by the attendant (designator theatralis). Such ejections are mentioned by Martial as following Domitian's ordinance (88/89 A.D.); e.g. ▼ 8, Edictum domini deique nostri, | quo subsellia certiora fiunt | et puros eques ordines recepit, | dum laudat modo Phasis in theatro, | Phasis purpureis ruber lacernis, | et iactat tumido superbus ore: | “Tandem commodius licet sedere, | nunc est reddita dignitas equestris; | turba non See 2 N premimur neque inquinamur”: | haec et talia dum refert supinus, | illas purpureas et adrogantes | iussit surgere Leitus lacernas.

: libellous verse was punished with the death-penalty under the xii Tables; cf. Cic. Rep. iv 10, 12, nostrae duodecim tabulae cum perpaucas res capite sanxissent in his quoque sanciendum putaverunt si quis occentavisset sive carmen condidisset quod infamiam faceret flagitiumve alteri: Hor. S. ii 1, 82, si mala condiderit in quem quis carmina, ius est | iudiciumque (cf. Ep. ii 1, 152); libel and slander against the leading men of the State were included under maiestas, or treason, by the lex Cornelia maiestatis of Sulla. A cognitio de famosis libellis was first established by Augustus; cf. Tac. A. i 72, primus Augustus cognitionem de famosis libellis specie legis eius (i.e. de maiestate) tractavit, commotus Cassii Severi libidine qua viros feminasque inlustres procacibus scriptis diffamaverat: Suet. Aug. 55: Dio lvi 27. Under Tiberius any writings or spoken words which could be construed as reflecting in any way on the emperor were held to be maiestas and punishable with death. Mayor, on Juv. i 152, gives many examples of writers of pasquils and lampoons who were punished by the emperors.

: prob. "burned"; cf. Tib. 61, 3, animadversum statim in auctores scriptaque abolita (= Tac. A. iv 35, libros per aediles cremandos censuere patres; Dio lvii 24, πρὸς τῶν ἀγορανόμων ἐκαύθη) : Plin. Εp. vii 19, 6, libros [Senecionis] abolitos (= Tac. Agr. 2, in libros [Senecionis] saevitum ut in comitio et foro urerentur).
: Caecilius Rufinus; Dio lxvii 13, ἔπραξε δέ τι καὶ ὡς τιμητὴς (censor) ἀξιόλογον, Καικίλιον γὰρ ῾Ῥουφῖνον ἀπήλασεν ἐκ τοῦ συνεδρίου (senatu movit) ὅτι ὠρχεῖτο. He is not mentioned elsewhere. A

: cf. Ner. 42, 2, iocularia carmina lasciveque modulata, quae vulgo notuerunt, etiam gesticulatus est (i.e. represented in pantomime) : Petron. Satyr. 36, scissor ("carver") ad symphoniam gesticulatus laceravit obsonium. The verb is post-Aug.; Cic. uses agere (facere) gestum. pantomimus in his dances had to depict by his various rhythmical motions and gestures different characters in different situations, generally of a passionate and erotic kind; hence such phrases as "speaking hands" (manus loquacissimae, linguosi digiti, Cassiod. Var. iv 51) and "eloquent dancing'' (saltare diserte, Tac. Dial. 26). A pantomimus is sometimes called gesticulator or gesticularius.

: movere, eiicere, praeterire (in recitando, i.e. at the public reading of the list) were the verbs used for the rejection and omission of senators by the censors. As censor the emperor could remove names from the senate for moral delinquencies, as was done in the old days by the ordinary censors at the lectio senatus; moreover, the revision of the lists of the senate and equites was an admitted right of the Princeps as such; Dio liii 17, καὶ τοὺς μὲν καταλέγουσι καὶ ἐς τὴν ἱππάδα καὶ ἐς τὸ βουλευτικόν, τοὺς δὲ καὶ ἀπαλείφουσιν, ὅπως ἂν αὐτοῖς δόξῃ. See Greenidge, op. cit. 347, 374.

: probrum often means unchastity, lewdness; cf. Iul. 43, 1, (quoted below): Vitell. 4: Tit. 10, 2: Cic. Phil. ii 38, 99, probri insimulasti pudicissimam feminam. Dio (lxvii 12) is sarcastic on Domitian, the adulterer, punishing adultery: συχνοὶ δὲ καὶ ἄνδρες καὶ γυναῖκες τῶν πλουσίων ἐπὶ μοιχείᾳ ἐκολάσθησαν, ὧν ἔνιαι καὶ ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἐμοιχεύθησαν.

: Julius Caesar prohibited the use of the lectica by women who had neither husbands nor children and who were under the age of 45 (Euseb.-Hieron. Chron. p. 137 Schoene); cf. Suet. Iul. 43, 1, Lecticarum usum, item conchyliatae vestis et margaritarum nisi certis personis et aetatibus perque certos dies ademit. One restriction on the use of the lectica was that it was confined to persons of free birth, fòr Suetonius mentions the “ius vehendi lectica per urbem” as one of the special privileges granted by Claudius to his freedman Harpocras (Claud. 28). The wives of senators were carried in a canopied lectica closed with curtains (σκιμπόδιον κατάστεγον, Dio lvii 15). ius capiendi legata ademit: this penalty was copied from that imposed on celibates by the lex Iulia de maritandis ordinibus of Augustus; cf. Gaius ii 111, caelibes qui lege Iulia hereditates legataque capere vetantur. ..

: although Domitian himself had done exactly the same thing in the case of his wife Domitia (see c. 3, 1). Julius Caesar, as a judge, showed a similar moral strictness; cf. Iul. 43, 1, diremit nuptias praetorii viri, qui digressam a marito post biduum statim duxerat, quamvis sine probri (= adulterii) suspicione.

: cf. Claud. 16, 2, non modo albo iudicum erasit, sed in peregrinitatem redegit. The iudices (see on Galb. 14, 3) in a quaestio were selected from an album compiled by the praetor from those qualified to serve. The word album (λεύκωμα) was used originally of the white board or tablet on which magisterial announcements, and especially the praetor's edict, were published; it then came to be used of any list or register, e.g. Tac. A. iv 42, albo senatorio erasit: Suet. Ner. 21, 1, nomen suum in albo profitentium citharoedorum (i.e. the list of competing lyre-players) iussit ascribi.
: senatorio et equestri.

: the lex Scantinia de venere nefanda (anterior to Cicero, but of uncertain date) punished with a fine of 10,000 sesterces (Quintil. iv 2, 69) unnatural offences against ingenui; cf. Cael. ad Cic. Fam. viii 12, 3; 14, 4: Juv. ii 44: Auson. Epigr. 91 (89), 4: Prudent. Peristeph. x 204. Domitian himself was not guiltless of such practices; see Stat. S. iii 4, 37. Dill (Roman Society from Nero to M. Aurelius p. 54) argues that Domitian, in spite of his own delinquencies, may have been sincere in his censorial regimen morum: “A voluptuary, with a calm outlook on his time, may have a wish to restrain vices with which he is himself tainted. A statesman may be a puritan reformer, both in religion and morals, without being personally severe and devout. Domitian may have had a genuine, if a pedantic, desire to restore the old Roman tone in morals and religion. He was, after all, sprung from a sober Sabine stock, although he may have sadly degenerated from it in his own conduct. And his attempt to reform Roman society may perhaps have been as sincere as that of Augustus."

: the Vestal virgins were regarded as daughters of the whole community, and so unchastity in relation to them was as heinous as incest. Their punishment by Domitian is referred to in Stat. S. i 1, 35 (on the equestrian statue of the emperor), ipse . . prospectare videris an tacita vigilet face Troicus ignis | atque exploratas iam laudet Vesta ministras. Dio (lxvii 3) mentions that during the investigation of the charges by the pontiffs (under Domitian as Pontifex Maximus) the 2N2 strain of the proceedings was such that one of the pontiffs, Helvius Agrippa, died suddenly of shock. Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vii 6) says that when news of the fate of the three Vestal virgins reached Ephesus, Apollonius made a public demonstration against Domitian, praying that as Vesta's fire was purified, so the Sun might be purified from the unjust murders with which Domitian was polluting the world.
: even during the censorship of Vespasian and Titus. For quoque = etiam cf. Vitell. 7, 3, n. ..

: the Vestals (Varronilla and the sisters Oculata) condemned in the earlier part of Domitian's reign (83/84 A.D.) were simply sentenced to death and given a choice of deaths; Dio (lxvii 3) says that Domitian prided himself on his clemency in not burying them alive: αὐτὸς δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἠγάλλετο, ὅτι τὰς ἀειπαρθένους ὡς ἠνδρωμένας οὐ κατώρυξεν ἀλλ᾽ ἄλλως ἀποθνήσκειν ἐκέλευσε. Six years later, in the case of Cornelia, he showed no such clemency.

: originally the condemned Vestal was beaten to death with rods, but Tarquinius Priscus introduced an even more awful penalty which continued in force in later times. The doomed culprit was borne like a corpse on a litter to the Campus Sceleratus outside the Colline Gate. She then had to descend into an underground stone cell which was immediately covered over with earth and she was left to a lingering death, having been provided with a little food and a lamp. Sometimes she was scourged before being buried alive, as in the case of Urbinia (Dion. Hal. ix 40). Cf. Plut. Num. 10, Quaest. Rom. 96; Liv. viii 15, 8: xxii 57, 3; Dion. Hal. ii 67, viii 8.

div.p: § 4. relegasset: see on Vesp. 15. This was a light penalty compared with that prescribed by ancient usage for a Vestal's paramours viz. to be beaten to death with rods while hanging on a cross (Mommsen, Strafr. 919).

p.note: : Pliny (Ep. iv 11) describes in a spirit of intense hostility to Domitian the condemnation and execution of Cornelia: Cum Corneliam, Vestalium maximam, defodere vivam concupisset (Domitianus), ut qui inlustrari saeculum suum eiusmodi exemplis arbitraretur, pontificis maximi iure seu potius immanitate tyranni, licentia domini, reliquos pontifices non in Regiam (i.e. the Pontifical palace) sed in Albanam villam convocavit. Nec minore scelere quam quod ulcisci videbatur absentem inauditamque damnavit incesti, cum ipse fratris filiam (i.e. Julia, daughter of Titus) incesto non polluisset solum verum etiam occidisset: nam vidua abortu periit. Missi statim pontifices qui defodiendam necandamque curarent. Illa nunc ad Vestam nunc ad ceteros deos manus tendens, multa, sed hoc frequentissime clamitabat, “me Caesar incestam putat, qua sacra faciente vicit, triumphavit?”” blandiens haec an irridens, ex fiducia sui an ex contemptu principis dixerit dubium est: dixit, donec ad supplicium, nescio an innocens, certe tamquam innocens, ducta est. Quin etiam cum in illud subterraneum cubiculum demitteretur haesissetque descendenti stola, vertit se ac recollegit, cumque ei carnifex manum daret, aversata est et resiluit foedumque contagium quasi plane a casto puroque corpore novissima sanctitate (“with a last display of sanctity'') reiecit, omnibusque numeris pudoris πολλὴν πρόνοιαν ἔσχεν εὐσχήμων πεσεῖν (Eur. Hec. 569, of Polyxena slain at Achilles' tomb).

: the “virgo Vestalis maxima'' (Iul. 83, C.I.L. vi 2127, 2129-2146) acquired the title by age; cf. Ov. F. iv 639, natu maxima virgo: Tac. A. xi 32, virginum Vestalium vetustissima: Dio liv 24, ἡ πρεσβεύουσα. The Vestals, who were six in number, were chosen between the ages of six and ten, and must serve for thirty years, after which they might retire and marry or continue priestesses for life. See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 336 sqq.
: see on repeti, c. 9, 2. stupratores virgis

: cf. Cato (Festus p. 241 M.), probrum virginis Vestalis, ut capite puniretur, vir qui eam incestavisset verberibus necaretur, lex fixa in atrio Libertatis. Pliny (l.c.) mentions only one of the alleged paramours of Cornelia as being thus punished: Celer, eques Romanus, cui Cornelia obiciebatur, cum in Comitio virgis caederetur, in hac voce perstiterat, “quid feci? nihil feci.” Licinianus (see below) was threatened with the same penalty. It is doubtful whether Juvenal (iv 8) means to include Crispinus among the paramours of Cornelia when he says of him: nemo malus felix, minime corruptor et idem | incestus, cum quo nuper vittata iacebat | sanguine adhuc vivo terram subitura sacerdos.

: cf. Liv. xxii 57, 3, L. Cantilius (a minor pontiff), qui cum Floronia (Vestali) stuprum fecerat, a pontifice maximo eo usque virgis in Comitio caesus erat, ut inter verbera expiraret. The Forum Romanum in its extended sense included the Comitium which originally was separated from it by the Rostra and lay to the north-western end of it, under the Capitol, close to the Curia Hostilia. The Comitium was the meeting-place of the comitia curiata, and in it was the tribunal where the praetor urbanus administered justice; cf. Varr. L.L. v 155, Comitium ab eo quod coibant eo comitiis curiatis et litium causâ.

: Valerius Licinianus, whose guilt was very doubtful according to Pliny (l.c.): Confessus est quidem incestum, sed incertum utrum quia verum erat an quia graviora metuebat si negasset. Fremebat enim Domitianus aestuabatque ingenti invidia destitutus (i.e. Domitian could get no one to support him in his odious conviction of Cornelia and Celer). Having described the executions of Cornelia and Celer, Pliny proceeds: Ardebat ergo Domitianus et crudelitatis et iniquitatis infamia. Arripit Licinianum quod in agris suis occultasset Corneliae libertam (whom Domitian wanted as a witness). Ille ab iis quibus erat curae praemonetur, si comitium et virgas pati nollet, ad confessionem confugeret, quasi ad veniam: fecit. Locutus est pro absente (Liciniano) Herennius Senecio tale quiddam quale est illud κεῖται Πάτροκλος (the terse words of Antilochus announcing the death of Patroclus to Achilles, Il. 18, 20). Ait enim “ex advocato nuntius factus sum: Licinianus recessit" (i.e. he offers no defence). Gratum hoc Domitiano, adeo quidem ut gaudio proderetur diceretque "absolvit nos Licinianus” (i.e. by his admission of guilt he clears me from the imputation of injustice). Domitian allowed Licinianus to rescue any effects he could before his goods were confiscated, and gave him an easy place of exile as a reward. Nerva transferred him to Sicily, where he was a professor of rhetoric at the time Pliny wrote. Henderson, Five Roman Emperors p. 15, says: “Much pity has recently been lavished upon the Vestal Cornelia, whom Domitian commanded to be buried alive, more maiorum, for incest. Pliny indeed inclines to believe her innocent, and declares that the Emperor condemned her to her ghastly doom unheard. His contemporary Suetonius has no doubt of her guilt, neither did any later Emperor recall her supposed paramour from exile."

: though a quaestio did not necessarily involve tormenta, the two generally went together; e.g. Calig. 32, 1, saepe in conspectu prandentis vel comissantis seriae quaestiones per tormenta habebantur: Claud. 34, 1, tormenta quaestionum repraesentabat. So quaestio is used in the sense of tormenta; e.g. Dom. 10, 5, novo quaestionis genere distorsit: Aug. 19, 2, nihil exprimi quaestione potuit. •
: profiteri indicium was the phrase for turning informer; Licinianus admitted his own guilt. Suetonius only uses -met with the reflexive pronoun (cf. sibimet, Vesp. 20).

: Plin. (l.c.), exilium molle velut praemium dedit. For the constr., which is post-Aug., cf. Claud. 24, 1, ornamenta consularia procuratoribus indulsit: Dom. 11, 3, ut damnatis liberum mortis arbitrium indulgeatis: Aug. 41, 1, usum eius (pecuniae) gratuitum iis indulsit.

div.p: § 5. templo Capitolini Iovis: see c. 5.

p.note: : see on c. 3, 1. Suetonius is referring to the period when Domitian, being little more than eighteen years of age, began his public career at Rome after the victory of Vespasian's forces over the Vitellians at the end of 69. See c. 1, 3.
: Stahr cites as a parallel the case of Robespierre, who in his youth could not bear the sight of blood and was a vehement opponent of the death-penalty.
: Vespasian did not arrive at Rome from Alexandria before the late summer or the autumn of 70.

: Georg. ii 536, Ante etiam sceptrum Dictaei regis (= Iovis) et ante | impia quam caesis gens est epulata iuvencis, | aureus hanc vitam in terris Saturnus agebat. To slay the ox, the fellow-labourer of the husbandman, was in primitive times an impiety to be punished with death; cf. Varr. R.R. ii 5, (Bos) socius hominum in rustico opere et Cereris minister; ab hoc antiqui manus ita abstineri voluerunt, ut capite sanxerint, siquis occidisset: Cic. N.D. ii 63, 159, quibus (bubus) cum terrae subigerentur fissione glaebarum, ab illo aureo genere, ut poetae loquuntur, vis nulla umquam afferebatur: “Ferrea tum vero proles exorta repente est | ausaque funestum prima est fabricarier ensem | et gustare manu vinctum domitumque iuvencum.” Tanta putabatur utilitas percipi e bubus, ut eorum visceribus vesci scelus haberetur. (Cicero's verses are a translation of Arat. Phaen. 129 sqq.) The same view is expressed in Ov. M. xv 120 sqq.; Plin. N.H. viii 45; Colum. vi praef.

: = contra, e contrario; cf. Iul. 86, 2, alii e diverso opinantur: Aug. 27, 2. In Virg., Liv., Vell. Pat., Quintil., etc., ex diverso means "from the opposite quarter," "on the opposite side," in which sense Pliny (N.H. iv 9) and Justin (xxx 4, 6) have e diverso, but Pliny elsewhere (cf. Sillig on N.H. xiv 35) always has e diverso with the same meaning as it has in Suetonius. See Thes. Ling. Lat. v 1585; Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 424.
: see on "abstinuit,” Tit. 7, 3.

div.p: § 2. circa: see on Tit. 4, 3. For prosecutus see on Tit. 2.

p.note: : used here of meanness in spending money, as in Ner. 30, 1, sordidos ac deparcos esse quibus impensarum ratio constaret; in c. 8, 2 it is used of meanness in exacting money.

: legacies from those who had children were refused also by Hadrian (Spart. Hadr. 18), Antoninus Pius (Capitol. Pius 8), and Pertinax (id. Pert. 7). Augustus, though valuing highly legacies from his friends, observed the same rule: Aug. 66, 4, legata vel partes hereditatium, a quibuscumque parentibus relicta sibi, aut statim liberis eorum concedere, aut si pupillari aetate essent, die virilis togae vel nuptiarum cum incremento restituere consuerat. The practice of Tiberius is described in Tac. A. ii 48: neque hereditatem cuiusquam adiit nisi cum amicitia meruisset: ignotos et aliis infensos eoque principem nuncupantes procul arcebat. Caligula insisted on being included in wills, and then, when through terror strangers named him as heir among their intimates, and parents among their children, he said that they were mocking him by not dying, and sent poisoned cakes to many (Calig. 38, 2). Nero ordered that the estates of those who were "ungrateful to their emperor (by leaving him nothing) should belong to the privy purse (Ner. 32, 2; cf. Tac. A. xiv 31, xvi 11). Domitian in his later days was grasping of legacies and claimed the estates of total strangers (see c. 12, 2). Tacitus (Agr. 43) mentions the will of Agricola “quo coheredem optimae uxori et piissimae filiae Domitianum scripsit," and says that Domitian was pleased by the compliment, his mind being so blinded by constant flatteries “ut nescireť a bono patre non scribi heredem nisi malum principem.”

: not mentioned elsewhere. The MSS. have rusci (so Preud'homme Rusci), but Torrentius rightly introduced Rusti, the form of the name attested by inscriptions (e.g. C.I.L. vi 2222) in the case of some others of the gens Rustia.

: cavere or testamento cavere was the regular expression used of providing for something by will; e.g. Cic. Fin. ii 103, dico magis fuisse vestrum agere ("to celebrate'") Epicuri diem natalem quam illius testamento cavere ut ageretur.

: two interpretations have been suggested, of which the first seems the more probable: (1) that a sum was to be given as a New Year's gift (strena) to all the senators every year when they entered the senate-house for the first time (so Burman and Bremi); (2) that a sum was to be given to each new senator when he first entered the senate-house (so Baumg.-Cr.). Mommsen (Staatsr. iii³ 895, n. 1) says that though such gifts were usual in the municipia, Domitian regarded them as lowering the dignity of the senate at Rome.
: the usual word for the payment of legacies; so the subst. praestatio, e.g. Paul. Dig. xxxii 98, heredes legatorum praestatione onerare.

: reos is generally explained as State debtors, but Casaubon and Ernesti seem right in taking it as accused persons of any kind; cf. Aug. 32, 2, where Suetonius mentions the remissions granted by Augustus, which included (1) the burning of all the records of old debts due to the Treasury: tabulas veterum aerarii debitorum, vel praecipuam calumniandi materiam, exussit; (2) the striking out of the names of all those who had long been under accusation without being tried: diuturnorum reorum et ex quorum sordibus (i.e. the mourning garb worn by rei) nihil aliud quam voluptas inimicis quaereretur nomina abolevit, condicione proposita, ut si quem quis repetere vellet, par periculum poenae subiret (i.e. the reviver of the charge, if he failed in his case, was to be liable to the same penalty as the accused would have to pay if he were convicted). The tabulae publicae containing the lists of accused persons, whose cases had not been tried, but whose names had been given in to the magistrates, were hung up in the aerarium, which was the record-office where were lodged all laws, decrees, acta of the magistrates, etc. (Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 546). In the aerarium were also posted the names of defaulters against whom the Treasury officials were proceeding to extremes: cf. Claud. 9, 2, ut, cum obligatam aerario fidem liberare non posset, in vacuum lege praediatoria venalis pependerit sub edicto praefectorum (i.e. the edictum announcing the sale of the securities was hung in the aerarium). Caligula wiped out arrears of criminal charges which remained untried when he became emperor: Calig. 15, 4, criminum, si quae residua ex priore tempore manebant, omnium gratiam fecit. The bona damnatorum went to the fiscus: see on Vesp. 16, 3.
: proximus was used of what is nearest in time, not merely in the future, but also in the past (Iul. 83, 1; Aug. 101, 3; Cic. Cat. i 1, etc.).

: repetere was the term used by the jurists for reviving an accusation; cf. Aug. 32, 2 (quoted above): Dom. 8, 4, Corneliam absolutam olim, dein longo intervallo repetitam convictamque. Both repetere reum and repetere crimen are found. causam causâ cadere.
: the regular phrase for winning a case, opp. to

div.p: § 3. scribas quaestorios: see on Vesp. 3. The quaestors referred to here are primarily those attached to the provincial governors (Mommsen, Staatsr. i 336, n. 3). Cicero lays great stress on the fact that the old Romans forbade any buying on the part of provincial governors “quod putabant ereptionem esse non emptionem, cum venditori suo arbitratu vendere non liceret” (Verr. ii 4, 5).

p.note: : nothing definite is known of this law. It may have been one of the many plebiscita of Publius Clodius in his tribuneship, 58 в.с. (Mommsen, l.c.). The old and very improbable view was that it is the lex Claudia de senatoribus, a plebiscitum of 218 B.c. directed against trading by senators, which forbade any senator or senator's son to own a ship of larger cubic capacity than 300 amphorae (Liv. xxi 63); Cicero says that in his time this law was "antiqua et mortua” (Verr. v 18, 45).

: these were oddments of land which were left over when a territory was portioned out to the colonies of veterans planted in Italy by Sulla, Julius Caesar, and the early emperors. These oddments had been usurped by the local communities or neighbouring holders, though they formed part of the ager publicus, the property of the State. Vespasian proceeded to reclaim and sell these subsiciva to aid the fiscus, but deputations came urging the upheaval occasioned by this disturbance of existing occupations (quassabatur universus Italiae possessor), and Vespasian suspended the sale; Titus proceeded anew with it, and later Domitian issued his edict securing possession to the existing occupiers of the subsiciva. For this conversion of these squatters' tenure into proprietorship see Heitland, Agricola p. 272.

: as if usucapio, or prescriptive right to a property by undisputed possession for a certain period, were legally possible in the case of illegal usurpers of State property; cf. Just. Inst. ii 6, 9, res fisci nostri usucapi non potest.

: this concession is often mentioned in the extracts from the Gromatici or Agrimensores; e.g. Siculus Flaccus De condicione agrorum p. 163, Non enim omnis ager centuriatus in assignationem cecidit, sed et multa vacua relicta sunt, quorum ea condicio est, quae subsicivorum; de quibus Domitianus finem statuit, id est, possessoribus ea concessit (a centuria was a square of land, 240 rods each way, containing 100 lots, originally of two iugera; any of the ager centuriatus not assigned would be in the same position as subsiciva): p. 284, quae cum vel communis iuris, aut publici essent, possessionibus vicinis tunc Domitianus imperator profudit: Frontinus, De controversiis agrorum p. 54, aeque et Titus imperator aliqua subsiciva in Italia recollegit: praestantissimus postea Domitianus ad hoc beneficium procurrit, et uno edicto totius Italiae metum liberavit: Hyginus, De controv. p. 133, Domitianus per totam Italiam subsiciva possidentibus donavit, edictoque hoc notum universis fecit. As early in his reign as July 82 Domitian had decided a dispute about subsiciva on the same principle which he afterwards embodied in his edict (C.I.L. ix 5420; Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2554). Augustus dealt in the same way with places in Rome which could not be clearly proved to be public or private property: Aug. 32, 2, loca in urbe publica iuris ambigui possessoribus adiudicavit.

: calumnia, which denoted legal chicanery of any kind, was specially used of false accusations and vexatious prosecutions; see Vitell. 7, 2. The delatores (Tit. 8, 5, n.) throve by giving information about property that might be claimed for the fiscus or imperial money-chest (Vesp. 16, 3, n.), and by promoting accusations which, if successful, would enable the fiscus to seize the property of the accused. In Ner. 32, 1 Suetonius tells us that Nero resorted to calumniae as a means of raising money. calumniae also occurred very frequently in connexion with the aerarium or public treasury; cf. Aug. 32, 2 (quoted above). On the subject of delationes fiscales and the property which could legally be claimed by the fiscus see Dig. xlix c. 14, entitled De iure fisci; also Cod. Iust. x 11 (De delationibus) containing rescripts of various emperors on the malpractices of the delatores.

: contrast c. 12, where we find every kind of accusations by delatores eagerly seized on by Domitian as grounds for his later extortions. For the attitude of earlier emperors towards delatores see on Tit. 8, 5. ferebatur vox eius: Dio (lxvii 1) says that Domitian used the words in an edict: τῇ δ᾽ αὐτῇ ταύτῃ διανοίᾳ καὶ προέγραψέ ποτε, ὅτι αὐτοκράτωρ ὅταν μὴ κολάζῃ τοὺς συκοφάντας, αὐτός σφας ποιεῖ τοιούτους. The form of Domitian's maxim recalls Seneca's Qui non vetat peccare, cum possit, iubet. Another saying of Domitian's was that those emperors who did not inflict punishment on many were not good emperors, but only fortunate (Dio lxvii 2). Paridis: see on c. 3, 1.
: so the Basle ed. of 1533; the MSS. have puberem.

: "at that very time"; only here in Suetonius, though in Tib. 14, 2, Thrasyllum mathematicum.. tum maxime expertus est (= tum expertus est maxime) there is a variant cum for tum. The words cum maxime frequently follow tum or nunc to emphasize them; e.g. Cic.
