Sen. 38, пипс сит тaxime conficio orationes (= cum maxime conficio orationes, nunc conficio "the time when I most of all compose is now," Reid ad loc.). Then cum maxime came to be used absolutely to express tum or nunc in a more emphatic fashion; so in Cicero, e.g. Verr. iv 38, 82, qui сит топиmenta rerum suarum cum maxime (= nunc) constituat: in Livy, e.g. xxix 17, 20, omnia quae captae urbes patiuntur passi sumus et cum maximé patimur: in Tacitus, e.g. H. i 29, ut qui adversas res expertus cum maxime ("at this moment'") discam ne secundas quidem minus discriminis habere. See also Hand Turs. iii 599 sqq., Kühner-Stegmann, ii 480. Düpow (op. cit. p. 17) wrongly explains cum maxime aegrum here as meaning "im höchsten Grade krank."
: see on Oth. 1, 2.

: there is no means of fixing this historian; he may be the Hermogenes (of uncertain date) who wrote a mythological account of Phrygia of which a few fragments have been preserved (see Müller, Frag. Hist. Graec. iii 523 sq.). The famous rhetorician Hermogenes of Tarsus lived later, as he declaimed at the age of 15 before the emperor M. Aurelius (161-180 A.D.).
: "satirical allusions," "indirect attacks"; see on Vesp. 13, causidicorum figuras lenissime tulit.

: slaves employed to copy books (scriptor librarius, Hor. A.P. 354). The author either had a sufficient number of copies produced for publication by his own librarii, or else he gave his work to an editor who published it for him. For the different classes of librarii see Marquardt, Privatl. 825 sqq. Stahr mentions as a parallel to the punishment of the librarii of Hermogenes the practice which obtains in many modern countries of punishing the printer as well as the author and publisher of a book that is condemned.

: cruci figere is post-Aug.; earlier we find cruci suffigere (Cic., cf. Suet. Iul. 74, 1) and cruci adfigere (Plaut., Liv.). Suetonius also uses cruce adficere (Galb. 9, 1); in crucem agere (Calig. 12, 2).

: a plain, ordinary citizen; cf. Cic. de or. i 132, Sicut unus paterfamilias (= unus e togatorum numero, i 111) his de rebus loquor: i 159, effudi vobis omnia quae sentiebam, quae fortasse, quemcumque patremfamilias adripuissetis ex aliquo circulo, eadem vobis percontantibus respondisset.
: for these two kinds of gladiators and their different equipment see on Tit. 8, 2, where the partiality of Titus for the Thraeces is described..

: the giver of the munus or gladiatorial show, i.e. Domitian himself. The point of the remark was that the Thraex, though a match for the murmillo, was not a match for him when backed by the favour of Domitian with whom the decision lay. Quintilian (viii 3, 34) says that the word munerarius was a coinage of Augustus: Quae vetera nunc sunt, fuerunt olim nova, et quaedam sunt in usu perquam recentia, ut Messala primus “reatum,””‘“munerarium” Augustus primus dixerunt. Florus (iii 20, 9) has munerator in this sense; later writers use editor.

: cf. Calig. 35, 3, hunc spectaculis detractum repente et in harenam deductum Thraeci comparavit ("matched him against'"). For spectacula in the sense of subsellia spectatorum cf. Plaut. Curc. 645, spectacula ruunt: Cic. Sest. 58, 124, ex omnibus spectaculis plausus est excitatus: Tac. A. xiv 13, exstructos spectaculorum gradus ("tiers"). It was also used = locus quo spectacula eduntur; e.g. Aug. 58, 1, ineunti (Augusto) Romae spectacula.
: among the offenders whom Caligula threw to the wild beasts were those who criticized his shows (male de munere suo opinatos, Calig. 27, 3).

: a label was hung from his neck, like the titulus on the neck of a slave exposed for sale which stated any special aptitudes, physical defects, previous misconduct, etc. (cf. Plin. Ep. v 19, Gell. N.A. iv 2, Prop. iv 5, 51, quorum titulus per barbara colla pependit). Sometimes a titulus stating his offence was carried before a malefactor as a placard; cf. Calig. 32, 2, Romae publico epulo servum ob detractam lectis argenteam laminam carnifici confestim tradidit, ut manibus abscisis atque ante pectus e collo pendentibus, praecedente titulo qui causam poenae indicaret, per coetus epulantium circumduceretur.

: impietas (ἀσέβεια, Dio) was synonymous with maiestas, lèsemajesté, high treason; cf. Tac. A. vi 47, defertur impietatis in principет. See on "pietas,” Vitell. 3, 1. Domitian claimed to be a deus (c. 13, 2). The incident in the amphitheatre is referred to in Plin. Pan. 33 (contrasting Trajan with Domitian): Iam, quam libera spectantium studia, quam securus favor! Nemini impietas, ut solebat, obiecta, quod odisset gladiatorem: nemo, e spectatore spectaculum factus, miseras voluptates unco et ignibus expiavit. Demens ille, verique honoris ignarus, qui crimina maiestatis in arena colligebat, ac se despici et contemni, nisi etiam gladiatores eius veneraremur, sibi male dici in illis, suam divinitatem, suum numen violari interpretabatur: cum se idem quod Deos, idem gladiatores quod se putabat. used the parma or Martial, to please

: an adherent of the Thraeces who parmula, a small round shield (see on Tit. 8, 2). Domitian, disparages the Thraeces and their infrequent victories: xiv 213, Haec quae saepe solet vinci, quae vincere raro, | parma tibi scutum pumilionis erit: ix 68, 7, Mitior in magno clamor furit amphitheatro | vincenti parmae cum sua turba favet. Marcus Aurelius (Comm. i 5) prides himself on his impartiality between the two kinds of shield in the arena and the two colours in the circus, he having been taught to be μήτε πρασιανὸς (= prasinus “green”) μήτε βενετιανός (= venetus "blue"), μήτε παλμουλάριος (parmularius) ἢ σκούταριος (scutarius, the scutum being carried by murmillones). Quintilian (ii 11, 2) tells of a rhetorician more interested in gladiators than in his own art, who, when asked whether he was a follower of Theodorus or Apollodorus (founders of different schools of rhetoric), replied that it was the Thraeces whom he followed: Alius percontanti, Theodoreus an Apollodoreus esset? Ego, inquit, parmularius sum.

div.p: § 2. complures senatores interemit: cf. Dio lxvii 3, 11, 12: Eutrop. vii 23, 2, interfecit nobilissimos e senatu: Oros. vii 10, 2, nobilissimos e senatu invidiae simul et praedae causa alios palam interfecit alios in exilium trusit ibique trucidari imperavit: Plin. Pan. 48, domo, quam nuper illa immanissima belua (Domitian) plurimo terrore munierat, cum nunc propinquorum sanguinem lamberet, nunc se ad clarissimorum civium strages caedesque proferret: Juv. iv 151, tempora saevitiae, claras quibus abstulit urbi | inlustresque animas impune et vindice nullo. Tacitus (Agr. 44) says that Domitian's savagery reached its climax in the years after Agricola's death (93 A.D.): postremum illud tempus, quo Domitianus non iam per intervalla ac spiramenta temporum, sed continuo et velut uno ictu rem publicam exhausit.

p.note: : this is the C. Vettulenus Civica Cerealis mentioned in a military diploma (Dessau 1995) as legatus of Moesia in 82 A.D. He was put to death by Domitian while he held the proconsulship of Asia (c. 88 A.D.); cf. Tac. Agr. 42, where his fate is referred to as furnishing a warning to Agricola not to accept the proconsulship when his turn came: Aderat iam annus, quo proconsulatum Africae et Asiae sortiretur, et occiso Civica nuper nec Agricolae consilium deerat nec Domitiano exemplum (i.e. a precedent for doing away with Agricola).

: consul (suffectus) under the Flavians, year unknown. Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vii 8 and 33, viii 7) says that Apollonius of Tyana, when he appeared before Domitian on the charge of conspiracy, maintained that Orfitus was just and temperate, averse from wealth, sluggish by nature, and no more capable of revolutionary designs than Apollonius' friend Nerva, the future emperor, who also was suspected by Domitian of intriguing against him. Orfitus and Rufus (who was alleged to be a fellow-conspirator) were banished to islands. Nerva was commanded to dwell at Tarentum. Apollonius was acquitted. Ser. Cornelius Scipio Salvidienus Orfitus, consul in 51, executed by Nero (Ner. 37), was probably the father of the (Ser. Cornelius Scipio) Salvidienus Orfitus mentioned here; and two consuls of the same name in 110 and 149 were probably his son and grandson.

: Manius Acilius Glabrio, who was consul along with Trajan in 91 A.D. The same portents appeared to them when they entered upon the consulship, predicting destruction for Glabrio but empire for Trajan (Dio lxvii 12). Glabrio's premature death is referred to in Juv. iv 94 sqq., where he is mentioned as hastening along with his father (aged about 80) to Domitian's consilium at his Alban fortress: properabat Acilius | cum iuvene (= filio) indigno, quem mors tam saeva maneret | et domini gladiis tam festinata. On the occasion of the Iuvenalia Domitian compelled him, though consul, to fight as a venator against a huge lion in the amphitheatre at the arx Albana; Glabrio dexterously despatched the lion, and according to Dio (lxvii 14) it was chiefly Domitian's jealousy of his skill in the arena which led to his exile and then to his death in 95 A.D. That Glabrio was also charged with "impiety" in the form of Judaism or Christianity seems a necessary inference from the words of Dio, who, after mentioning that several, including Flavius Clemens (see с. 15, 1), were condemned on this charge, goes on to say: τὸν δὲ δὴ Γλαβρίωνα . . . κατηγορηθέντα τά τε ἄλλα καὶ οἷα οἱ πολλοὶ καὶ ὅτι καὶ θηρίοις ἐμάχετο, ἀπέκτεινεν. See von Rohden in Pauly-Wissowa, i 267. Hardy (Studies in Rom. Hist. p. 67) says: “archaeological discoveries have now established the fact that the family of the Acilii Glabriones were buried in a crypt, the centre of a series of catacombs clustered round the tomb of some saint or martyr, whom, considering the evidence of Dio Cassius, it is not altogether rash to identify with the Acilius Glabrio of Domitian." Cf. Ramsay, The Church in the Roman Empire p. 262.
: causal, see on Tit. 5, 1.

: though Suetonius uses the phrase res novas moliri several times (e.g. Galb. 11, Dom. 7, 3), he only uses the subst. molitor here; he coins a fem. molitrix in Ner. 35, 4, Antoniam Claudi filiam quasi molitricem novarum rerum interemit. For molitor cf. Sen. Tranq. 7, maximorum molitores scelerum: Tac. A. xi 29, Appianae caedis molitor Narcissus: Cic. Univ. 5, effector mundi molitorque Deus.
: whose wife (Domitia Longina) Domitian took away and married; see c. 1, 3.
: Domitian himself may have praised Lamia's voice, or someone else in the presence of Domitian.

: i.e. εὐτακτῶ, disciplinam servo, continenter vivo, Venere abstineo. Gronovius correctly explained the jest of Lamia: "Non mirari te oportet me bene canere: servo enim disciplinam: et, ut servare possim, tu fecisti uxore abducta"; he aptly cites Aelian, V.H. iii 30, ᾿Αμοιβεὺς ὁ κιθαρῳδὸς σωφρονέστατος ἐλέγετο καὶ γυναῖκα ὡραιοτάτην ἔχων μὴ ὁμιλεῖν αὐτῇ. For εὐτακτεῖν of obeying a trainer's regulations cf. Epictet. Ench. xxix 2, θέλεις Ὀλύμπια νικῆσαι; . δεῖ σ' εὐτακτεῖν, ἀναγκοτροφεῖν, κ.τ.λ. A trainer for singing and declamation was called phonascus (φωνασκός), e.g. Aug. 84, 2; Ner. 25, 3. μὴ καὶ σὺ γαμῆσαι θέλεις ; : Lamia's first wife had been carried off by Domitian, and so he sarcastically suggests that Titus, in recommending him to marry again, was looking forward to carrying off the second wife as his bride.

div.p: § 3. Salvium Cocceianum: his full name was Lucius Salvius Otho Cocceianus (C.I.L. vi 2002; Plutarch, Oth. 16, erroneously calls him Κοκκήιος); he was the son of L. Salvius Otho Titianus, who was brother of the emperor Otho (see Oth. 1, 3, n.). Tacitus (H. ii 48) describes how Otho on the eve of his suicide comforted his nephew Salvius Cocceianus, concluding with the words "proinde erecto animo capesseret vitam neu patruum sibi Othonem fuisse aut oblivisceretur umquam aut nimium meminisset." Cf. Plut. l.c., Suet. Oth. 10, 2. Cocceianus neglected this wise advice, and the suspicious mind of Domitian interpreted the nephew's celebrations of his dead uncle's birthday as a sign that he too was cherishing hopes of empire.

p.note: : April 28; see Oth. 2, 1. The birthday of Julius Caesar became a State festival after his death (Dio xlvii 18). Dio mentions the celebrations of the birthdays of the emperors Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Vitellius, Titus, Hadrian, Commodus, Severus, and Geta; such celebrations being doubtless continued after their death in so far as they were not specially forbidden. Domitian forbade memorial games on the birthday of Titus (Dio lxvii 2); so too Caracalla in the case of Geta (Dio lxxvii 12). See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 268, n. 10.

: for the different way in which Vespasian treated Pompusianus and his imperatoria genesis see Vesp. 14. Dio (lxvii 12) says that Domitian first banished him to Corsica and afterwards put him to death.

: the indic. is used, though quod circumferret, quodque..indidisset follows, because it is a compressed form of expression representing quod, ut ferebatur (ferebant), haberet imperatoriam genesim; see on quod constabat, Tit. 7, 1. In giving the reasons for the different executions the construction varies between the indie. (quod dixerat, quodque responderat, quod celebraverat) and the subjunct. (in this and the following clauses); the indic. expressing the writer's statements of facts, the subjunct. expressing the considerations actuating Domitian (Trachmann, op. cit. p. 26).

: Dio (lxvii 12) describes the map which Pompusianus had, not as a portable parchment, but as a painting on the walls of his bed-chamber (τὴν οἰκουμένην ἐν τοῖς τοῦ κοιτῶνος τοίχοις εἶχεν ἐγγεγραμμένην). It would be a general map of the world such as those referred to in Prop. iv 3, 37, Cogor et e tabulis pictos ediscere mundos, and Vitruv. viii 2, 6, capita fluminum, quae orbe terrarum chorographiis picta itemque scripta inveniuntur. Maps were frequently painted on the walls of porticoes; e.g. the map of Italy in the temple of Tellus at Rome (Varr. R.R. i 2), and the map of the Roman Empire painted (7 A.D.) in the portico of Polla, sister of Agrippa, at Rome (Plin. N.H. iii 3, Dio lv 8). Pompusianus was not put to death merely for having a map in his possession, but for using it to aid his alleged treasonable designs by studying the points at which the Empire could best be attacked, or by acquiring a knowledge which would be essential to him when emperor. contiones. ex Tito Livio: Quintilian praises Livy as “in contionibus supra quam enarrari potest eloquens” (x 1, 101); he also recommends to the orator the study of the contiones in the historians (iii 8, 67). Twice elsewhere Suetonius mentions Livy, telling us that he encouraged the youthful Claudius to write a history (Claud. 41, 1), and that Caligula was very near removing his writings and busts from all the libraries, censuring him as a long-winded and careless historian: ut verbosum in historia neglegentemque carpebat (Calig. 34, 2).

: the Carthaginian general Mago, son of Hamilcar Barca, was the youngest brother of Hannibal and accompanied him in the Carthaginian invasion of Italy in 218 B.C. at the beginning of the second Punic war.

: the name appears as C. Sallustius Lucullus in a spurious inscription, Eph. Epigr. vii 1185.* He was one of the successors of Agricola as legatus of Britain, for the predecessors of Agricola are named by Tacitus, and so his command must have been at some period between 84 (when Agricola left Britain) and 96 (when Domitian died). The reason given by Suetonius for his execution was probably only a part of a more general charge of inciting the army in Britain to revolt from Domitian.

: Domitian may have thought that these lances should have been called after him as head of the army (Bremi). For the naming of weapons after individuals cf. Δρουσιανὰ ξίφη (Dio lvii 13; see note on "ferramenta,” Tit. 9, 2). Iphicrates, an Athenian general, invented a new sort of military boots or leggings called after him ᾿Ιφικρατίδες.

: Quintus (?) Iunius Arulenus Rusticus was an unflinching adherent of the Stoic school and a pupil of Thrasea Paetus. As tribunus plebis in '66 A.D. he wished to use his veto (intercessio) on the senate's condemnation of Thrasea, but Thrasea forbade him, as it would not save his life and it would involve the death of Rusticus (Tac. A. xvi 26, where Rusticus is described as a flagrans iuvenis, actuated “cupidine laudis''). He was praetor in 69, and was one of the envoys sent by Vitellius and the senate to the forces of Vespasian which were advancing on Rome, but they received him with derision and even wounded him (Tac. H. iii 80; cf. Vitell. 16). In 93 he was condemned by the senate for treason to Domitian and was executed. The younger Pliny was a warm admirer of his (see Ep. i 14, ii 18, iii 11). For the difficulty in determining his praenomen see Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii 233. Both Tacitus and Pliny call him Rusticus Arulenus or Arulenus Rusticus or simply Rusticus.

: P. Clodius Thrasea Paetus, who took the younger Cato as a model (cf. Plut. Cat. min. 25, 37), put his Stoical principles into practice by the stubborn opposition which he offered in the senate to Nero's tyrannous conduct. He was consul (suffectus) in 56. In 63 he was excluded from the receptions of Nero, and for the next three years he took no part in public life; his retirement, however, did not placate Nero's animosity, and in 66, after the conspiracy of Piso and the many executions which followed it, Nero 'aspired to extirpate Virtue itself” (virtutem ipsam exscindere concupivit) by putting to death Thrasea Paetus and his friend Barea Soranus (Tac. A. xvi 21). Thrasea was condemned for treason, and was only allowed to choose the manner of his death. Tacitus enumerates the various charges brought against him at his trial; Suetonius (Ner. 37, 1) says that Nero charged him with having a "dour and pedagogic look” (tristior et paedagogi vultus). The full form of his name was learned from a tablet found at Pompeii (Mommsen, Hermes xii 128).

: son-in-law of Thrasea Paetus; for his career and character see on Vesp. 15. If the text here is sound, Suetonius seems inaccurate in attributing the panegyric on him to Junius Rusticus, for Tacitus, Pliny, and Dio say that it was composed by Herennius Senecio: Tac. Agr. 2, Legimus, cum Aruleno Rustico Paetus Thrasea, Herennio Senecioni Priscus Helvidius laudati essent, capitale fuisse, neque in ipsos modo auctores, sed in libros quoque eorum saevitum, delegato triumviris (capitalibus) ministerio ut monumenta clarissimorum ingeniorum in comitio ac foro urerentur: Plin. Ep. vii 19, cum Senecio reus esset, quod de vita Helvidi libros composuisset: Dio lxvii 13, τὸν γὰρ δὴ ῾Ρούστικον τὸν ᾿Αρουλῆνον ἀπέκτεινεν (ὁ Δομιτιανός) ὅτι ἐφιλοσόφει καὶ ὅτι τὸν Θρασέαν ἱερὸν (= sanctissimum, Suet.) ὠνόμαζε, καὶ ῾Ερέννιον Σενεκίωνα... ὅτι τοῦ Πρίσκου τοῦ ῾Ἑλουιδίου τὸν βίον συνέγραψεν. Macé (Suétone, p. 413) proposed to insert Herennium Senecionem quod before Helvidi, and to read the pl. edidissent appellassentque, thinking that the copyist jumped from HErennium to HElvidi, and that later a corrector changed the verbs to the sing. in agreement with the only subject which was left. Janssen would force the text into meaning that Rusticus wrote a biography of Thrasea Paetus and not of Helvidius Priscus, but that in this biography he described both of them as sanctissimi viri.

: Dio (l.c.), ἄλλοι τε ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς ταύτης τῆς κατὰ τὴν φιλοσοφίαν αἰτίας συχνοὶ διώλοντο, καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ πάντες ἐξηλάθησαν αὖθις ἐκ τῆς ῾Ρώμης: Tac. (l.c.), Scilicet illo igne (i.e. the burning of the panegyrics on Thrasea Paetus and Helvidius Priscus) vocem populi Romani et libertatem senatus et conscientiam generis humani aboleri arbitrabantur, expulsis insuper sapientiae professoribus atque omni bona arte in exilium acta, ne quid usquam honestum occurreret. This expulsion of philosophers took place in 93 A.D. Pliny (Ep. iii 11) describes the risks which he as praetor incurred in that year (cum essent philosophi ab urbe summoti) by lending aid to the philosopher Artemidorus: atque haec feci, cum septem amicis meis aut occisis aut relegatis, occisis Senecione, Rustico, Helvidio, relegatis Maurico, Gratilla, Arria, Fannia, tot circa me iactis fulminibus quasi ambustus mihi quoque impendere idem exitium certis quibusdam notis augurarer. Among those banished was Epictetus, "That halting slave, who in Nicopolis Taught Arrian, when Vespasian's brutal son Cleared Rome of what most shamed him" (M. Arnold). The Armenian version of Eusebius (p. 160, Schoene) dates the expulsion correctly in the year Oct. 92-Sept. 93; Hieronymus puts it two years later (94–95) ‘“Domitianus rursum philosophos et mathematicos Roma per edictum extrusit," and mentions an earlier expulsion by Domitian, not known otherwise, in the year Oct. 88-Sept. 89 ‘mathematicos et philosophos Romanos urbe pepulit,” which Furneaux-Anderson on Tac. l.c. suggest may arise from a confusion with the expulsion under Vespasian (see on Vesp. 13) or may indicate that a number of philosophers and astrologers were charged with complicity in the revolt of L. Antonius Saturninus on the Rhine (Dom. 6, 2). words ἐξηλάθησαν αὖθις in Dio (l.c.) seem to imply some earlier expulsion by Domitian, and Janssen surmises that in 88-89 they were expelled from Rome, in 93-95 from Italy. The

div.p: § 4. Helvidium filium: this Helvidius (Priscus), whose praenomen and cognomen do not occur, was a son of Helvidius Priscus (see above) and a stepson of Fannia. Pliny (Ep. ix 13) says that he lived in retirement owing to the perils of the times (metu temporum nomen ingens, pares virtutes secessu tegebat). Pliny speaks of him as consularis and he may have been consul suffectus in Sept. 87 (Mommsen). When he was accused by Domitian, the servile senate condemned him and even dragged him to prison (nostrae duxere Helvidium in carcerem manus, Tac. Agr. 45). After Domitian's death Pliny impeached Publicius Certus, a senator of praetorian rank, who had been the principal supporter of the delatores against Helvidius and had laid violent hands on Helvidius in the senate. Certus escaped by a death so opportune as to suggest suicide, and Pliny afterwards published his speech de ultione Helvidi, which was modelled on that of Demosthenes against Meidias (Ep. vii 30, cf. iv 21).

p.note: : causal, see on Tit. 5, 1.

: exodium (ἐξόδιον) denoted an after-piece, especially a merry farce after a serious play, the actors being called exodiarii; cf. the Schol. on Juv. iii 175: exodiarius apud veteres in fine ludorum intrabat, qui ridiculus foret, ut quicquid lacrimarum atque tristitiae, quae exissent ex tragicis affectibus, huiusce spectaculi risus detergeret. After the disappearance of the old saturae, the Atellanae and mimi were frequently used for this purpose; hence Atellanicum exodium (Suet. Tib. 45), exodium Atellanae (Juv. vi 71).

: Oenone, the daughter of the river-god Cebren, was the first wife of the Trojan Paris and was deserted by him for Helen. After the capture of Troy and the recovery of Helen by the Greeks Paris resought Oenone, that she might cure a wound which he had received from an arrow of Philoctetes. Domitian suspected that his own separation from, and subsequent reunion with, Domitia (c. 3, 1) and his passion for Julia (c. 22), wife of Flavius Sabinus (see below), were burlesqued in the farce of Helvidius. Furthermore, Paris happened to be the name of the paramour of Domitia.
: see on retaxare in Vesp. 13. ...

: T. Flavius Sabinus, son of the praefectus urbis Flavius Sabinus, who was an elder brother of Vespasian (Vesp. 1, 3). Like his cousin Domitian he escaped from the Capitol when it was stormed by the Vitellians and his father was captured and slain (Tac. H. iii 69–73; cf. Dom. 1, 2). Sabinus appears in the consular Fasti as consul ordinarius for 82 A.D. along with the emperor Domitian, and their names are used for dating that year in C.I.L. vi 3828, Dessau 6105: Imp. Domitiano [Aug. viii] T. Flavio Sabi[no cos.] idibus Iu[n] Presumably, therefore, Sabinus actually held the office at least for the earlier part of 82, so that if the verbal slip on the part of the herald occurred in 81 when Sabinus was designated as consul, his execution did not follow immediately as one might naturally infer from the words of Suetonius. Possibly, as Gsell (op. cit. 248) and others assume, the contretemps happened in some later year when Sabinus was designated consul for a second time but was executed before entering on the office. See Stein in Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2614 sq. Sabinus was married to Julia, daughter of the emperor Titus, and on his death Domitian took Julia as his mistress; cf. Philostr. vit. Apollon. vii 7, Σαβῖνον ἀπεκτονώς, ἕνα τῶν ἑαυτοῦ συγγενῶν, Ἰουλίαν ἤγετο. ἡ δὲ Ἰουλία γυνὴ μὲν ἦν τοῦ πεφονευμένου, Δομετιανοῦ δὲ ἀδελφιδῆ (“niece”), μία τῶν Τίτου θυγατέρων. See c. 22.
: the other cousin of Domitian was Flavius Clemens (c. 15, 1), brother of the Flavius Sabinus mentioned here.

: Tiberius took away from the people the election of magistrates and transferred it to the senate (Tac. A. i 15, tum primum e campo comitia ad patres translata sunt). In the days of the Republic the announcement of the result (renuntiatio) was made by the magistrate presiding over the comitia or by the voice of a herald (perhaps by both); cf. Cic. Mur. 1, where Cicero says that he as presiding consul announced the return of Murena (L. Murenam consulem renuntiavi) : Gell. xii 8, censores illi voce praeconis renuntiati sunt. Though in 14 A.D. the people were deprived of any active part in the elections, they 20 still assembled as comitia centuriata or tributa to hear the formal announcement of the result of the voting in the senate (Dio lviii 20), and this custom continued down to the 3rd cent. A.D.

: for destinare = designare cf. Dom. 15, 1: Tib. 31: Iul. 1, 1; Calig. 12, 1; it is used in this sense by Livy first. On designations to the consulship under the Empire see Mommsen, Staatsr. i³ 588. =

: imprudenter, per errorem; cf. Plaut. Most. 968, ne ad alias aedes perperam deveneris: Auct. Bell. Hisp. 12, Tabellarii, qui ad Pompeium missi erant, perperamque ad castra nostra pervenerant: Varr. R.R. i 69, perperam facere "to make a mistake."

div.p: § 5. civilis belli: the revolt of L. Antonius Saturninus in Upper Germany (c. 6, 2).

p.note: : see on c. 8, 4.
: cf. Apul. Met. vii 28, ardentem titionem (= facem) gerens mediis inguinibus obtrudit: x 24, titione candenti inter media femora detruso crudelissime necavit. manus

: cf. Galb. 9, 1, nummulario amputavit. This verb (= circumsecare, circumcidere) in Cicero means to prune trees; in the sense of cutting off parts of the body it occurs in Lucilius, but not in class. Lat.

: Julius Calvaster; cf. Dio lxvii 11, eἷς δ᾽ οὖν τις νεανίσκος Ιούλιος Κάλουαστρος κεχιλιαρχηκὼς ἐς βουλείας ἐλπίδα (i.e. he had held the military tribuneship in the hope of becoming a senator) παραδοξότατα ἐσώθη. ἐπειδὴ γὰρ πολλάκις κατὰ μόνας συμμεμιχὼς (τῷ ᾿Αντωνίῳ) ἠλέγχετο, καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν ὅπως ἄλλως τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς συνωμοσίας ἀπολύσηται, ἔφη κατ' ἐρωτικὴν χρείαν αὐτῷ συγγεγονέναι· καὶ γὰρ ἦν οἷος ἐρᾶσθαι δύνασθαι. καὶ ὁ μὲν οὕτως ἀφείθη.

: a tribune of senatorial birth and entitled to wear the tunica laticlavia, for which see on Vesp. 2, 2. The tribunes of the legion were young men preparing for either a senatorial or an equestrian career. Those of equestrian birth were called tribuni angusticlavii, e.g. the father of Suetonius (Oth. 10, 1). A year's service as tribune was sufficient military qualification for entering on the political cursus honorum of senators; but those qualifying for the equestrian cursus usually had to serve as praefectus cohortis, tribunus legionis, and praefectus alae (Parker, Rom. Legions, p. 189).
: i.e. the guilt of treasonable conspiracy.

: see on Vesp. 13. In the reign of Claudius, during the executions which followed the downfall of Messalina in 48 A.D., Caesoninus escaped the death-penalty by the same shameful defence; cf. Tac. A. xi 36, Suillio Caesonino et Plautio Laterano mors remittitur, huic ob patrui egregium meritum: Caesoninus vitiis protectus est, tamquam in illo foedissimo coetu passus muliebria.

: Dio lxvii 1, Δομιτιανὸς δὲ ἦν μὲν καὶ θρασὺς καὶ ὀργίλος, ἦν δὲ καὶ ἐπίβουλος καὶ κρυψίνους, ὥστε ἀφ᾽ ἑκατέρων τῶν μὲν· τὸ προπετὲς τῶν δὲ τὸ δόλιον ἔχων, πολλὰ μὲν ὥσπερ σκηπτός (instar fulminis) ὀξέως ἐμπίπτων τισὶν ἐλυμαίνετο, πολλὰ δὲ καὶ ἐκ παρασκευῆς ἐκακούργει .... ἐπλάττετο δὲ ἀγαπᾶν ἀεὶ ὃν ἀεὶ μάλιστα ἀποσφάξαι ἤθελεν. The treacherous smoothness and blandness (like the "placidi pellacia ponti'") of emperors such as Domitian (and Tiberius) is denounced by Pliny, Pan. 66, Erant sub oculis naufragia multorum, quos insidiosa tranquillitate provectos improvisus turbo perculerat. Quod enim tam infidum mare quam blanditiae principum illorum, quibus tanta levitas (al. lenitas), tanta fraus, ut facilius esset iratos quam propitios cavere? Cf. also the description in Tac. Agr. 39 of the way in which Domitian "fronte laetus, pectore anxius” disguised his hatred of Agricola. The gruesome humour he displayed in the treatment of his destined victims is compared by Henderson (Five Roman Emperors p. 19) with that of Louis XI described in Quentin Durward.

: = actorem in rationibus (C.I.L. v 8237), a steward, cashier, accountant, who would be a slave or at most a freedman. Sometimes, as here, actor is followed by a defining genitive, cf. actor praedii, fundi, bonorum, rerum; more frequently it is used absolutely for a "manager." The varieties of actores are enumerated by Marquardt, Privatl.2 139; see also Mayor on Plin. Ep. iii 19.
: in pre-class. and class. Lat. with perf. indic.; in Livy and later writers with the subjunct. (always imperf. in Suet., cf. с. 16, 1).
: see on c. 10, 1.

: a very high honour; to sit unbidden on an emperor's seat was to court death: cf. Spart. Hadr. 23, Servianum quasi adfectatorem imperii quod in sedili regio iuxta lectum posito sedisset mori coegit. ..

: sending food from the royal table to absent friends was an honour shown by the Persian kings; cf. Xen. Anab. i 9, where Cyrus is said to have sent half-eaten geese and half loaves to his friends. Other references to the custom under Roman emperors are in Spart. Caracalla 3, fratrem patruelem Afrum, cui pridie partes de cena miserat, iussit occidi: Capitol. Pertinax 12, amicis si quando de prandio suo mittere voluit, misit offulas binas, aut omasi partem, aliquando lumbos gallinaceos. “pars" was the regular word for a "portion" or "helping" of a dish; cf. Suet. Calig. 18, qua epulatione equiti Romano contra se hilarius avidiusque vescenti partes suas misit: Petron. Satyr. 33, ego quidem paene proieci partem meam.

: Marcus Arrecinus Clemens, brother of Arrecina Tertulla the first wife of Titus (Tit. 4, 2). He was consul (suffectus) in 73 A.D., and again under Domitian (year uncertain) along with L. Baebius Honoratus (C.I.L. xii 3637). In 70 A.D. he was appointed by Mucianus to be prefect of the praetorian guards, an office held by his father under Caligula; cf. Tac. H. iv 68, Utque Domitiani animum.. deleniret, Arrecinum Clementem, domui Vespasiani per adfinitatem innexum et gratissimum 202 Domitiano, praetorianis praeposuit, patrem eius sub C. Caesare egregie functum ea cura dictitans. His appointment to this post was quite exceptional, as he was a senator and not an eques; see on Tit. 6, 1.

: emissarius meant a scout, spy, or secret agent, especially for the purpose of securing materials for accusations; cf. Galb. 15, 2, ex omnibus Neronis emissariis maleficentissimos: Cic. Verr. ii 22, Itaque apponit, qui petat Veneri Erycinae illam hereditatem. Petit Naevius Turpio quidam, istius excursor et emissarius, homo omnium ex illo conventu quadruplatorum (= delatorum) deterrimus: v 108, quem iste in rebus capitalibus in omni calumnia praecursorem habere solebat et emissarium: Cic. Fam. viii 8, de vi reus a quodam suo emissario Sex. Tettio factus. ...

: for such gestatio or riding in a litter (the lectica held two) or carriage see on Vesp. 21. Verbs like gestor and vehor come under the head of those passives which Kühner-Stegmann (i 105, 108) call "deponential" passives, differing from ordinary passives in having a present participle and a gerund; cf. Galb. 8, 1, ne ad gestandum quidem iter ingressus: Ulp. Dig. vii 8, 12, gestandi ius: Gaius Dig. xl 2, 7, сит gestandi gratia prodierit: Suet. Claud. 28, lectica per urbem vehendi ius: Gell. v 6, 27, equo vehens: Cic. Brut. 331, adulescentiam per medias laudes quasi quadrigis vehentem: Cic. N.D. i 78, Triton natantibus invehens beluis.

div.p: §2. contemptius: comparative of contemptim “contemptuously," not of contempte "contemptibly"; see Thes. Ling. Lat. iv 655.

p.note: : cf. Cic. Cat. i 1, Quousque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?

: “an especially severe sentence"; cf. Liv. viii 21, 2, interrogatus a quodam tristioris sententiae auctore, quam pоепат meritos Privernates censeret: Ov. M. xv 43, Tunc quoque sic lata est sententia tristis, et omnis | calculus inmitem demittitur ater in urnam. as

: Baumg.-Cr. explains exitus here “finis vitae, mors," and Rolfe translates "no more certain indication of a cruel death," but exitus means the "ending" of Domitian's judgement as opp. to principium; cf. Cic. Imp. Pomp. 1, 3, huius orationis difficilius est exitum quam principium invenire.

: cf. Ner. 49, 12, where Nero on his flight from Rome learns that he has been condemned by the senate as a public enemy (hostis) and sentenced to be punished more maiorum; he inquires the nature of the punishment, and is told "nudi hominis cervicem inseri furcae, corpus virgis ad necem caedi"; when he hears the horsemen approaching to arrest him, he stabs himself. Claudius on one occasion when he was at Tibur wished to witness an antiqui moris supplicium, but no executioner could be found after the criminals had been tied to the stake; he sent for one from Rome and continued to wait for him until nightfall (Claud. 34, 1). On the antiquity of this punishment see Mommsen, Strafr. 916 sqq. puniendi is the gerund, and more maiorum puniendi = ad poenam (supplicium) antiqui moris “condemned to the old-fashioned method of punishing"; for the double gen. with more cf. Cic. Brut. 163, Scaevolae dicendi elegantia. The gerundive with condemnare is found only in Rufin. Hist. 5, 1, quem praeparandum bestiis condemnavit; with damnare in Ulp. Dig. xlviii 19, 3: 24, 1.

div.p: § 3. intercessit: in virtue of his tribunician power (Tit. 6, 1, n.) the emperor possessed the right of vetoing a decree of the senate (Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 879). Tacitus mentions two cases of an emperor interposing his veto where the senate had decreed the punishment "more maiorum'': A. iv 30, dictis sententiis ut Serenus more maiorum puniretur, quo molliret invidiam, (Tiberius) intercessit: A. xvi 11, decretum ut more maiorum punirentur, at Nero mortem sine arbitro (= liberum mortis arbitrium) permittens intercessit. Cf. also A. xiv 48, where Nero hopes for an opportunity of using his intercessio tribunicia in the event of Antistius being condemned by the senate to this penalty.

p.note: : = alienum, lit. "away from the matter in hand," and so "unprofitable" "useless," opposed to in rem or ex re; cf. Aug. 94, 1, non ab re fuerit subtexere quae ei prius quam nasceretur ... evenerint : Liv. xxxv 32, non ab re esse Quinctio visum est sociorum aliquos legatos interesse ei consilio. This use of ab re is nearly confined to negative sentences; see Kühner-Stegmann, i 493.
: loyalty" to the emperor; see on Vitell. 3, 1: Dom. 10, 1..

: as though the senators themselves were eager to punish any alleged maiestas with the severest penalties of the law, and were not merely obeying the dictates of the tyrant. Tacitus says that Nero spared the senate the humiliation of his being present to witness them passing shameful sentences, whereas Domitian loved to be present and to gloat over their servility: Agr. 45, Nero tamen subtraxit oculos suos iussitque scelera, non spectavit: praecipua sub Domitiano miseriarum pars erat videre et aspici, cum suspiria nostra subscriberentur, cum denotandis tot hominum palloribus sufficeret saevus ille vultus et rubor, quo se contra pudorem muniebat.

: parcere oculis meant to avoid unpleasant or unlawful sights"; cf. Prop. iv 9, 53, parce oculis, hospes, lucoque abscede verendo: Tibull. i 2, 33, parcite luminibus, celari vult sua furta Venus. Contrast pascere oculos in Vitell. 14, 2. ...
: from the fact that the senate had decreed such a “mild" penalty.

: like Nero; cf. Ner. 32, 1, destitutus atque ita iam exhaustus et egens ut stipendia quoque militum et commoda (rewards or bounties) veteranorum protrahi ac differri necesse esset, calumniis rapinisque intendit animum; also like Caligula; cf. Calig. 38, 1, exhaustus igitur atque egens ad rapinas convertit animum vario et exquisitissimo calumniarum et auctionum et vectigalium genere. stipendio quod adiecerat: see c. 7, 3.

: cf. Zonar. xi 19, μεταμεληθεὶς δὲ τὴν μὲν ποσότητα (i.e. the amount of pay) οὐκ ἐμείωσε, τὸ δὲ πλῆθος τῶν στρατευομένων συνέστειλε· καὶ ἑκατέρωθεν μεγάλα τὸ δημόσιον ἔβλαψε, μήθ' ἱκανοὺς τοὺς ἀμύνοντας αὐτῷ, καὶ τούτους μεγαλομίσθους ποιήσας.

: obnoxius (= noxae expositus, damno subiectus) is a favourite word with Suetonius in the sense of "exposed to"; e.g. Aug. 28, 3, Urbem inundationibus incendiisquc obnoxiam: Tib. 63, 1, contumeliis obnoxius: Tib. 54, 2, omnium criminationibus obnoxios reddidit: Iul. 45, 2, obtrectatorum iocis obnoxiam expertus calvitii (“baldness'") deformitatem. He once uses it absolutely in the sense of humilis, demissus, "subservient”: Tib. 12, 2, non privatum modo, sed etiam obnoxium et trepidum egit; cf. Cic. ad Brut. i 17, 6, supplex et obnoxius.
: see on Tit. 5, 3.

: cf. Ner. 34, 1, neque in divexanda (matre) quicquam pensi habuit: Sall. Cat. 5, neque id quibus modis assequeretur quicquam pensi habebat: Liv. xxvi 15, 4, quibus neque quid dicerent neque quid facerent quicquam pensi fuisset. In these phrases pensum means what is weighed or considered, and the partitive genitive depends on nihil or quicquam; in Tac. A. xiii 15, neque fas neque fidem pensi habere, the gen. is a gen. of price or value (so too in Val. Max. ii 9, 3, non pensi ducere). See Kühner-Stegmann, i 457, ii 262; Roby Lat. Gr. 1301 (where it is suggested that Tac. misunderstood the construction of the phrase).

: cf. Pliny's contrast between Domitian and Trajan, Pan. 41, Nam quid est causae cur aliis quidem, cum omnia raperent et rapta retinerent, ut si nihil rapuissent, nihil retinuissent, defuerint omnia: tibi, cum tam multa largiaris et nihil auferas, omnia supersint? Numquam principibus defuerunt qui fronte gravi et tristi supercilio utilitatibus fisci contumaciter adessent, et erant principes ipsi sua sponte avidi et rapaces et qui magistris non egerent, plura tamen semper a nobis contra nos didicerunt.

: cf. Ner. 32, 2, instituit (Nero) ut lege maiestatis facta dictaque omnia, quibus modo delator non deesset, tenerentur. Tacitus (A. iii 38) says that under Tiberius the maiestatis crimen was the complementum (“makeweight'') omnium accusationum. The abuse of the charge of maiestas to enrich the Treasury under Domitian is denounced in Plin. Pan. 42: Locupletabant et fiscum et aerarium non tam Voconiae et Iuliae leges quam maiestatis singulare et unicum crimen eorum qui crimine vacarent. Huius tu (i.e. Trajan) metum penitus sustulisti. For the various offences made indictable under the law of maiestas see Furneaux, Tac. Ann. Vol. i² p. 141.

div.p: § 2. confiscabantur: = in fiscum redigebantur. The verb confiscare (cf. publicare, δημεύειν) is first found in Suetonius, either c. acc. pers., e.g. Calig. 41, 2, duos equites R. locupletes corripi confiscarique iussit (so Cic. dom. 8, cum lege nefaria Ptolemaeum publicasses), or c. acc. rei, as here and in Calig. 16, 3, sestertium milies confiscatum; he also uses it of money kept in the emperor's “fiscus” (Vesp. 16, 3, n.) as opposed to the “aerarium publicum': Aug. 101, 2, quam summam confiscatam semper repositamque habuerat. ..

p.note: : the estates of those who were in no way related to the emperor, and to which the fiscus had not the slightest claim (see on fiscales calumniae, c. 9, 3). Contrast Domitian's earlier scrupulousness in the matter of inheritances (c. 9, 2). Pliny (Pan. 43) with epigrammatic neatness and sting describes him as “unus omnium, nunc quia scriptus, nunc quia non scriptus, heres.”

: cf. Calig. 38, 2, testamenta primipilarium, qui ab initio Tiberi principatus neque illum neque se heredem reliquissent, ut ingrata rescidit; item ceterorum (testamenta) ut irrita et vana quoscumque quis diceret herede Caesare mori destinasse.
: for the pleonasm cf. Galb. 9, 1, multo praeter ceteras altiorem.. crucem: Vitell. 13, 2, famosissima super ceteras cena.

: in inscriptions of the early Empire fiscus is thus used as a name for the imperial exchequer (or central chest) of separate provinces or finance departments; e.g. fiscus Asiaticus (C.I.L. vi 8570), Gallicus (vi 5197), frumentarius (vi 544); cf. Suet. Aug. 101, quantum pecuniae in aerario et fiscis et vectigaliorum residuis. Jewish communities, wherever they might be situated, were in the habit of levying a didrachm (half-shekel) each year from every adult male Jew to increase the treasures of the Temple at Jerusalem. The sums collected were centralised and exported in gold by trusted agents to Jerusalem (Philo Leg. ad Gaium 23). This export of gold roused opposition in the Greek towns and also in Italy where the Roman senate on several occasions forbade all export of gold, and the propraetor Flaccus confiscated the sums collected for the Temple by the communities in Asia Minor (Cic. Flac. 28). Julius Caesar issued edicts, confirmed by Augustus, authorizing anew the sending of these gifts to Jerusalem from Rome and the provinces, and when the cities of Asia Minor and Cyrene made a show of opposition, Agrippa intervened in favour of the Jews (Joseph. Ant. Iud. xvi 16, Phil. Leg. 40). After the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Temple in 70 A.D. this annual tribute was transferred to Jupiter Capitolinus and to his earthly representative the Roman emperor (Mommsen, Prov. Rom. Emp. ii 217; cf. Dio lxvi 7, Joseph. Bell. Iud. vii 6, 6, Mart. vii 55). All the circumcised were bound to register their names, and there were procurators to collect this capitation tax (procuratores ad capitularia Iudaeorum, C.I.L. vi 8604). abolished the abuses and "delations" connected with it under Domitian, as is shown by coins of his with the inscription fisci Iudaici calumnia sublata, but the tax itself was still being levied at the beginning of the 3rd cent.; cf. Orig. Ep. ad Afr. 14, καὶ νῦν ᾿Ιουδαίων τὸ δίδραχμον αὐτοῖς (τοῖς Ῥωμαίοις) τελούντων. Julian (c. 360 A.D.) forbade exactions from the Jews and destroyed the fiscal registers of their names (Julian Ep. 23). See Daremberg-Saglio, iii 625; Hirschfeld, Kais. Verwaltungsb.2 p. 73. Nerva
: see on Vitell. 14, 4. The delatores (Tit. 8, 5) gave information to the Treasury officials who controlled the Iudaicus fiscus of attempts to evade payment by those who could be held liable.

p.mentioned: qui vel inprofessi Iudaicam viverent vitam
p.note: : vel inprofessi is a correction by I. Fr. Gronovius of velut inprofessi (MG Υδ), veluti professi (X). Gronovius interprets inprofessi as proselytes who were not of Jewish extraction and so had not registered themselves on the fiscal register of Jews, but who observed the Sabbath and various Jewish rites and purifications; they are here distinguished from those who were born of Jewish parents but disguised the fact to avoid the tax. Janssen follows Bremi in taking inprofessi as referring especially to the Christians, the Jews being referred to in the clause beginning vel dissimulata origine, while others (e.g. Baumg.-Cr.) think that this latter clause refers to the Christians, and that the inprofessi are proselytes to Judaism. The adj. inprofessus is used in post-Aug. writers either in an active (or middle) sense "not declaring oneself," as here and Dig. xxxix 4, 16, 1, si quis inprofessus servus fuerit, or passively, e.g. Quintil. in lemm. Decl. 341, res furtiva inprofessa apud publicanos. The words intra urbem, which are found in some of the MSS. after Iudaicam, appear in the old editions but were rightly rejected by Oudendorp as an explanatory gloss.

: the pres. inf. might be expected as in Cic. Rep. i 23, memini me admodum adulescentulo perturbari exercitum nostrum, but there are many instances even in Cicero of the perf. inf. with memini to express a past event of which one was a witness or contemporary, and it is usual in post-class. Latin (Kühner-Stegmann, i 703).

: in Ner. 57, 2 Suetonius says that twenty years after the death of Nero (68 A.D.), "adulescente me,” there arose a false Nero who won support in Parthia; thus he describes himself as an adulescens in 88; but it is improbable that he is referring to any earlier period here, adulescentulus being often a mere synonym of adulescens (e.g. in Vesp. 8, 3). Bentley would omit me adulescentulum.
: see on c. 8, 1.

: = circumcisus, a very rare use, for which the only other reference in the Thes. Ling. Lat. is Mar. Victorin. in Gal. 5, 12. For circumcision as the distinguishing mark of the Jews cf. Tac. H. v 5, Circumcidere genitalia instituerunt, ut diversitate noscantur. Transgressi (i.e. proselytes) in morem eorum idem usurpant, nec quicquam prius imbuuntur quam contemnere deos, exuere patriam, parentes liberos fratres vilia habere. Other synonyms of circumcisus are recutitus (Pers. v 184) and verpus (Juv. xiv 104). Horace, Sat. i 9, 70, has curti Iudaei.

div.p: §3. iuventa: this poet. form (cf. Dom. 18, 1; Aug. 61, 1; 68) is used by Livy. Suetonius has iuventus more frequently; he always uses senecta (not in Cic.), e.g. Galb. 4, 1: 17 (in Tib. 24, 2 senectus occurs in an utterance of Tiberius).

p.note: : see on Vesp. 9, 2.

: = audax, impudens, temerarius; cf. Calig. 51, 1, diversissima in eodem vitia, summam confidentiam et contra nimium metum. As an adj., confidens is not used in a good sense in any writer between Plautus and Apuleius; cf. Cic. Tusc. iii 14, Qui fortis est, idem est fidens, quoniam confidens mala consuetudine loquendi in vitio ponitur, ductum verbum a confidendo, quod laudis est.
: a mistress of Vespasian, who treated her almost as a lawful wife; see Vesp. 3.
: a peninsula at the north-eastern corner of the Adriatic sea, running out from the coast of Liburnia between Tergeste (Trieste) and the Sinus Flanaticus (Gulf of Quarnero). osculum

: as though she were the wedded wife of Vespasian. It was customary at Rome for women to kiss their own relations and those of their husband as far as the degree of second cousins; cf. Polyb. in Athen. x 440, πρὸς δὲ τούτοις (τὴν γυναῖκα) φιλεῖν δεῖ τοὺς συγγενεῖς τοὺς ἑαυτῆς καὶ τοὺς τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἕως ἐξανεψίων (sobrinorum). See Marquardt, Privatl.2 31.
: sc. osculandam, as a sign of respect due from one in an inferior station. See on Oth. 6, 2, osculo exceptus.
: Flavius Sabinus, married to Julia daughter of Titus; see c. 10, 4.

: the imperial attendants (aulici ministri) wore a white tunic adorned with a border or lace of gold; cf. Amm. Marc. xxxvi 6, 5, tunica auro distincta, ut regius minister: Cod. Iust. xi 9, 2, Nemo vir auratas habeat aut in tunicis aut in lineis paragaudas (= limbos, i.e. borders, fringes) nisi in tantummodo quibus hoc propter imperiale ministerium concessum est. Marcus Aurelius allowed the more prominent citizens to give banquets with the same pomp as himself, and with servants like his own: Capitol. M. Antoninus 17, 5, Tunc viris clarioribus permisit ut eodem cultu quo et ipse vel ministris similibus convivia exhiberent. Οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη: words used by Odysseus in Hom. Il. ii 204. The rest of this verse and the beginning of the next were quoted by Caligula at the time when he was claiming absolute monarchy: Calig. 22, 1, Compluribus cognominibus adsumptis-nam et “pius” et “castrorum filius” et ‘“pater exercituum’”et‘optimus maximus Caesar'' vocabatur— cum audiret forte reges, qui officii causa in urbem advenerant, concertantes apud se super cenam de nobilitate generis, exclamavit : Εῖς κοίρανος ἔστω, εἷς βασιλεύς.

p.mentioned: et patri se et fratri imperium dedisse
p.note: : Martial, in an adulatory poem (ix 101) on Domitian as the greater Hercules (maior Alcides), praises him for surrendering a world-empire, which was his own, to his father Vespasian and for subordinating himself to his elder brother Titus: Solus Iuleas cum iam retineret habenas, | tradidit inque suo tertius orbe fuit. Both Vespasian and Titus were absent in the East at the time when the army of Vespasian under Antonius Primus entered Rome. Domitian (aged 18) was installed in the Palace and received the title of "Caesar' as Vespasian's son (see c. 1, 3). He was appointed praetor with consular power and comported himself with tyrannical arrogance (omnem vim dominationis licenter exercuit), though the real authority rested with Mucianus until Vespasian arrived in person.
: used not only in the sense of giving back, but also of paying one his due (ἀποδιδόναι).
: see c. 3, 1.
: so Salmasius for vocatam of the MSS., re- having been lost by haplography after edicere.

: a sacred couch on which the statues of the gods rested, as distinct from the lectus of a mere mortal. A pulvinar was among the divine honours bestowed on Julius Caesar (Iul. 76, 1). The imperial box built by Augustus in the Circus Maximus was also called a pulvinar (Aug. 45, 1; Claud. 4, 3).

: this verb is used of cries of disapproval in Cicero; of cries of approval first in Livy (xxxiv 50). Suetonius uses it in a favourable sense here and in Vitell. 15, 4: Claud. 7; 27, 2; in an unfavourable sense in Aug. 70, 2; Tib. 52, 3; Galb. 20, 2. So adclamatio favourable in Iul. 79, 1; Aug. 58, 1; Oth. 6, 3; unfavourable in Dom. 23, 1. See Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 67.
: see on c. 4, 5.

: Statius (Silv. i 6, 84) in his description of a banquet given by Domitian to the people in the amphitheatre says that the delighted recipients raised shouts of “dominus" and adds “Hoc solum vetuit licere Caesar." It would seem therefore that the epulum mentioned by Suetonius must have been given at a later date when Domitian was less rigorous in this respect. Cf. Gsell, op. cit. 49, n. 5.

: the title "dominus,” which suggested both a slave-master and a political tyrant, was rejected with loathing by Augustus; cf. Aug. 53, 1, Domini appellationem ut maledictum et obprobrium semper exhorruit. Cum spectante eo ludos pronuntiatum esset in mimo: “O dominum aequum. et bonum!" et universi quasi de ipso dictum exultantes comprobassent, et statim manu vultuque indecoras adulationes repressit et insequenti die gravissimo corripuit edicto; dominumque se posthac appellari ne a liberis quidem aut nepotibus suis vel serio vel ioco passus est, atque eius modi blanditias etiam inter ipsos prohibuit. So too Tiberius: Tib. 27, Dominus appellatus a quodam denuntiavit ne se amplius contumeliae causa nominaret: Dio lvii 8, (ὁ Τιβέριος) πολλάκις ἔλεγεν ὅτι δεσπότης (dominus) μὲν τῶν δούλων, αὐτοκράτωρ (imperator) δὲ τῶν στρατιωτῶν, τῶν δὲ δὴ λοιπῶν πρόκριτος (princeps) εἰμί. Caligula, whom Dio (lix 3) describes as μοναρχικώτατος, claimed the title of ‘dominus”; cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 3, his elatus dominum dici, atque insigne regni capiti nectere tentaverat. Juvenal (iv 96) uses “dominus” of Domitian, and Pliny (Pan. 55) says of Trajan in contrast with him: sedem obtinet principis, ne sit domino locus; cf. ib. 45, scis, ut sunt diversa natura dominatio et principatus, ita non aliis esse principem gratiorem quam qui maxime dominum graventur. See below on "dominus et deus."

: cf. Claud. 7, adclamante populo: ‘‘Feliciter” partim ‘“patruo imperatoris, partim “Germanici fratri!”: Petron. Satyr. 50, familia "Gaio feliciter!'” conclamavit: ib. 60, consurreximus patri patriae, feliciter!'' diximus. sed et see on Galb. 4, 1.
: see c. 4, 4. et "Augusto,

: a notorious delator under Domitian; cf. Juv. iv 53, Si quid Palfurio, si credimus Armillato, | quidquid conspicuum pulchrumque est aequore toto, | res fisci est, ubicumque natat. The Schol. on Juv. l.c. gives us particulars of his career, on the authority of Marius Maximus the historian: Palfurius Sura, consularis filius, sub Nerone luctatus est cum virgine Lacedaemonia in agone (i.e. a public contest): post inde a Vespasiano senatu motus transivit ad Stoicam sectam, in qua cum praevaleret et eloquentia et artis poeticae gloria, abusus familiaritate Domitiani acerbissime partes delationis exercuit: quo interfecto, senatu accusante damnatus est.

: = de numero oratorum (certantium); cf. Ov. Am. iii 3, 46, non de tetricis dicerer esse deus, and other passages cited by KühnerStegmann, i 499. Bremi explains de oratoribus coronatum as propter victoriam de oratoribus reportatam coronatum (cf. Iul. 11, tropaea Gai = Mari de Iugurtha). The contest in which Palfurius was successful is that described in c. 4, 4, certabant prosa oratione Graece Latineque, where the "coronae" are also mentioned.

: for this as a sign of arrogance cf. Cicero 's jesting remark to the jurisconsult Valerius, Fam. i 10, Qui istinc veniunt, partim te superbum esse dicunt quod nihil respondeas, partim contumeliosum, quod male respondeas; also to another jurisconsult Trebatius, Fam. vii 16, superbiam tuam accusant, quod negent te percontantibus respondere (resp. meaning "to answer" and "to give counsel's opinion''). tacere iussit voce praeconis: a precedent followed by Hadrian; cf. Dio lxix 6, ἦγε δὲ καὶ τὸν δῆμον τῶν Ῥωμαίων ἐμβριθῶς μᾶλλον ἢ θωπευτικῶς, καί ποτε ἰσχυρῶς αὐτοῦντί τι ἐν ὁπλομαχίᾳ (ludis gladiatoriis) οὔτε ἔνειμε καὶ προσέτι ἐκέλευσε τοῦτο δὴ τὸ τοῦ Δομιτιανοῦ κηρυχθῆναι “ σιωπήσατε.” οὐκ ἐλέχθη μὲν γάρ, ὁ γὰρ κῆρυξ ἀνατείνας τὴν χεῖρα καὶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ τούτου ἡσυχάσας, ὥσπερ ἐιώθασι ποιεῖν (οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ὁπότε ὑπὸ κηρύγματος σιγάζονται), ἐπειδὴ ἐσιώπησαν, ἔφη “ τοῦτ᾽ ἐθέλει.”

div.p: §2. formalem epistulam: formalem is explained by Baumg.-Cr. as “forma sollemni conscriptam, cum formulis titulisque sollemnibus"; by Forcellini as "quae eadem forma ad plures scribebatur’' (ἐγκύκλιος, α circular letter). The Thes. Ling. Lat. (vi 1081, 1088) connects formalis here with forma in its special sense of an emperor's decree or rescript, which afforded a basis and model for magisterial ordinances. In M the reading is formaul emdictaret, and Bentley conjectured formulam dictaret epistula.

p.note: : sc. to his secretary (ab epistulis). The head of the imperial secretariate under Domitian was Abascantus, and the multitudinous duties of his office are described by his friend the poet Statius (Silv. v 1, 85 sqq., quoted in Introd., p. 11).

: cf. Dio Chrysost. Οr. 45, 1, τὸν ἰσχυρότατον καὶ βαρύτατον καὶ δεσπότην ὀνομαζόμενον καὶ θεὸν παρὰ πᾶσιν Ἕλλησι καὶ βαρβάροις : Dio Cass. lxvii 5, ἤδη γὰρ καὶ θεὸς ἠξίου νομίζεσθαι, καὶ δεσπότης καλούμενος καὶ θεὸς ὑπερηγάλλετο. ταῦτα οὐ μόνον ἐλέγετο ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐγράφετο: 1xvii 13, προσκυνήσας (ὁ Κέλσος) αὐτῷ, δεσπότην τε καὶ θεὸν (ἃ παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἤδη προσηγορεύετο) πολλάκις ὀνομάσας, κ.τ.λ.: Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, 2, maior libidinum flagitio ac plus quam superbe utens patribus, quippe qui se dominum deumque dici coegerit: [id.] Epit. 11, 6, more C. Caligulae dominum sese deumque dici coegit: Eutrop. vii 23, 2, dominum se et deum primus appellari iussit: Oros. vii 10, 2, in tantam superbiam prolapsus fuit, ut dominum sese ac deum vocari scribi colique iusserit. The date at which Domitian claimed these titles is between Oct. 1, 85 A.D. and Sept. 30, 86 according to Euseb.-Hieron. Chron. p. 161 Schoene. Martial first uses them of him in Bk. v (89 A.D.) 8, 1, edictum domini deique nostri; contrast x 72, 3, where on the accession of Trajan he writes: dicturus dominum deumque non sum |... non est hic dominus sed imperator. Pliny (Pan. 2) praises Trajan for making no such claim to divinity: Nusquam ut deo, nusquam ut numini blandiamur: non enim de tyranno, sed de cive, non de domino, sed de parente loquimur: ib. 52, Tu delubra non nisi adoraturus intras, tibi maximus honor excubare pro templis, postibusque praetexi. Sic fit ut tibi di summum inter homines fastigium servent, cum deorum ipse non appetas. See also note on “domino” above; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 759.

: cf. Suidas (s.v. Δομετιανός), οὐχ ὑπέμεινεν ἑτέρων αὐτοῦ γενέσθαι κατὰ τὸ Καπιτώλιον ἀνδριάντων στάσιν ἢ ἐκ χρυσοῦ τε καὶ ἀργύρου πεποιημένων: Dio lxvii 8, τοσαῦτα δὲ αὐτῷ ἐψηφίσθη, ὥστε πᾶσαν ὀλίγου δεῖν τὴν οἰκουμένην, τὴν ὑπ᾿ αὐτὸν οὖσαν, εἰκόνων αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀνδριάντων καὶ ἀργυρῶν καὶ χρυσῶν ἐμπλησθῆναι: Eutrop. vii 23, 2, Nullam sibi nisi auream et argenteam statuam in Capitolio passus est poni: Plin. Pan. 52, Itaque tuam (i.e. Trajan's) statuam in vestibulo Iovis Opt. Max. unam alteramve et hanc aeneam cernimus. At paulo ante aditus omnes, omnes gradus, totaque area hinc auro, hinc argento relucebat, seu potius polluebatur, cum incesti principis (i.e. Domitian) statuis permixta deorum simulacra sorderent. (Pliny goes on to say that the road leading to the Capitol used to be blocked by the herds of victims intended to honour the hideous effigies of the tyrant with as much blood as he himself had shed.) Martial, i 70, 5, refers to the gleaming statues of Domitian on the Palatine: Inde sacro veneranda petes Palatia clivo, | plurima qua summi fulget imago ducis. The colossal equestrian statue of Domitian in the Forum, described by Statius (S. i 1), was of bronze. These statues were all destroyed in the exultant outburst at his death described in c. 23. On the subject of imperial statues see Friedlaender, Sitteng. iii¹º 58 sqq.

: Lipsius was the first to suggest that this means centenum pondus (100 lbs.), the weight mentioned in Stat. S. v 1, 190, where the dying Priscilla charges her husband Abascantus to set up a golden image of Domitian on the Capitol: Da Capitolinis aeternum sedibus aurum, | quo niteat sacri centeno pondere vultus | Caesaris. Vollmer, however, in his note there, infers that centenum pondus must have exceeded the weight fixed by Domitian, otherwise Statius would not have mentioned the weight at all.

: vaulted passages or open archways were called Iani (or iani); cf. Cic. N.D. ii 24, 67, principem in sacrificando Ianum esse voluerunt, quod ab eundo nomen est ductum, ex quo transitiones perviae “iani,” foresque in liminibus profanarum aedium “ianuae” nominantur. There were many Iani at Rome; cf. Ov. F. i 257, where the poet addresses the god Ianus: Cum tot sint Iani, cur stas sacratus in uno? Suetonius mentions one built by Augustus: Aug. 31, 5, Pompei statuam marmoreo Iano superposuit. The most famous was the medius Ianus, the Roman Exchange, in the Forum; on the vexed question whether this was an arcade or four archways joined in a square (Ianus quadrifrons), and on the relation between it and the imus and summus Ianus see Jordan, Topogr. Rom i 2, 214 sqq., and the commentators on Hor. S. ii 3, 18: Ερ. i 1, 54. arcus: cf. Plin. Pan. 54, Quasi prolatis imperii finibus nunc ingentes arcus excessurosque templorum fastigium titulos, nunc menses etiam nec hos singulos nomini Caesarum dicabamus. Arches to celebrate victories in war, and later as a mark of honour, were characteristically Roman structures. The first recorded instance is that of the three fornices (fornix being the older Latin term) erected in 196 B.c. by L. Stertinius for victories in Spain (Liv. xxxiii 27). In 190 B.c. Scipio Africanus built another on the Clivus Capitolinus, surmounted by seven gilded statues and two figures of horses (Liv. xxxvii 3). Arches were erected in honour of the Caesars and the members of the imperial house, not only for military successes but also for great public works; e.g. the arch in honour of Domitian at Sinuessa, where the Via Domitia began, mentioned in Stat. S. iv 3, 97, arcus, belligeris ducis tropaeis | et totis Ligurum nitens metallis, | quantus nubila qui coronat imbri (i.e. a rainbow). There are still in Rome itself five arcus triumphales of Drusus, Titus, Septimius Severus, Gallienus, and Constantine. For illustrations of these, as restored, see Baumeister, Denk. d. class. Alt. iii 1865 sqq.; Daremberg-Saglio, i 391 sqq.

: the entablature, resting on columns against the piers of the arch, was surmounted by an "attica," on the front of which was the titulus or dedicatory inscription, and on the top of it the statue of the triumphator, at first on horseback and later standing in a chariot. The statues of victors standing in their four-horsed chariots above an arcus triumphalis are mentioned in Prudent. c. Symm. ii 556, Frustra igitur currus summo miramur in arcu | quadriiugos stantesques duces in curribus altis | Fabricios, Curios, hinc Drusos, inde Camillos. Juvenal mentions similar statues set up in the front courts of illustrious Roman houses: vii 125, huius enim stat currus aeneus, alti | quadriiuges in vestibulis: viii 3, stantes in curribus Aemilianos. The Arch of Trajan at the entrance of the Forum Traianum was crowned by a statue of the emperor in a triumphal chariot drawn by six horses, as is seen from his coins.
: see on c. 1, 1.
: dat. of agent (App. i. § 3. C. c).

: i.e. the Gr. ἀρκεῖ = satis est, a play on the Lat. arci which is used as the pl. of arcus by Varro (Non. p. 108 Lindsay). With a play on the word "arch" one might render "Arch-builder, enough!" Bentley hazarded a conjecture APK (= MCXX), but thinks it more probable that some Latin word is to be read: Latinum verbum quaerendum, non Graecum ἀρκεῖ. Nam cum auctor “Graece” dicit, non ponit nisi Latina. But the practice of Suetonius varies: at times he gives merely a Latin version of what he says was written or spoken in Greek (e.g. in Ner. 45), at times he gives the original Greek (e.g. in Claud. 43).

: six in the reign of his father Vespasian, in the years 71, 73, 75, 76, 77, 79; one with his brother the emperor Titus, in 80; ten when he himself was emperor, in 82-88 (inclusive), 90, 92, 95. See also c. 2, 1. After his victory over the Chatti (c. 6, 1) the senate decreed to Domitian the consulship for ten years, but this sequence was interrupted in 89. Statius hymns Domitian's 17th consulship in Silv. iv 1, 1, Laeta bis octonis accedit purpura fastis | Caesaris insignemque aperit Germanicus annum, etc.

: in 82-88 A.D. Ausonius, Grat. Act. 6, speaks loosely of Domitian's 17 consulships as continuous: Scis, imperator doctissime (i.e. Gratianus), septem ac decem Domitiani consulatus, quos ille invidia alios provehendi continuando conseruit, ita in eius aviditate derisos, ut haec eum pagina fastorum suorum, immo fastidiorum, fecerit insolentem nec potuerit praestare felicem. Pliny (Pan. 58) denounces these "continuous" consulships: Non te (i.e. Trajan) ad exemplar eius voco, qui continuis consulatibus fecerat longum quemdam et sine discrimine annum: his te confero, quos certum est, quoties consules fuerunt, non sibi praestitisse Contigit ergo privatis aperire annum fastosque reserare, et hoc quoque redditae libertatis indicium fuit, quod consul alius quam Caesar esset. Miseros ambitionis, qui ita consules semper ut semper principes erant! Quamquam non tam ambitio quam livor et malignitas videri potest omnes annos possidere summumque illud purpurae decus non nisi praecerptum praefloratumque transmittere. The flatterer Statius pretends that the reluctant Domitian was only yielding to an insistent senate and people: Silv. iv 1, 10, Curia Caesareum gaudet vicisse pudorem; 1, 18, talem (i.e. consul) te cernere semper | mense meo (i.e. January) tua Roma cupit; 1, 33, flectere (fut.) tamen precibusque senatus | promittes hunc saepe diem.
: see on c. 1, 3.

: cf. Iul. 59, 1, ne religione quidem ulla a quoquam incepto absterritus. Cicero and the writers of his and the Augustan age do not use quisquam adjectivally except with names of persons or classes; see Neue-Wagener, Formenlehre ii³ 505, Tyrrell and Purser on Cic. Att. v 10, 4. It is found with other nouns in Plaut., Lucr., and post-Aug. writers; e.g. Tac. Dial. 29, 3, cuiquam ministerio: Quintil. x 2, 6, cuiusquam rei.

: a practice condemned by Pliny, Pan. 65, Quam diversum consuetudine illorum qui pauculis diebus gestum consulatum, immo non gestum, abiciebant per edictum! An example of Domitian's resigning the consulship on the Ides (13th) of Jan. is in 92 A.D. when he (for the 16th time) and Q. Volusius Saturninus were elected on Jan. 1, and on Jan. 13 L. Venuleius Apronianus took Domitian 's place (C.I.L. xiv 243, Dessau 6126). Caligula held four consulships, one from the Kalends of July for two months, a second from the Kalends of Jan. for 30 days, a third up to the Ides of Jan., and the fourth until Jan. 7 (Calig. 17). Tiberius, when emperor, was thrice consul, once for a few days, once for 3 months, once until the Ides (15th) of May (Tib. 26). Augustus held 13 consulships, 5 for the full year, the rest for 9, 6, 4, or 3 months, except the second (33 B.C.) which he held only for a few hours, resigning it on the Kalends of Jan. (Aug. 26). For the brief tenure of consulships by private individuals under the Empire see on c. 2, 1.

: for autem placed immediately after the prep. cf. Iul. 46, post autem pontificatum. This order of words, which is very rare, is found in Cic. Orat. 154, dicitur cum illis, cum autem nobis non dicitur, sed nobiscum: N.D. ii 52, Tim. 26, Off. ii 8: Auct. Bell. Afr. 59: Nep. Eum. 13. Suetonius has autem in the fourth place in Vesp. 22, 1, et super cenam autem; this is frequent in Plautus, and there are several instances in Cicero, e.g. Quinct. 44, quid a nobis autem refertur?
: over the Chatti in 83 and over the Dacians in 86; see on c. 6, 1, duplicem triumphum egit.

: Vollmer (op. cit. p. 45, n. 6) points out that these words are not to be taken with post duos triumphos (as Domitian assumed the cognomen of “Germanicus" after the one triumph of 83), but are introduced to explain why he chose the name "Germanicus'' for September. Gsell (p. 45, n. 4) thinks that the two triumphs mentioned here are the double triumph of 89 (see on c. 6, 1), and makes Suetonius guilty of the blunder of asserting that it was not till after this double triumph that Domitian assumed the cognomen of “Germanicus" and gave that name to September. The date when he took the cognomen is fixed by two diplomata militaria (C.I.L. iii pp. 1962, 1963: Dessau, 1996, 1997), the first dated June 9, 83, in which he is still "Domitianus Augustus," and the second dated Sept. 3, 84, in which he appears as "Domitianus Augustus Germanicus." Also on the coins of 84 he is styled Germanicus, but not on those of 83. His new title is referred to in Frontin. Strateg. ii 11, 7, Imperator Caesar Augustus Germanicus eo bello quo victis hostibus cognomen Germanici meruit, etc.: Mart. ii 2, 3, Nobilius (nomen) domito tribuit Germania Rheno, | et puer hoc dignus nomine, Caesar, eras (cf. Dom. 2, 1). | Frater Idumaeos meruit cum patre triumphos, | quae datur ex Chattis laurea, tota tua est: xiv 170, cui nomina Rhenus | vera dedit.

: the date of the renaming of these months is uncertain. Dio (lxvii 4) notices only the change of October to "Domitianus'' after Domitian's first triumph over the Chatti. According to Euseb.-Hieron. the changes were made between Oct. 1, 86 and Sept. 30, 87; but the old names occur in the Acta Arvalia for 87 (C.I.L. vi 2065). Janssen mentions that “Domitianus” is found in a Latin papyrus of 88 (Nicole-Morel, P. Gen. Lat. i 8); the first appearance of either of the new names in a Greek papyrus is in 90 (P. Oxyr. ii p. 164, μηνὸς Δομιτιανοῦ δ'). An inscription of 89 in the Florence Museum has "Germanicus" for September: exces(sit) viii k[al(endas)] Germ[anic(as)] Saeniano et Blaeso co(n)s(ulibus). Martial and Statius do not help to fix the date, as the poems in which they refer to the new names were not published till 94 and 95: Mart. ix 1, 1, Dum Ianus hiemes, Domitianus autumnos | Augustus annis commodabit aestates, | dum grande famuli nomen asseret Rheni | Germanicarum magna lux Kalendarum, etc.: Stat. S. iv 1, 42, nondum omnis honorem | annus habet, cupiuntque decem tua nomina menses. The months recovered their old names at Domitian's death; cf. Plut. Num. 19: Macrob. S. i 12, 36, Mensis September principalem sui retinet appellationem, quem Germanici appellatione, Octobrem vero suo nomine Domitianus invaserat. Sed ubi infaustum vocabulum (i.e. Domitian's name) ex omni aere vel saxo placuit eradi, menses quoque usurpatione tyrannicae appellationis exuti sunt: cautio postea principum ceterorum diri ominis infausta vitantium mensibus a Septembri usque ad Decembrem prisca nomina reservavit. Tiberius refused to allow the name "Tiberius" to be given to September and "Livius" to October (Tib. 26). Nero called April "Neroneus" (Ner. 55). Julius Caesar was honoured by having Quintilis (July) changed to "Iulius” (Iul. 76), and Augustus changed Sextilis (August) to "Augustus" (Aug. 31). Commodus (c. 192 A.D.) called all the months by his own names and titles, Amazonius, Invictus, Felix, Pius, Lucius, Aelius, Aurelius, Commodus, Augustus, Herculeus, Romanus, Exsuperatorius (Dio lxxii 15). The compound transnominare is first found in Suetonius.
: he received the imperium on Sept. 14, 81 A.D.; see on c. 17, 3.
: on Oct. 24, 51 A.D.

: Eutrop. vii 23, cum ob scelera universis exosus esse coepisset, interfectus est suorum coniuratione in Palatio: Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, magis magisque saevitia nimius eoque suspectior etiam suis libertorum consilio uxore non ignara ... poenas luit.

: Dio (lxvii 15) says that those who planned and carried out the plot against Domitian were Parthenius (see c. 16, 2) and Sigerius, who were both Domitian's cubicularii or a cubiculo, Entellus who was a libellis, and Stephanus a freedman (steward of Domitilla, Domitian's niece, see c. 17, 1); he also mentions that Norbanus and Petronius Secundus, praefecti praetorio, were said to have been privy to the plot.
: the reading of YON, adopted by Roth and Preud 'homme. G has insidiis before amicorum, and this is preferred by Ihm. The other MSS. omit the substantive on which the genitives depend.

: Domitia, who lived in continual fear of his vengeance for her infidelity (c. 3, 1); cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, Igitur metu crudelitatis et conscientiae suae coniuravere plerique adscita etiam in consilium tyranni uxore Domitia, ob amorem Paridis histrionis a Principe cruciatus formidante. Dio (l.c.) mentions the report (ὡς λέγεται) that she was aware of the conspiracy: αὐτὸ οὔτε ἡ Δομιτία, ἡ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ, ἠγνόησε . . : ἥ τε γὰρ Δομιτία ἀεί ποτε ὑπ' αὐτοῦ ἐμισεῖτο, καὶ διὰ τοῦτ᾽ ἐφοβεῖτο μὴ καὶ ἀποθάνῃ. goes on to say that Domitian kept under his pillow a list of doomed suspects; while he slept, this was stolen by a page, in whose hands Domitia found it and communicated the contents to the conspirators.
: see on Tit. 5, 2.
: see on Vitell. 14, 4.
: see on Tit. 8, 1. Dio

: the emperor Claudius was poisoned with a boletus (mushroom) medicatus (Claud. 44, 2); cf. Tac. A. xii 67, infusum delectabili cibo boleto venenum: Juv. v 147, boletus (ponetur) domino, sed quales Claudius edit | ante illum uxoris, post quem nihil amplius edit: Mart. i 20, 4, boletum, qualem Claudius edit, edas. Nero, who was a party to the poisoning of Claudius, used afterwards to praise mushrooms as "the food of the gods" (Ner. 33, 1).

div.p: §2. edicti de excidendis vineis: see c. 7, 2.

p.note: : = remitteret; cf. Gell. i 12, gratia Papiae legis per senatum fit. Sonnenschein, on Plaut. Rud. 1414, shows that the phrase gratiam facere alicui alicuius rei or de aliqua re means "to renounce something in favour of someone" and may be used (1) literally "to give up," or (2) "to let off," e.g. Plaut. Cas. 372, de istac Casina huic nostro vilico gratiam facias, ‘‘give up"; Rud. 1414, iuris iurandi volo gratiam facias, "let off"; so in Suet. Tib. 35, 1, equiti Romano iuris iurandi gratiam fecit: Aug. 17, 2, Bononiensibus gratiam fecit coniurandi cum tota Italia pro partibus suis (= concessit ut ne coniurarent, coniurare' remisit, ‘“excused them from joining the general confederation to support his cause'"): Aug. 38, 3, reddendi equi gratiam fecit eis, qui maiores annorum quinque et triginta retinere eum nollent (where see Shuckburgh).

: for this method of defaming an emperor cf. Aug. 55, Etiam sparsos de se in curia famosos libellos nec expavit et (al. nec) magna cura redarguit ac ne requisitis quidem auctoribus id modo censuit, cognoscendum posthac de iis, qui libellos aut carmina ad infamiam cuiuspiam sub alieno nomine edant: Tib. 66, nullo non damnatorum omne probri genus coram vel per libellos in orchestra (where the senators sat in the theatre) positos ingerente.

: these verses are a famous epigram by Evenus of Ascalon, Anth. Pal. ix 75. The second line is the same as the last line of an epigram by Leonidas of Tarentum which gives the full fable, Anth. Pal. ix 99, Ἴξαλος εὐπώγων αἰγὸς πόσις ἔν ποθ᾽ ἁλωῇ | οἴνης τοὺς ἁπαλοὺς πάντας ἔδαψε κλάδους. | τῷ δ᾽ ἔπος ἐκ γαίης τόσον ἄπυε· κεῖρε, κάκιστε, | γναθμοῖς ἡμέτερον κλῆμα τὸ καρποφόρον· | ῥίζα γὰρ ἔμπεδος οὖσα, πάλιν γλυκὺ νέκταρ ἀνήσει, | ὅσσον ἐπισπεῖσαι σοί, τράγε, θυομένῳ. This is imitated by Ovid, F. i 355 sqq., (caper) quem spectans aliquis dentes in vite prementem | talia non tacito verba dolore dedit: "Rode, caper, vitem: tamen hinc, cum stabis ad aram, | in tua quod spargi cornua possit erit." | Verba fides sequitur; noxae tibi deditus hostis | spargitur affuso cornua, Bacche, mero. custom of sacrificing to Bacchus the vine-gnawing goat is referred to in Varr. R.R. i 2; Verg. G. ii 380, non aliam ob culpam Baccho caper omnibus aris | caeditur. The κἄν: a correction by Roth (also in C.I.L. iv 3407, 6) of KAI. Politian read κήν, which is the form in Anth. Pal. ix 75. σοί, τράγε : so Roth (and earlier Bentley) from Anth. Pal. for CΟΙΚΑΡΘΕ (MGLP). Politian, followed by the old editors, read Καίσαρι. Bücheler conjectured σοί, κάπρε, (“nescio an rectius,” Ihm). Alexander, op. cit. 28 sqq., defending σοί, κάπρε, (which he proposes independently) says: "Suetonius may have misquoted, particularly in a place where the Greek τράγε would suggest the Latin caper with a natural reflex again to the Greek κάπρος, or an alteration in the original may have been made designedly by those who scattered abroad the defamatory libelli, to emphasize some point the meaning of which is now obscure." though the boar (κάπρος) is mentioned as devastating vines (Alexander cites Psalm 80 and Ov. M. viii 294), the words φάγῃς ἐπὶ ῥίζαν, “eat away to the root," seem much more appropriate when used of the goat. But

div.p: § 3. excogitatum: Suetonius is peculiar in using excogitatus (= cogitando inventus, ἐπινενοημένος) in the sense of exquisitus, to denote something carefully devised and distinctive; cf. Calig. 22, 3, templum numini suo proprium et sacerdotes et excogitatissimas hostias instituit (these victims including flamingoes, peacocks, guinea-fowl, etc.).

p.note: : see on Galb. 10, 2.

: the trabea was a variety of toga ornamented with trabes, bands or stripes, the arrangement of the stripes being uncertain. Three kinds of trabea were distinguished by Suetonius according to Servius (on Aen. vii 612): Suetonius in libro de Genere vestium (see Introd. c. iv) dicit tria esse genera trabearum: unum diis sacratum, quod est tantum de purpura; aliud regum, quod est purpureum, habet tamen album aliquid; tertium, augurale, de purpura et cocco. Dion. Hal. (ii 70, vi 13) says that the trabea of the Salii was bordered with purple and had scarlet παρυφαί (trabes), while that of the knights was entirely of purple with the same scarlet παρυφαί. The trabea was worn by the kings at Rome; then by consuls at the opening of the temple of Janus; by the Salii in their dance in armour; by knights (trabeata agmina, Stat. S. iv 2, 32), especially on the occasion of a transvectio or decursio equitum (cf. Tac. A. iii 2); and by augurs, the Flamen Dialis, and the Flamen Martialis. See Daremberg-Saglio, v 382; Marquardt, Privatl. 507.

: after his victory over the Chatti in 83 (c. 6, 1) Domitian was 2 P granted 24 lictors (Dio lxvii 4), and this number may have been continued under subsequent emperors. Augustus seems to have had 24 lictors down to 29 B.C.; from then until 23 B.c. he had the 12 consular lictors at Rome, and until 19 B.C. he had 12 lictors outside Rome as proconsul; in 19 в.с. he received for ever the right of having 12 lictors on all occasions (Dio liv 10, ταῖς δώδεκα ῥάβδοις ἀεὶ καὶ πανταχοῦ χρῆσθαι). Cf. Mommsen, Staatsr. i³ 387, ii³ 807; Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2004. apparitores: this word is more frequently used as a general term for the public officers attached to, and in immediate attendance upon, the magistrates at Rome (qui apparent magistratibus), and included the five classes: scribae, accensi, lictores, viatores, praecones; sometimes it is used in a more limited sense excluding the lictores (as here and in Val. Max. vii 3, 9), or the scribae (as in Cic. Verr. iii 66, Plut. Cat. min. 16). Mommsen, op. cit. i 332 sqq.

div.p: § 4. tempore suspecti periculi: i.e. the time foretold by the Chaldaei.

p.note: : cf. Plin. N.H. xxxvi 163, Nerone principe in Cappadocia repertus est lapis duritia marmoris, candidus atque translucens etiam qua parte fulvae inciderant venae, ex argumento phengites (i.e. φεγγίτης from φέγγος, light, brightness) appellatus. Hoc construxerat (Nero) aedem Fortunae amplexus aurea domo (i.e. enclosing this temple in the precincts of his Golden House, see Oth. 7, 1), quare etiam foribus opertis interdiu claritas ibi diurna erat alio quam specularium modo, tamquam inclusa luce, non transmissa. In N.H. xxxvi 196 Pliny mentions wallmirrors made from another stone, Obsian or Obsidian, which he describes as “nigerrimi coloris, aliquando et translucidi, crassiore visu atque in speculis parietum pro imagine umbras reddente.” Guillaume (in Daremberg-Saglio, i 176) says that phengites was probably a gypseous alabaster of a peculiar transparence; Lenz (Mineralogie der alten Griech. und Römer p. 153) describes it as a colourless calcareous spar. Agricola (16th cent.), De Natura Fossilium vii 307, considers it a marble; cf. Chandler, Travels in Greece (1776) с. 63: "The gallery (of the monastery of St. Luke at Stiris) is illuminated with pieces of the transparent marble called Phengites, fixed in the wall in square compartments, and shedding a yellow light." Phengite is a modern name for the species of mica known as Muscovy-glass. The Greek σεληνίτης or moonstone was used as a material for windows and so was called φεγγίτης. •

: cf. Dio lxvii 12, συνεγίγνετο δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς τοῖς κατηγορήσουσι καὶ τοῖς καταμαρτυρήσουσι, καὶ συνέπλαττε καὶ συνετίθει πάνθ' ὅσα λεχθῆναι ἔδει· καὶ πολλάκις καὶ τοῖς δεσμώταις κατὰ μόνας ἐλάλει, τὰ δεσμὰ αὐτῶν ἐν ταῖς χερσὶ κατέχων, οὔτε γὰρ ἄλλοις τὰ λεχθησόμενα ἐπίστευε, καὶ ἐκείνους καὶ δεδεμένους ἐδεδίει. Suetonius uses custodiae in the sense of ii qui custodiuntur in Tib. 61, 5, Calig. 27, 1, and similarly the collective singular in Ner. 31, 3, quod ubique esset custodiae in Italiam deportari praeceperat. Servius (on Aen. xi 184), noting custodia in the sense of qui custodit, condemns the passive use : ut hi qui custodiuntur ‘‘custodiae” dicantur, usurpatum est; unde male est in usu “custodiae audiuntur.” This passive use occurs in Seneca, Ep. 5, 7, eadem catena et custodiam et militem copulat: Dial. ix 11, 12, Ptolemaeum inter Gaianas custodias vidimus; also in Plin. Ep. x 19: Modest. Dig. xlviii 1, 12, praetor custodias auditurus. For other abstract substantives used in a concrete sense by Suetonius see App. i. § 2. α.

: ablative of manner. Cf. Sen.
