Ep. 77, 7, describing how the slaves of the suffering Marcellinus were unwilling to help him to commit suicide, and a Stoic friend of his pointed out to the slaves that it was as bad to prevent one's master from killing himself as it was to kill him (tam mali exempli esse occidere dominum quam prohibere). See also on Vitell. 10, 1, ut pessimi exempli.
: this reading is found only in some of the later MSS., and as a correction in L; audiendam, the reading of the rest, is due to audiebat at the end of the preceding sentence.

: first mentioned in Tac. A. xv 55 in connexion with the discovery of Piso's conspiracy against Nero in 65 A.D. He remained. faithful to Nero to the end, and was one of the three freedmen who accompanied him on his last flight from Rome, and when Nero (hearing that he had been declared a public enemy and sentenced to be scourged to death) wished to kill himself but lacked strength and courage, Epaphroditus aided him: cf. Ner. 49, 3, ferrum iugulo adegit iuvante Epaphrodito a libellis. The Stoic philosopher Epictetus was a slave of his, and he is probably the Epaphroditus at whose suggestion Josephus wrote his Jewish Antiquities, and to whom he dedicates his work against Apion (Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii 36).

: the same office as he had held under Nero, succeeding Doryphorus who died in 62. The expression a libellis denoted both the department of petitions and the head of the department. The emperor Claudius organised the a libellis (ἐπὶ ταῖς βίβλοις) as a distinct office along with the ab epistulis and a cognitionibus. Under Claudius, as under Nero and the Flavian emperors, the a libellis were freedmen; Hadrian and his successors appointed equites. The libelli with which the department dealt were petitions to the emperor from individuals or communities for benefactions or protection, hearing of cases, relief from imposts, etc. In the phrases a libellis, ab epistulis, etc., there is an ellipse of servus (or libertus); cf. Iul. 74, 1, a manu servus (= amanuensis in Tit. 3, 2), the force of a or ab being "on the side of" "in respect of'" "in the department of"; see Kühner-Stegmann i 495, where ab epistulis is explained as ein Sklave von seiten des Briefschreibens.

: Dio (lxvii 14) says that Domitian first banished and later (in 95) executed him as a deterrent to his own freedmen. For the rare abl. with condemnare cf. Vitruv. vii praef. 3, non modo sunt reprehendendi, sed etiam poena condemnandi: Cic. Verr. iii 34, condemnari quadruplo. Suetonius also uses ad, e.g. Claud. 14, ad bestias condemnavit, and in, e.g. Tib. 51, 2, uno in antliam ("the treadmill'') condemnato; in Dom. 11, 1, he has the usual gen. capitis condemnaturus.
: cf. Ner. 40, 1, talem principem paulo minus quattuordecim annos perpessus terrarum orbis tandem destituit.

: cf. Fronto p. 233 N., Quanto quisque eam (sc. mortem) natu minor adeptus est, tanto beatior . . existimandus est: Carm. epigr. 466, 2, Quam praemature sim mortis adeptus. Death in Nero's case was really a boon. adipisci is very rarely used of evils: Cic. Fin. i 32, neque.. quisquam est, qui dolorem amet, consectetur, adipisci velit: Liv. vi 8, 8: Tac. A. i 74: Apul. Plat. ii 11. Cf. febrim nancisci in Tit. 10, 1. 2P2

: a cousin of Domitian, being son of Vespasian 's elder brother Flavius Sabinus (Vesp. 1, 3; Dom. 1, 2); he was a brother of the Flavius Sabinus mentioned in c. 10, 4 as put to death by Domitian. Hardy (Studies in Rom. Hist. p. 67) points out that Clemens was a possible danger to Domitian from a political point of view, being the second personage in the empire as Domitian had no heir of his own. contemptissimae inertiae: this laziness and apathy, which might have rendered Domitian inapprehensive of any revolutionary design on his part, would be urged as a proof that Clemens was a Christian (see below), inactivity and indifference to all public affairs and duties being one of the charges regularly brought by heathen opponents against the Christians; cf. Minuc. Oct. 8, 4, latebrosa et lucifuga natio, in publico muta, in angulis garrula: Tertull. Apol. 42, sed alio quoque iniuriarum titulo postulamur, et infructuosi in negotiis dicimur (a charge which Tertullian indignantly refutes; see Mayor ad loc.). Such aloofness from public life and the interests of their fellow-men formed the charge of "odium humani generis” for which the Christians were condemned in Nero's reign (Tac. A. xv 44). The evidence for the alleged general persecution of Christianity by Domitian is critically examined by Henderson, Five Roman Emperors 45 sqq.

: Clemens was married to Flavia Domitilla, a niece of Domitian (see c. 17, 1), who bore him at least seven children (cf. C.I.L. vi 8942); one, a daughter whose name is unknown, is mentioned in C.I.L. vi 948. The two sons referred to by Suetonius were entrusted (about 90 A.D.) to Quintilian to educate (Quint. iv prooem. 2, quoted on c. 8, 3), and Clemens secured for Quintilian the ornamenta consularia (Auson. Grat. Act. 31). These sons' earlier names are unknown; when designated by adoption as the successors of Domitian their names would be (T. Flavius) Domitianus and (T. Flavius) Vespasianus; some find a reference to this adoption in Stat. S. iv 3, 18, qui (i.e. Domitian) genti patriae futura semper | sancit lumina (but see Vollmer's note).

: by adoption. Such an adoption did not necessarily follow the legal forms; a public pronouncement by the emperor in the Forum, the senate, or the camp was sufficient. See on Galba's adoption of Piso, Galb. 17. There were three other methods used by the emperors in nominating a successor, though theoretically the constitution did not recognize either heredity or designation: (1) giving a co-regency (consortium imperii), see on Tit. 9, 3; (2) designating the intended successor as the emperor's heir; (3) from the time of Hadrian, bestowing on him the name of "Caesar," see on Dom. 1, 3.
: sor and Preud'homme; MGX have abolito; Ihm adopts abolitoque the reading of N.

: sorN; the other MSS. omit iusserat, and it is omitted in Ihm's text, appellari being thus left dependent on destinaverat ; but the passive infin. with destinare is not found in Suetonius and is very rare elsewhere (Thes. Ling. Lat.). Preud 'homme suggested appellare (omitting iusserat), and Bentley would read abolito ... appellans.

: it is a disputed point whether the bronze coins from Smyrna with a figure of a boy or youth and round it the name Οὐεσπασιανὸς νεώτερος (Eckhel vi 402, Cohen i² 539) are to be referred to this adopted son, or to Domitian's own son (mentioned in c. 3, 1) who died young and whose name is unknown. See Stein in Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2623; Gsell, op. cit. p. 53, n. 3.

: Dio (lxvii 14) says that Clemens and his wife Domitilla were charged with ἀθεότης, i.e. neglect of the gods of the State, and adoption of the practices of the Jewish faith (which Dio does not differentiate from Christianity) : κὰν τῷ αὐτῷ ἔτει (95 A.D.) ἄλλους τε πολλοὺς καὶ τὸν Φλάβιον Κλήμεντα ὑπατεύοντα (consulem), καίπερ ἀνεψιὸν ὄντα καὶ γυναῖκα καὶ αὐτὴν συγγενῆ ἑαυτοῦ Φλαβίαν Δομιτίλλαν ἔχοντα, κατέσφαξεν ὁ Δομιτιανός. ἐπηνέχθη δὲ ἀμφοῖν ἔγκλημα ἀθεότητος, ὑφ' ἧς καὶ ἄλλοι ἐς τὰ τῶν ᾿Ἰουδαίων ἤθη ἐξοκέλλοντες (aberrantes) πολλοὶ κατεδικάσθησαν, καὶ οἱ μὲν ἀπέθανον, οἱ δὲ τῶν γοῦν οὐσιῶν ἐστερήθησαν, ἡ δὲ Δομιτίλλα ὑπερωρίσθη μόνον ἐς Πανδατερίαν. Schiller (Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit i 2, 537, n. 6) and Weynand (in Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2578) less probably explain ἀθεότης as a synonym of ἀσέβεια (impietas, c. 10, 1, n.) in the sense of lèse-majesté. With regard to Domitilla's banishment Dio seems to confuse Pandateria with Pontia, another island in the Tuscan sea, also a place of exile, as Hieron. (Epist. 108, 7) says that Pontia is famous as the place of exile of the Christian Domitilla; so too Euseb. (Hist. Eccl. iii 18). See note on Domitillae, c. 17, 1.

p.mentioned: tantum non in ipso eius consulatu
p.note: : Clemens was consul ordinarius along with Domitian in the latter's 17th consulship in 95 A.D., and probably held the office till April 30, four months being the usual tenure in Domitian's reign (Gsell. op. cit. 303). He was put to death in a later part of that year when, strictly speaking, he was not consul but ex-consul. Dio (l.c.) and Philostratus (cited below) are inaccurate in saying that he was consul (ὑπατεύων, ὕπατος) when executed, his real position being ὑπατικός (consularis); see Stein in Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2539. Imhof (Domitianus, p. 116) holds that Clemens as consul ordinarius retained the title of consul for the whole year, even though he was succeeded by consules suffecti, and that he was not put to death till Jan. 96. Gsell makes quite a different use of the same argument in order to reconcile the statements of Dio and Suetonius. He thinks that Dio is speaking of Clemens as consul for the whole of 95, the year of his execution, while Suetonius limits his consulship to the earlier months of that year, when he was actually in office.

: cf. Eutrop. vii 23, 3, (Domitianus) consobrinos suos (i.е. Flavius Clemens and Flavius Sabinus) interfecit: Plin. Pan. 48, illa immanissima belua (i.e. Domitian), сит propinquorum sanguinem lamberet. ... ..

: Philostratus (vit. Apollon. viii 25) says that the intention of the gods to depose Domitian from the presidency of mankind was manifest when he went so far as to slay Clemens: ἐώθουν οἱ θεοὶ Δομετιανὸν ἤδη τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων προεδρίας. ἔτυχε μὲν γὰρ Κλήμεντα ἀπεκτονὼς ἄνδρα ὕπατον, κ.τ.λ.

div.p: § 2. continuis octo mensibus: i.e. the eight months preceding his death on Sep. 18, 96 A.D. Imhof says that they were the eight months intervening between the execution of Clemens (which, according to his theory, took place in Jan. 96) and the death of Domitian, and Schiller takes the same view.

p.note: : = fulmina, lightning-flashes that descend and strike, thunderbolts, a use of fulgura found in poetry and post-Aug. prose, e.g. Verg. G. i 487 (of the portents at Caesar's death), non alias caelo ceciderunt plura sereno | fulgura. Cf. Galb. 4, 2.
: sc. Iuppiter; cf. Luc. ii 60 (an appeal to Jove), utrasque simul partesque ducesque feri: Sen. N.Q. ii 46, quare Iuppiter aut ferienda transit aut innoxia ferit?

: cf. Calig. 57, 2, futurae caedis (i.e. the murder of Caligula) multa prodigia extiterunt Capitolium Capuae de caelo tactum est, item Romae cella Palatini atriensis; Claud. 46 (among the praesagia of the death of Claudius), tactum de caelo monumentum Drusi patris: Galb. 1 (in Nero's last days), tacta de caelo Caesarum aede, capita omnibus statuis simul deciderunt, Augustique sceptrum e manibus excussum est. Other instances of this portent are found in Cic. Div. ii 21, 47; Liv. xxv 7, xxix 14, etc. Seneca, N.Q. ii 49, gives different classifications of fulmina with their significance as portents.
: = templum Iovis Capitolini; both it and the templum Flaviae gentis had been built by Domitian himself (see c. 5).

: Domitian's magnificent restoration of the Palatina domus (see on Vesp. 25), completed in 92 A.D., was the work of the architect Rabirius; cf. Mart. vii 56, 1, Astra polumque pia cepisti mente, Rabiri, | Parrhasiam (= Palatinam) mira qui struis arte domum. The part of the imperial palace on the Palatine which still exists above ground is mainly due to this reconstruction under Domitian; see Platner-Ashby, Topogr. Dict. Rome 158 sqq. Ancient writers give no account of the whole building, but are lavish in their praises of its splendour; e.g. Mart. viii 36, 1, Regia pyramidum, Caesar, miracula ride; | iam tacet Eoum barbara Memphis opus: | pars quota Parrhasiae labor est Mareoticus (= Aegyptius) aulae? | Clarius in toto nil videt orbe dies: Stat. S. iv 2, 18, Tectum augustum, ingens, non centum insigne columnis, | sed quantae superos caelumque Atlante remisso | sustentare queant. Stupet hoc vicina Tonantis | regia teque pari laetantur sede locatum | numina. Cf. also Plut. Poplic. 15, Philostrat. vit. Apollon. vii 32.
: see on Vesp. 23, 3.
: probably the colossal equestrian statue (described in Stat. S. i 1) which was decreed to Domitian by the senate and people for his victories over the Chatti and Dacians (c. 6, 1).

: this inscription was not carved on the marble base of the statue, but must have been on a plate of bronze fastened to it. Among the omens prophetic of the death of Augustus was the blotting out by a thunderbolt of the letter C from the name Caesar in the inscription on one of his statues, the haruspices declaring that this foretold that he would live 100 (C = centum) days and would then become a god, as the word aesar in Etruscan denoted a god (Aug. 97, 2).
: the cypress-tree which earlier had fallen and risen erect again as an omen of Vespasian's rise to power (Vesp. 5, 4).

: at Praeneste (Palestrina) 20 miles E. of Rome there was a famous temple and oracle of Fortuna primigenia (an epithet explained as meaning the mother of life or the firstborn daughter of Jove). Cicero (Div. ii 41, 85) tells the tale of the foundation of the oracle. A Praenestine, Numerius Suffucius, was bidden by a dream to cleave a rock, and a great number of wooden lots (sortes), inscribed in antique characters, fell out, while honey flowed from an olive-tree close by. The haruspices ordained that the olive-tree should be made into a box, in which the lots were enclosed, and one was drawn by a child when the oracle was consulted. Cicero says that in his day only the vulgar had resort to it, but under the Empire it came into favour again. Tiberius tried to do away with all oracles near Rome, but desisted through fright at the divine power of the Praenestine lots, for though he had them conveyed in a sealed chest to Rome, they could not be found till the chest was taken back to the temple of Fortuna (Tib. 63). The future greatness of Alexander Severus was foretold by the Praenestine oracle with a sors bearing the words of Virgil "si qua fata aspera rumpas, | tu Marcellus eris” (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 4). For other references to the oracle see Prop. ii 32, 3: Luc. ii 193: Juv. xiv 88: Sil. Ital. viii 365.

: on the Kalends of January Domitian sent gifts to the goddess and made sacrifice at the temple at Praeneste. In Rome on that day, in accordance with old Republican usage, there was a solemn votorum nuncupatio pro incolumitate reipublicae on the Capitol, and on Jan. 3 vows were offered pro incolumitate principis. As the goddess Fortuna deserted Domitian, so she had deserted Galba when his doom was approaching; see Galb. 18, 2.

div.p: § 3. Minervam colebat: for the special honours paid by Domitian to Minerva, whose son he claimed to be, see on c. 4, 4.

p.note: : Dio (lxvii 16) gives a different version of the dream: ἄλλα τε αὐτῷ σημεῖα ἐγένετο, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ ὕπνῳ τόν τε ῾Ρούστικον (i.e. Junius Rusticus, whom he had put to death, see c. 10, 3) ξίφει προσιέναι οἱ, καὶ τὴν ᾿Αθηνῶν, ἣν ἐν τῷ κοιτῶνι (cubiculo) ἱδρυμένην εἶχε, τὰ ὅπλα ἀποβεβληκέναι, καὶ ἐπὶ ἅρματος ἵππων μελάνων ἐς χάσμα ἐσπίπτειν ἔδοξεν. excedere was the word regularly used of the gods leaving a doomed place; cf. Tac. H. v 13, Exapertae repente delubri (i.e. the Temple at Jerusalem) fores, et audita maior humana vox, excedere deos; simul ingens motus excedentium: Verg. A. ii 351, Excessere omnes, adytis arisque relictis, | di, quibus imperium hoc steterat.

: if the reading is sound, Suetonius here combines two of the constructions which he uses with somniare: the inf. (e.g. Aug. 91, 2, somniavit queri Capitolinum Iovem) and the pres. ptc. (Galb. 4, 3, somniavit Fortunam dicentem). He couples the inf. with the passive ptc. (esse omitted) in Calig. 57, 3, somniavit consistere se in caelo iuxta solium Iovis impulsumque ab eo dextri pedis pollice et in terras praecipitatum. Roth and Preud'homme mark a lacuna before negantemque; Stephanus read negantem; Oudendorp proposed, negantem quoque; P. Thomas would insert lacrimantem before negantemque. exarmata. a love: according to the old Greek legend Zeus himself gave birth to Athena, who sprang fully armed from his head. In Homer she appears as the protectress of heroes, and in Il. v 736 she is described as arming herself with the shield (aegis), helmet, and spear of her father Zeus. ..

: this is the only place where Suetonius uses perinde with quam instead of with ac, atque, ut, ac si, which he has elsewhere. Tacitus often has perinde . quam, mainly in neg. sentences; see Heraeus on H. i 30: Draeger, Synt. Tac. 175.

: this is the reading of all the MSS., but the name is not found elsewhere. Bentley conjectured Ascleparionis, a correction suggested also by Kumanudis and approved by Boissevain (on Dio lxvii 16) who says: "forma ᾿Ασκληταρίων nihili est nec usquam reperitur, ᾿Ασκληπαρίων redit C.I.A. 3, 3521." Cumont (Catal. codd. astrol. Graec. v p. 205) would read Asclationis, assuming that the astrologer mentioned by Suetonius is Asclation, an astrologer cited by Vettius Valens (astrological writer c. 140 A.D.).
: see on Vitell. 14, 4. The predictions by astrologers of Domitian's death are mentioned in c. 14, 1.
: see on Vitell. 14, 4.
: the acc. with sciscitari (instead of ex or ab) is first found in Livy; cf. Vitell. 7, 3, Calig. 28.

: Dio (lxvii 16) says that he was sentenced to be burnt alive, and when this was being done a torrent of rain quenched the pyre: ἕτερος τέ τις πρότερόν ποτε εἰπὼν αὐτῷ καὶ ὁπότε καὶ ὅπως φθαρήσεται, ἔπειτα ἐρωτηθεὶς ὁποίῳ αὐτὸς τέλει τοῦ βίου χρήσεται, καὶ ἀποκρινάμενος ὅτι ὑπὸ κυνῶν ἀναλωθήσεται, ἐκελεύσθη μὲν ζῶν κατακαυθῆναι, καὶ τὸ πῦρ αὐτῷ προσήχθη. ὑετοῦ δὲ ἐν τούτῳ πολλοῦ καταρρυέντος ἥ τε πυρὰ ἐσβέσθη καὶ ἐκεῖνον κύνες ὀπίσω τὼ χεῖρε δεδεμένον καὶ ἐπικείμενον ἐπ' αὐτῆς εὑρόντες διεσπάραξαν. The burning alive and the quenching of the pyre by rain are reminiscent of the story of the deliverance of Croesus when Cyrus ordered him to be placed upon the pyre (Hdt. i 86 sq.).
: see on Tit. 5, 3.

: though sepelire denoted more especially inhumation (cf. Cic. Legg. ii 23, where it is opposed to urere), it was also used of performing the funeral rites by burning; even humare could be used of burning not of burying, e.g. Nep. Eumen. 13, Antigonus Eumenem mortuum propinquis suis sepeliendum tradidit: hi militari honestoque funere . humaverunt, ossaque eius in Cappadociam deportanda curaverunt. ..

: funus is used vaguely here to include the pyre and the body placed upon it. Servius has three notes explaining the word: (1) on Aen. iii 62, proprie “funus” est incensum cadaver; (2) on Aen. ii 539, “funus” est iam ardens cadaver, quod dum portatur “exequias” dicimus, crematum iam “reliquias,” conditum iam ‘‘sepulcrum”; (3) on Aen. iii 22, apparatus mortuorum “funus” dici solet: exstructio lignorum “rogus”: subiectio ignis “pyra”: crematio cadaveris ‘“bustum”: locus “ustrina”: operis exstructio “sepulcrum”: nomen inscriptum ‘‘monumentum.”

: Latinus, an archimimus, is named as a powerful delator under Domitian by the Schol. on Juv. iv 53, on the authority of the historian Marius Maximus. Juvenal mentions Latinus as a delator (i 36) and as an actor (mimus) playing the part of an adulterer concealed in a trunk (vi 44). Martial refers to his acting (i 4, 5: ii 72, 3: iii 86, 3: 61, 11: xiii 3, 2) and has one whole epigram (ix 28) in which he combines the praises of Latinus with those of Domitian his "master" and his "god": Dulce decus scaenae, ludorum fama, Latinus | ille ego sum plausus deliciaeque tuae, | qui spectatorem potui fecisse Catonem, | solvere qui Curios Fabriciosque graves. | Sed nihil a nostro sumpsit mea vita theatro, | et sola tantum scaenicus arte feror: | nec poteram gratus domino sine moribus esse; | interius mentes inspicit ille deus. | Vos me laurigeri parasitum dicite Phoebi, Roma sui famulum dum sciat esse Iovis (i.e. Domitian). On the favour enjoyed by actors, especially mimi or pantomimi, in the imperial household see Friedl. Sitteng. ii¹º 143 sqq. This is the only passage in which Suetonius uses mimus for the actor (histrio), elsewhere it denotes the play or farce (see on Oth. 3, 2); archimimus for a principal actor occurs in Vesp. 19, 2.

: "gossip"; cf. Aug. 70, 1, cena eius secretior ("private") in fabulis fuit ("was a subject of gossip'): Juv. i 145, it nova nec tristis per cunctas fabula cenas: Plin. Ep. viii 18, habes omnes fabulas urbis.
: for this constr. see on c. 11, 1.

: Pliny describes these as African apples, more like berries than apples, of two kinds, one white, the other a deep red. They were introduced into Italy about 36 A.D., and Martial mentions them as grown in Italy. Cf. Plin. N.H. xv 47, (māla) peregrina sunt zizypha ("jujubes') et tubures, quae et ipsa non pridem venere in Italiam, haec ex Africa, illa ex Syria. Sex. Papinius, quem consulem vidimus, primus utraque attulit, divi Augusti novissimis temporibus, in castris sata, bacis similiora quam malis, sed aggeribus praecipua decora, quoniam et in tecta iam silvae scandunt. Tuberum duo genera: candidum et a colore Syricum dictum: Mart. xiii 42, Non tibi de Libycis tubures et apyrina (i.e. pomegranates with soft kernels) ramis, | de Nomentanis sed damus arboribus: xiii 43, Lecta suburbanis mittuntur apyrina ramis | et vernae ("home-grown'') tubures. Quid tibi cum Libycis? Harduin explains tubures as nucipersica "nut-peaches"; Stahr translates it in our passage by "Trüffeln (truffles), but that would be tubera. The form tubures (not tuberes) is the better attested in Suetonius, Pliny, and Martial.

: Domitian was assassinated on Sept. 18, 96 A.D. In that year the moon would enter Aquarius on Sept. 15/16 and leave it on Sept. 18/19. A red moon usually betokened wind; cf. Arat. Phaen. 784; Verg. Georg. i 431, vento semper rubet aurea Phoebe; Luc. v 549, ventorumque nota rubuit (luna). Domitian predicted that by reason of his murder the moon on the morrow would be red with blood. The adjs. cruentus and sanguineus were used of the heavenly bodies in the sense of "blood-red," e.g. Sen. N.Q. vii 17, 3, cruenti cometae omen post se futuri sanguinis ferunt: Verg. Aen. x 273, cometae | sanguinei lugubre rubent: Ov. Am. ii 1, 23, sanguineae cornua lunae. The ominous significance of the moon being in Aquarius is perhaps to be deduced from Macrob. Comm. in Somn. Scip. i 12, Et quia in Leone sunt rudimenta nascendi et quaedam humanae naturae tirocinia, Aquarius autem adversus Leoni est et illo oriente mox occidit: ideo, cum sol Aquarium tenet, Manibus parentatur, utpote in signo quod humanae vitae contrarium vel adversum feratur. Janssen cites an explanation given by Prof. Van Wageningen: Luna in Aquario tum erat, cuius tertius decanus est Lunae, cf. Firm. Mat., Math. ii 3: “Aquarii primus decanus Veneris est, secundus Mercurii, tertius Lunae.'" Decanus autem dicitur in lingua astrologorum qui decem ex triginta partibus orbis signiferi praeerat. Eadem autem pars Aquarii arbitrio paret Martis et Saturni stellarum vagarum, cf. Firm. ii 5, 12, qui dicit etiam “Aquarii dominus est Saturnus.” Hic cum esset omnium errantium pessimus, iure suspicabatur Domitianus dirum quoddam exstiturum. Domitian's prediction resembles that of the prophet Joel (2, 31): “The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord be come."
: see on Vesp. 5, 5.

: Dio (lxvii 16) gives the name of the soothsayer as Larginus Proclus, and says that the death-penalty was postponed in order that it might be inflicted when Domitian had survived the danger; after Domitian had been slain, the soothsayer was set free and rewarded by Nerva with 400,000 sesterces: ὁ δὲ δὴ μάλιστα διὰ πάντων ἄξιον θαυμάσαι ἐστί, Λαργῖνός τις Πρόκλος, δημοσίᾳ προειπὼν ἐν Γερμανίᾳ ὅτι τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ, ἐν ᾗ ἀπέθανε, τελευτήσει, ἀνεπέμφθη τε ἐς τὴν ῾Ρώμην ὑπὸ τοῦ ἄρχοντος, καὶ ἐσαχθεὶς πρὸς τὸν Δομιτιανὸν ἔφη καὶ τότε τοῦθ' οὕτως ἕξειν, καὶ καταδικασθεὶς τὴν ἐπὶ θανάτῳ ἀνεβλήθη τε ὅπως διαφυγόντος αὐτοῦ τὸν κίνδυνον ἀποθάνῃ, κὰν τούτῳ τοῦ Δομιτιανοῦ σφαγέντος ἐσώθη καὶ δέκα μυριάδας δραχμῶν παρὰ τοῦ Νέρουα ἔλαβεν. For other predictions of the time of Domitian's death see c. 14, 1.
: by the governor of the province, as Dio states.

: a change of government; cf. Galb. 8, 2, пес defuerunt qui interpretarentur significari rerum mutationem, etc.: Cic. Att. viii 3, 4, multi mutationis rerum cupidi: Justin xl 2, quod prodigium mutationem rerum portendere haruspices responderunt.

div.p: § 2. verrucam: “wart'” (ἀκροχορδών), a word familiar from the proverbial expression in Hor. S. i 3, 74, Qui ne tuberibus propriis offendat amicum | postulat, ignoscet verrucis illius. Serenus Sammonicus (Poet. Lat. Min. Baehrens iii 158) describes the nature and treatment of verrucae (Interdum existit turpi verruca papilla, etc.), and the means of stopping the flow of blood if they burst (Si rupta inmensos fundet verruca cruores, etc.). =

p.note: : utinam nihil amplius (et gravius) accidat; cf. Sil. Ital. ix 347, sitque hactenus, oro. The various uses of hactenus are fully illustrated in Hand Turs. iii 4 sqq. Suetonius has it five times followed by ut (e.g. Vesp. 13, where see note); he also uses it in Calig. 22, 1, Hactenus quasi de principe, reliqua ut de monstro narranda sunt ("Thus far forth as of a prince; now forward relate we must as of a monster" Holland), and in vit. Ter. 5, 2, Cicero in Limone hactenus ("to this extent'") laudat (Terentium).

: for the plural cf. Cic. Brut. 54, 200, videt oscitantem iudicem, loquentem cum altero, nonnumquam etiam circulantem, mittentem ad horas; Plin. N.H. vii 182 (quoted below): the sing. is used in Hor. S. ii 6, 44, hora quota est?
: not merely the day but the very hour of his death had been predicted to him by the astrologers; see c. 14, 1. .. ..

: from the middle of the 2nd cent. B.C. sundials (solaria) and water-clocks (clepsydrae) were in use at Rome, every wealthy house having special slaves to announce the hours, from whom the master asked the time; cf. Plin. N.H. vii 182, obiit Cn. Bebius Tamphilus cum a puero quaesisset horas: Mart. viii 68, 1, horas quinque puer nondum tibi nuntiat, et tu | iam conviva mihi, Caeciliane, venis: Juv. x 215, clamore opus est ut sentiat auris, | quem dicat venisse puer, quot nuntiet horas: Plin. Ep. iii 1, ubi hora balinei nuntiata est: Sen. de brev. vit. 12, 6, quos quando lavari debeant, quando natare, quando cenare, alius admonet: Sidon. Ep. ii 9, nuntium per spatia clepsydrae horarum incrementa servantem. Marquardt, Privatl.2 256 sqq., 788 sqq. tertia

: the refreshing of the body by the siesta (meridiatio), which came at the sixth hour, i.e. noon; cf. Martial (iv 8) on the division of the hours of the day between social duties, business, and recreation: Prima salutantes atque altera continet hora, | exercet raucos causidicos; | in quintam varios extendit Roma labores, | sexta quies lassis, septima finis erit; etc. Stahr translates our passage, “er eben im Begriff war sich eilig zum Bade zu begeben," and so Rolfe, he was hastening to the bath," but the meaning is fixed by Dio lxvii 17, ἀναπαύσεσθαι τὸ μεθημερινόν, ὥσπερ εἰώθει, ἔμελλε.

: freedman and chamberlain of Domitian, who gave him the high privilege of wearing the sword or dagger (pugio, see on Galb. 11) which was usually granted only to military officers such as the praefectus praetorio; cf. Dio lxvii 15, ἐπέθεντο δὲ αὐτῷ (i.e. Domitian) καὶ συνεσκευάσαντο τὴν πρᾶξιν Παρθένιός τε ὁ πρόκοιτος (cubicularius) αὐτοῦ, καίπερ οὕτω τιμώμενος παρ' αὐτοῦ ὡς καὶ ξιφηφορεῖν, κ.τ.λ. The murder of Domitian secured the throne for Nerva, but the new emperor was unable to protect Parthenius and his fellow-conspirators when their punishment was demanded by the praetorians in 97 A.D., and Parthenius was first mutilated and then slain; [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 12, 8, demptis prius genitalibus et in os coniectis, iugulavere. He was a patron of Martial and presented him with a toga (Mart. viii 28, ix 49); Martial asks him to introduce his books to the emperor's notice (v 6, xi 1, xii 11), and speaks in extravagant terms of the poetic talents of Parthenius himself: xii 11, Parthenio dic, Musa, tuo nostroque salutem: | nam quis ab Aonio largius amne bibit? | Cuius Pimpleo lyra clarior exit ab antro? | Quem plus Pierio de grege Phoebus amat? He may be the Parthenius "Aug. libertus a cubiculo” mentioned in C.I.L. vi 8764 (= Dessau 1736).

: even under the Republic the cubicularii, or grooms of the bedchamber, filled positions of confidence and exercised. 'great influence; Cicero (Att. vi 2, 5) boasts that he as governor of Cilicia was not approachable for any purpose through his cubicularii. In the imperial household the cubicularii were a numerous body of slaves or freedmen with a special commissariat and medical service (see Marquardt, Privatl.2 144). They were divided into a prima statio and a secunda statio, but it is doubtful whether these relieved each other on duty, or were distinguished by different degrees of access to the emperor's person as Friedlaender suggests. These two classes were subdivided into decuries (see Dom. 17, 2), and at their head was a supra cubicularios or praepositus cubiculo (πρόκοιτος, ὁ ἐπὶ τοῦ κοιτῶνος), always in close attendance on the emperor and having his ear more than any other man. One of the duties of a chamberlain was to supervise the introduction of visitors; so Parthenius announced to Domitian the arrival of Stephanus.
: = ab corporis cura avertit et alii rei intendit (Baumg.-Cr.).

: i.e. Stephanus, who pretended that he had a conspiracy to reveal; see c. 17, 1. Philostratus (vit. Apollon. viii 25) says that Stephanus in person accosted Domitian as he was returning from the law-court and asked him for a private audience, as he had something important to say; Domitian then took him aside privately into the men's apartment (ἀνδρών) of the palace, where Stephanus stabbed him. (lxvii 17) simply says that when Domitian left the court for his midday rest Parthenius removed the blade of the dagger which was always under the emperor's pillow, and then introduced Stephanus. Dio
: for the indirect question with cunctari see on c. 2, 3, diu cunctatus an offerret.
: see on Galb. 19, 2. For the names of the principal conspirators see on Dom. 14, 1. minimi

p.mentioned: quando et quo modo, id est, lavantemne an cenantem
p.note: : Burman and Baumg.-Cr. would delete id est, while Ernesti would change id est to item, on the ground that lavantemne an cenantem would correspond rather with quando et quo loco. If change is necessary, quando ex commodo “when most conveniently'' might be suggested. According to the MSS. Suetonius several times uses id est or hoc est in giving an explanation or limiting more definitely a general expression; e.g. Iul. 19, 2, provinciae negoti, id est, silvae callesque: Aug. 26, 2 magno, id est, septemdecim annorum intervallo: Aug. 88, orthographiam, id est, formulam rationemque scribendi a grammaticis institutam: Vesp. 11, neve filiorum familiarum faeneratoribus exigendi crediti ius umquam esset: hoc est, ne post patrum quidem mortem. In all such passages editors are naturally inclined to regard the words introduced by id est or hoc est as mere glosses. But it must be remembered that Suetonius was a grammaticus, to whom exposition would become a second nature.

: Philostratus (vit. Apollon. viii 25) says that this freedman of Domitilla, who had been signified by the portent of a στέφανος (corona) surrounding and dimming the orb of the sun, brooded on the murder of Flavius Clemens, or on the wrongs of the Romans generally, and attacked Domitian in a spirit worthy of the Athenian champions of liberty (such as Harmodius and Aristogeiton). The fact which Suetonius mentions, that Stephanus was to be tried for embezzlement, probably influenced him much more than any general considerations. Dio (lxvii 18) has a remarkable story that Apollonius of Tyana on the very day and at the very hour when Domitian was murdered assembled the multitude at Ephesus or elsewhere and exclaimed “καλῶς, Στέφανε, εὖγε, Στέφανε, παῖε τὸν μιαιφόνον. ἔπληξας, ἔτρωσας, ἀπέκτειναs." Dio avers that this was so, however incredible it may seem (κἂν μυριάκις τις ἀπιστήσῃ). Stephanus himself was slain by those who rushed in to the aid of Domitian and were not privy to the plot (Dio c. 17).

: Flavia Domitilla, a granddaughter of Vespasian (C.I.L. vi 948, 8942) and niece of Domitian; her mother Flavia Domitilla, sister of Domitian, died before the accession of Vespasian (see Vesp. 3), and so in Philostrat. vit. Apollon. viii 25, where the Domitilla of our passage is spoken of as a sister of Domitian, ἀδελφιδῆν ‘“niece" must be restored for ἀδελφήν. Domitilla was wedded to Flavius Clemens, who was put to death by Domitian, and she herself was banished as a Christian (see c. 15, 1, and note). According to Philostratus she was ordered by Domitian within a few days after her husband's execution “ ἐς ἀνδρὸς φοιτᾶν” (“to join her husband in death"; Gsell explains "to wed again"). For her history and a discussion of the improbable theory that one Flavia Domitilla, wife of Clemens, was banished for political reasons to Pandateria, and that another Flavia Domitilla, niece of Clemens (Euseb. Hist. Eccl. iii 18), was banished as a Christian to Pontia see Stein in Pauly-Wissowa, vi '2733; Gsell, op. cit. 298 sqq.; Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii 81.

: “embezzled," in which sense intervertere (e.g. Vitell. 7, 2) is much more common. Suetonius also uses intercipere of literary plagiarism; Gramm. 5, commentarios, quorum tamen pars maxima intercepta dicitur. In [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, 11 we are told (if the reading is correct) that it was Clodianus (mentioned below by Suet. as a cornicularius) who was charged with embezzlement: Coniuravere plerique, impulsoribus Parthenio procurante cubiculum, et Stephano, et tum ob fraudem interceptae pecuniae supplicium suspectante Clodiano (probably et should be removed before tum and inserted before Clodiano).

: for the comparative cf. Tib. 6, 4, where sinisterior funalis equus means the trace-horse on the left side as opp. to the dexterior, the trace-horse on the right; SO in Claud. 7, dexteriore umero: Galb. 21, in dexteriore latere eius. Suetonius more frequently uses the positives dexter and sinister. Earlier instances of dexterior and sinisterior are found in Varr. L.L. ix 34, Galba in Cic. Fam. x 30, 3, Ον. M. ii 138, vii 241, xii 303, Cels. iv 1, and other passages collected by Neue-Wagener, Formenlehre ii³ 187.

: the bandages may have been rolled round the wool to keep it in its place, or lanis fasciisque may be a hendiadys for laneis fasciis "woollen bandages." For fascia "bandage" cf. Galb. 21: Cic. Brut. 60, 217, devinctus fasciis et multis medicamentis propter dolorem artuum delibutus. See also on galbeo in Galb. 3, 1.

: a certain restoration by Ferrarius for dolum or dolo of the MSS. A dolo was a sword-cane with a blade in it that might be used as a stiletto (Hesych., δόλωνες· ξιφίδια ἐν ξύλοις ἀποκεκρυμμένα); cf. Claud. 13, 1 (of assassins lying in wait for Claudius), reperti et equestris ordinis duo in publico cum dolone ac venatorio cultro praestolantes. As a weapon of war dolo meant a pole with a short iron point, e.g. Aen. vii 664, pila manu saevosque gerunt in bella dolones, where Servius comments, "dolo est aut flagellum intra cuius virgam latet pugio; aut, secundum Varronem, ingens contus cum ferro brevissimo.” professus conspirationis indicium: Philostratus (vit. Apollon. viii 25) says that what Stephanus revealed to Domitian was that Flavius Clemens (see c. 15, 1) was not dead as the emperor thought, but was still alive in a place known to Stephanus, and was planning to attack Domitian.

: for libellus used of a written information lodged by an informer (delator) cf. Plin. Ep. vii 27, nihil notabile secutum, nisi forte, quod non fui reus: futurus, si Domitianus, sub quo haec acciderunt, diutius vixisset. Nam in scrinio eius datus a Caro de me libellus inventus est.

: cf. Philostr., l.c., μέγα δ' αὐτοῦ βοήσαντος περὶ ὧν ἤκουσε, τεταραγμένῳ προσπεσὼν ὁ Στέφανος καὶ τὸ ξίφος τῆς ἐσκευασμένης χειρὸς ἀνασπάσας διῆκε τοῦ μηροῦ πρὸς μὲν τὸν αὐτίκα θάνατον οὐ καιρίαν, πρὸς δὲ τὸν μετὰ ταῦτα οὐκ ἄκαιρον (i.e. the wound was fatal, though not immediately so): Suidas, δ.υ. Δομετιανόs, says that Domitian was stabbed during his siesta: Στέφανον προσπεσόντα Δομετιανῷ καθεύδοντι τὸ μεθημερινὸν πατάξαι μέν, οὐ μὴν καιρίαν, ἀναπηδήσαντος γοῦν ἐκείνου.

div.p: § 2. Clodianus: cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, 11 (quoted above on interceptarum); he is not mentioned elsewhere.

p.note: : a title derived from corniculum, a decoration consisting of one or two small horns fastened to the side of the helmet, conferred on soldiers for distinguished service; e.g. Liv. x 44, equites omnes ob insignem multis locis operam corniculis armillisque argenteis donavit. Suetonius (Gramm. 9) tells us that the famous "plagosus" Orbilius gained this distinction when serving in Macedonia. From such distinguished soldiers were chosen the adjutants attached to the principal officers, and cornicularius is regularly used for an adjutant. Under the Republic one was attached to the tribunus militum whose turn it was to command (cf. Val. Max. vi 1, 11), and in inscriptions under the Empire we frequently find references to the cornicularius of the legates legionis, the tribunus militum, the praefectus praetorio, etc. Civil officials, e.g. the praefectus annonae, when their departments came to be organised in military form, had their cornicularii; see Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 546. In the Thes. Ling. Lat. our passage is cited as an instance of cornicularius used de officio civili, but Clodianus in all probability was attached to one of the praefecti praetorio, Norbanus and Petronius Secundus, who took part in the conspiracy; see on c. 14, 1.

: cf. Dio lxvii 17 (when Domitian was struggling with Stephanus and had thrown him to the ground), Παρθένιος, δείσας μὴ διαφύγῃ (ὁ Δομιτιανός), ἐπεισεπήδησεν, ἤ, ὥς γέ τισι δοκεῖ, Μάξιμον ἐξελεύθερον (libertum) ἐπεισέπεμψε.

: the person denoted by this name (or the variant "Saturius" read by Roth and Preud'homme) is elsewhere called Sigerus or Sigerius. Dio mentions Sigerus, a chamberlain (πρόκοιτος), as a prominent conspirator along with Parthenius (see c. 16, 2), and the two are coupled in Tertull. Apol. 35, unde qui armati palatium inrumpunt, omnibus tot Sigeriis atque Partheniis audaciores?; cf. also Mart. iv 78, 8 (addressing a fussy old fool who is always visiting the Palace and talks of nothing but the chamberlains): Sigeriosque meros Partheniosque sonas, where Friedlaender and others prefer the correction Sigerosque, both forms of the name occurring in inscriptions, “Sigerus" much more frequently.
: see on c. 16, 2, cubiculo praepositus.
: this participant in the murder is not mentioned elsewhere. For the emperor's ludus gladiatorius see on c. 4, 1.

: this is Ernesti's correction of curae, and is approved by *Oudendorp and adopted in their texts by Wolf, Baumg.-Cr., Roth, Preud 'homme, and Janssen. Burman conjectured cui cura, but this involves the insertion of et before hoc amplius. C. G. Müller proposed cura, in the sense of curator. The reading of the MSS., curae assistens, is retained by Ihm; though it lacks any parallel in Suetonius, it may possibly be defended by Minuc. Fel. Oct. 26, angelos, id est ministros et nuntios dei venerationi eius novit adsistere. ...

: there was a shrine for the worship of the Lares either in or attached to the imperial bedchamber; cf. Aug. 7, 1, where we read of a bronze statuette of the young Augustus presented by Suetonius himself to the emperor Hadrian (whose secretary he was) and worshipped by Hadrian among his Lares: puerilem imagunculam Augusti aeream quae dono a me principi data inter cubiculi Lares colitur. As loyal citizens associated the Genius of Augustus with the Lares (cf. Hor. C. iv 5, 31), and included likenesses of the reigning emperor among the "gods of their family," so we find the emperors themselves introducing among these gods the images of those whom they specially revered: cf. Capitol. M. Anton. Philos. 3, tantum honoris magistris suis (i.e. his teachers of philosophy) detulit, ut imagines eorum aureas in larario haberet: Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 29, matutinis horis in larario suo in quo et divos principes, sed optimos electos, et animas sanctiores, in quis Apollonium et Christum, Abraham, et Orpheum et huiuscemodi ceteros habebat, ac maiorum effigies divinam faciebat: c. 31, Vergilium autem Platonem poetarum vocabat eiusque imaginem cum Ciceronis simulacro in secundo larario habuit ubi et Achillis et magnorum virorum. Alexandrum vero Magnum inter optimos et divos in larario maiore consecravit. The word lararium for a shrine of the Lares is first used by these Scriptores Historiae Augustae; aedicula is used earlier, e.g. Petron. Satyr. 29, Juv. viii 111. See also Vitell. 2, 5. rem

: in the Thes. Ling. Lat. (i 2016) this is given as an instance of hoc (abl.) amplius = praeterea (see Appendix i. § 6); but Howard and Jackson (Index Suet.) are much more probably right in taking hoc as acc. here and in Aug. 27, 2, Iulius Saturninus hoc amplius tradit.
: sc. lecti, as in Iul. 84, 1, lectus et ad caput tropaeum.

: only the hilt was left, the blade having been withdrawn by Parthenius; Dio lxvii 17, τοῦ ξίφους, ὁ ἀεί ποτε ὑπὸ τῷ προσκεφαλαίῳ (pulvino) ἔκειτο, τὸ σιδήριον ὁ Παρθένιος ἐξεῖλεν, ὅπως μὴ χρήσηται. deducto ad terram: καταβληθεὶς ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ (Δομιτιανοῦ) ἔκειτο (Dio, l.c.). For this use of deducere cf. Stat. Th. viii 851 (of wrestlers), deducit in aequum et celsum procurvat Agyllea Tydeus: Petron. Satyr. 127, implicitum me brachiis deduxit in terram.

: the desperate struggling of the wounded Domitian, until he was finally overcome by numbers, is described with further details by Philostratus (l.c.): ὁ δ᾽ ἐρρωμένος μὲν καὶ ἄλλως τὸ σῶμα, γεγονὼς δὲ περὶ τὰ πέντε καὶ τετταράκοντα ἔτη, ξυνεπλάκη τρωθείς, καὶ καταβαλὼν τὸν Στέφανον ἐπέκειτο, τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ὀρύττων καὶ τὰς παρειὰς ξυντρίβων πυθμένι χρυσῆς κύλικος αὐτοῦ κειμένης περὶ τὰ ἱερά, ἐκάλει δὲ καὶ τὴν ᾿Αθηνῶν ἀρωγόν. συνέντες οὖν οἱ δορυφόροι κακῶς πράττοντος ἐσῆλθον ἀθρόοι, καὶ τὸν τύραννον ἀπέκτειναν λιποθυμοῦντα ἤδη (the δορυφόροι are the praetorian bodyguard of Domitian). .. ... .. •

: the right reading is uncertain: LPOS have tum, T has cum; conatur is given by r, conatum by the other MSS. Some of the old editors read conatum and omit dum (Ihm says of this, "nescio an verius''). Ernesti proposed dum conaretur. If dum conatur is correct, it is the only instance in Suetonius of dum with the pres. indic. in Orat. Obliq. (Bagge and Dalmasso cite as other instances Tib. 14, 4, cum illum eo ipso momento, dum spatiatur una, praecipitare in mare destinasset: Tib. 51, 2, et dum adventus sui spem facit, prohibuit consecrari; but in neither passage is dum really in Orat. Obliq.). Such a constr. with dum is found once in Cicero, but in verse, Tusc. i 101, Dic, hospes, Spartae nos te hic vidisse iacentes | dum sanctis patriae legibus obsequimur; in Sall. Cat. 58, Liv. xxiv 19, Ον. Μ. iv 776; most frequently in Tac. (e.g. H. i 33, iii 38, v 17; 4. ii 81, xiii 15, xiv 58, xv 59, etc.). Draeger (Hist. Synt. ii² 605) says that this constr. is avoided by Val. Max., the two Plinies, Quintil., Suet., Apul., Gell., and the Scriptores Hist. Aug. Suetonius has the normal subjunctive in Aug. 94, 4, lego Atiam posita in templo lectica, dum ceterae matronae dormirent, obdormisse; cf. Calig. 38, 3: Ner. 35, 5.
: see on Tit. 7, 2.
: a very common phrase in Plautus, used also in Cic., Caes., Virg., etc.; cf. ὀφθαλμοὺς ὀρύττειν οι ἐξορύττειν.

div.p: § 3. xiv Kal. Octb.: i.e. Sept. 18 (96 A.D.).

p.note: : his age at death was 44 years, 10 months, 26 days, as Dio (lxvii 18) states precisely: Δομιτιανὸς δὲ ἔζησε ἔτη τέσσαρα καὶ τεσσαράκοντα καὶ μῆνας δέκα καὶ ἡμέρας ἓξ καὶ εἴκοσιν. He was born on Oct. 24, 51 A.D. (see c. 1, 1).

: an inaccurate statement, as strictly speaking he was in the 16th year of his reign; his dies imperii was Sept. 14, 81 A.D. (the day after the death of Titus, see Tit. 11) when the senate gave to him the imperium, the title of "Augustus," and the tribunicia potestas, and so he had reigned 15 years and 5 days, as Dio correctly calculates: ἐμονάρχησε δὲ ἔτη πεντεκαίδεκα καὶ ἡμέρας πέντε. Eutropius (vii 23, 6) repeats the incorrect statement of Suetonius, but Aurelius Victor (Caes. 11, 7) says: poenas luit quinto et quadragesimo vitae anno, dominationis circiter quinto decimo.

: the rude bier on which the bodies of the poor were borne to burial (the rich being borne on a lectus or lectica funebris); cf. Juv. viii 175, Mart. ii 81, viii 75, 14, ix 2, 12 (in Mart. x 5, 9 it is called Orciniana sponda). The sandapila was provided with a cheap wooden coffin (capulus) or shell in which the body was placed; this was spoken of contemptuously as a "box" (arca), cf. Hor. S. i 8, 8, Luc. viii 736; the arca was not burned with the body, nor buried with it in cases of interment, but was used again and again (cf. Val. Max. ii 6, 7). The Schol. on Juv. l.c. mentions that sandapilae were used for removing slain gladiators from the amphitheatre; so Aur. Vict. (Caes. 11, 8) says of Domitian: Senatus gladiatoris more funus ferri (al. efferri), radendumque nomen decrevit.

: Eutrop. vii 23, 6, funus eius ingenti dedecore per vespillones exportatum, et ignobiliter est sepultum: Euseb.-Hieron. Chron. p. 163 Schoene, Domitianus occisus in palatio et per vespillones ignobiliter exportatus anno aetatis xxxxv. The vispillones were hireling corpse-bearers who carried the sandapila (Mart. i 30, 1: 47, 1: ii 61, 3); they were generally four in number (Mart. viii 75, 9) and were also known as sandapilarii (Sidon. Apoll. Ep. ii 8). Festus (p. 369 M.) says: vespae et vespillones dicuntur, qui funerandis corporibus officium gerunt, non a minutis illis volucribus (wasps, vespae), sed quia vespertino tempore eos efferunt, qui funebri pompa duci propter inopiam nequeunt. Hi etiam vespullae vocantur. The form vispillo (not ves-) is supported by the MSS. of Martial and Suetonius.
: efferre (ἐξάγειν, ἐκκομίζειν) was the regular word for carrying out to burial; for exportare cf. Verg. G. iv 255 (of bees), tum corpora luce carentum | exportant tectis et tristia funera ducunt.
: Dio lxvii 18, αὐτοῦ τὸ σῶμα Φυλλὶς ἡ τροφὸς κλέψασα ἔθαψεν. She is not mentioned elsewhere.

: this road issued from the Porta Capena along with the Via Appia, and diverging to the left from it, ran more inland, passing through the Alban hills and touching Ferentinum, Aquinum, and Casinum, ending at Casilinum in Campania, where it rejoined the Via Appia. Juvenal refers to the tombs which lined it and the other great roads leading out of Rome: i 170, experiar quid concedatur in illos, | quorum Flaminia tegitur cinis atque Latina; v 55, clivosae veheris dum per monumenta Latinae.
: a like regard for the ashes of Nero was shown by his two nurses: Ner. 50, reliquias Egloge et Alexandria nutrices cum Acte concubina gentili Domitiorum monumento condiderunt.
: see c. 1, 1 (also c. 5 and c. 15, 2).
: daughter of Titus by his second wife Marcia Furnilla (Tit. 4, 2). Domitian's illicit passion for Julia, which led to her death, is described in c. 22.
: see on Galb. 21.

: cf. Tac. H. iv 40, Quo die senatum ingressus est Domitianus, de absentia patris fratrisque ac iuventa sua (he was aged 18) pauca et modica disseruit, decorus habitu (“graceful in mien'"); et ignotis adhuc moribus creba oris confusio pro modestia accipiebatur.

: Tacitus (Agr. 45) says that Domitian used this natural flush as a screen against shame, in that it prevented him showing the blush of shame: saevus ille vultus et rubor quo se contra pudorem muniebat; so Pliny, Pan. 48, inveighs against Domitian's “superbia in fronte, ira in oculis, femineus pallor in corpore, in ore impudentia multo rubore suffusa.” Blushing was regarded as a sign of gentle breeding; cf. Plin. Ep. i 14, Est illi (i.e. Acilianus) facies liberalis multo sanguine multo rubore suffusa, "His countenance is that of a gentleman, the blood coming readily to his cheeks, which are not seldom suffused with a blush" 20 (Lewis). Seneca, Ep. 11, discourses on blushing and in particular on the blush of modesty (verecundia) which he describes as “bonum in adulescente signum''; some men are most dangerous when they redden: quidam (e.g. Sulla) numquam magis quam cum erubuerint, timendi sunt, quasi omnem verecundiam effuderint; Pompey was remarkable for extreme mollitia oris; he blushed in the presence of any gathering. Cf. also Juv. x 300, vultumque modesto | sanguine ferventem.
: cf. Ner. 51, oculis hebetioribus. hebes (opp. to acutus, acer) was used of dim sight; cf. ἀμβλύς, ἀμβλὺ ὁρᾶν, ἀμβλυωπός. For Suetonius' descriptions of the eyes of the Caesars see on Galb. 21.
: the use of decens in the sense of "comely" is poetical (Hor., Ov., etc.), and very rare in prose (Plin. Ep. i 21, 2: Quintil. viii 3, 10).
: "toes"; cf. Iul. 61, equo insigni pedibus prope humanis et in modum digitorum ungulis fissis.

: this may mean that the toes were too short or too bent inward. Pitiscus assumes that Domitian had the claw-like curvature of the big-toes which disfigured those known as “falcones”; cf. Fest. p. 88 M., falcones dicuntur, quorum digiti pollices in pedibus intro sunt curvati, a similitudine falcis.

: cf. Iul. 45, 2, calvitii deformitas: Apul. Apol. 74, in pueritia priusquam isto calvitio deformaretur: Petron. Satyr. 108, deformis praeter spoliati capitis dedecus superciliorum etiam aequalis cum fronte calvities. Juvenal (iv 37) describes Domitian as the "bald Nero" in the lines which, according to the Schol. there (differing from the Schol. on i 1, vii 92, see note on “Paridis” Dom. 3, 1), led to the poet's banishment to Egypt: Cum iam semianimum laceraret Flavius orbem | ultimus et calvo serviret Roma Neroni; cf. Auson. 257, 12, quem calvum dixit sua Roma Neronem.
: cf. Vitell. 17, 2; Ner. 51. Titus also was inclined to corpulence (Tit. 3, 1).

: Nero and Caligula also were spindle-legged: Ner. 51, gracillimis cruribus; Calig. 50, 1, gracilitate maxima cervicis et crurum. Germanicus, father of Caligula, in his early years had the same defect but remedied it: Calig. 3, 1, formae minus congruebat gracilitas crurum, sed ea quoque paulatim repleta assidua equi vectatione post cibum.

: the compound remacrescere does not occur elsewhere, and the prefix re- can only be explained as having an intensive force "to grow very lean or thin." For a list of similar compounds (e.g. refervescere, refercire, resciscere) in which re- must be so explained or else regarded as pleonastic see Roby, Lat. Gramm. § 2103. Bentley and Duker conjectured emacruerant, Iernstedt longiore macruerant. Marcilius suggested that gracilitate should be omitted, taking obesitate with crurum as well as with ventris, and giving to re- the sense of "again." Oudendorp, though preferring emacruerant, explains the reading of the MSS. as meaning “crura natura quidem gracilia, nihilominus macriora erant facta longa valetudine.” Bremi takes remacruerant as macruerant.

div.p: §2. calvitio ita offendebatur: the sensitiveness of Julius Caesar on the same subject is well known; Iul. 45, 2, Circa corporis curam morosior, ut calvitii deformitatem iniquissime ferret, saepe obtrectatorum iocis obnoxiam expertus. Ideoque et deficientem capillum revocare (“to draw • forward'') a vertice adsueverat et ex omnibus decretis sibi a senatu populoque honoribus non aliud aut recepit aut usurpavit libentius quam ius laureae coronae perpetuo gestandae. Otho had recourse to wearing a wig (Oth. 12, 1.) ..

p.note: : the usual phrase is in (ad) contumeliam accipere aliquid; in Aug. 68, populus accepit in contumeliam eius versum, the meaning is that the people took the verse as a reflection on Augustus. For trahere in the sense of interpreting cf. Tac. H. ii 20, ornatum ipsius (ducis) in superbiam trahebant: A. iii 22, quod quidam ad saevitiam trahebant. Friedlaender notices that Martial's repeated jests 1 baldness (e.g. in v 49, a book dedicated to Domitian) are very strange in the light of what Suetonius says here.

: nothing more is known of this treatise by Domitian. Οὐχ ὁράᾳς, κ.τ.λ.: Hom. Il. xxi 108, part of the reply of Achilles refusing quarter to Priam's suppliant son Lycaon. The preceding line is the famous κάτθανε καὶ Πάτροκλος, ὅπερ σέο πολλὸν ἀμείνων, and the succeeding lines are πατρὸς δ᾽ εἴμ᾽ ἀγαθοῖο, θεὰ δέ με γείνατο μητηρ· | ἀλλ᾽ ἔπι τοι καὶ ἐμοὶ θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κραταιή.

: cf. the little dirge on Hair (capillorum elegidarion) recited by Eumolpus in Petron. Satyr. 109: Quod solum formae decus est, cecidere capilli, | vernantesque comas tristis abegit hiemps. | Nunc umbra nudata sua iam tempora ("the temples'') maerent, | areaque (i.e. the bald expanse of the head) attritis ridet adulta (so Bücheler for adusta) pilis. | O fallax natura deûm: quae prima dedisti | aetati nostrae gaudia prima rapis. Eumolpus adds an epigram in hendecasyllables on the same theme: -Infelix, modo crinibus nitebas | Phoebo pulchrior et sorore Phoebi (i.e. the Sun and Moon). | At nunc levior aere vel rotundo | horti tubere ('mushroom'"), quod creavit unda, | ridentes fugis et times puellas. | Ut mortem citius venire credas, | scito iam capitis perisse partem.

p.mentioned: nec gratius quicquam decore nec brevius
p.note: : for this commonplace cf. Sall. Cat. 1, 4, formae gloria fluxa atque fragilis est: Ov. A.A. ii 113, forma bonum fragile est: Sen. Phaedr. 773, res est forma fugax: Nemes. Ecl. 4, 24, donum forma breve est.
: cf. Dio lxvii 6, τό τε σῶμα ἄπονος, καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ἄτολμος ἦν. Pliny (Pan. 14) calls Domitian “iners.” Contrast the activity of Julius Caesar, Iul. 57, laboris ultra fidem patiens erat.

: for non temere see on Tit. 6, 2. Pliny (Pan. 24) praises Trajan for differing in this respect from his predecessors (especially Domitian): Incedebas pedibus, incedis: laetabaris labore, laetaris; nihil in ipso te fortuna mutavit. Liberum est ingrediente per publicum principe subsistere, occurrere, comitari, praeterire: ambulas inter nos, non quasi < non > contingas, et copiam tui, non ut imputes, facis... Ante te principes fastidio nostri et quodam aequalitatis metu usum pedum amiserant. Illos ergo umeri cervicesque servorum super ora nostra (vehebant), etc. For the practice of Augustus cf. Aug. 53, 2, 202 In consulatu pedibus fere, extra consulatum saepe adaperta sella per publicum incessit. Ammianus (xxii 7) says of the emperor Julian: Humilior princeps. visus est in officio pedibus gradiendo cum honoratis: quod laudabant alii, quidam ut affectatum et vile carpebant.

: Trajan on his campaigns led his legions on foot; cf. Plin. Pan. 14, Cum legiones duceres seu potius (tanta velocitas erat) raperes, non vehiculum umquam, non equum respexisti. Julius Caesar generally marched with his soldiers; cf. Iul. 57, in agmine nonnumquam equo, saepius pedibus anteibat. Tacitus (H. ii 11) says of Otho: Nec illi segne aut corruptum luxu iter; sed lorica ferrea usus est et ante signa pedes ire.

: the lectica was carried on poles (asseres) by six or eight lecticarii (Oth. 6, 3, n.: Mart. vi 77, 4: ix 2, 11); the emperor's lecticarii, who formed part of the familia Augusta, are often mentioned in inscriptions (C.I.L. vi 8872-8875, etc.). ..

: arma here are the campestria arma (Hor. A.P. 379), the weapons used in the soldierly exercises in the Campus Martius, which are referred to e.g. in Aug. 83, Exercitationes campestres equorum et armorum statim post civilia bella omisit: Hor. Ep. i 18, 52, Adde virilia quod speciosius arma | non est qui tractet: scis quo clamore coronae ('ring of spectators'") proelia sustineas campestria: Ov. Tr. iii 12, 19, Usus equi nunc est, levibus nunc luditur armis. By arma in the strict sense the Romans meant defensive weapons (the scutum, etc.) and such offensive weapons as were used at close quarters (especially the gladius); missile weapons were tela not arma, and we find the iaculum which was used in the exercitationes campestres (cf. Hor. C. i 8) distinguished from the arma in Ov. A.A. iii 383, Sunt illis celeresque pilae, iaculumque, trochique, | armaque, et in gyros ire coactus equus. Titus was “armorum et equitandi peritissimus’(Tit. 3, 2).

: the use of the bow was not part of the Roman military training, the bowmen (sagittarii) being supplied by the auxiliaries, mainly those from Crete and the Balearic isles. Titus, like Domitian, excelled in bowmanship, slaying 12 of the defenders of Jerusalem with 12 arrows (Tit. 5, 2). The emperor Julian was destinandi sagittas mire promptus” (Aur. Vict. Caes. 42, 23), and Honorius also was skilled with the bow (cf. Claud. iv Cons. Hon. 527 sqq.).

: Suetonius is very fond of using the intensive vel with praecipuus, as though it were a superlative adj. like maximus; cf. Aug. 10, 2, quem vel praecipuum adiutorem speraverat: Aug. 32, 2, vel praecipuam calumniandi materiam: Iul. 21: Aug. 29, 1: Claud. 20, 1: Galb. 16, 1; so with the adv., e.g. Vitell. 13, 1, vel praecipue luxuriae Ner. 22, 1. There are two instances in Tacitus: Dial. 6, vel praecipua iucunditas est: A. xii 60, сит Marius et Sulla de eo vel praecipuе bellarent. deditus:

: for the venationes in the amphitheatre attached to Domitian's arx Albana see c. 4,4. Pliny (Pan. 81) says that Trajan found relaxation in hunting wild beasts in their native haunts, whereas the beasts on which Domitian showed his skill had their spirit broken by captivity (domitas fractasque claustris feras).

: the use of figere in the sense of transfigere (of bowmen, spearmen, etc.) is found in poetry and post-Aug. prose; e.g. Juv. iv 99. comminus ursos | figebat Numidas, Albana nudus harena | venator: Tac. A. ii 17, quidam .. admotis sagittariis per ludibrium figebantur.

: scopulus is a dim. of scopus (σκοπός), a mark or target. The dim. is not found elsewhere, and Stephanus read scopo, adopted by many subsequent editors; Roth rightly restored scopulo, which also appears in the texts of Preud'homme and Ihm. The Greek σκοπός was not naturalised as a Lat. word, but occurs in its Gr. form in Cic., e.g. Att. viii 11, sed neutri σκοπός est ille, ut nos beati simus; also in Macrob. Somn. Scip. 4, somnii mentem, ipsumque propositum, quem Graeci σκοπὸν vocant, tentemus aperire. For the great number of diminutives in Suetonius see App. i. § 1. d. •

: the accusative has to do double duty with in and praebentis. For the meaning of palma cf. Isid. Diff. 2, 62, ‘‘palma” manus est dispansis digitis, sicut et arbor dispansis ramis: Orig. 11, 69, "palma” est manus expansis digitis, sicut contractis “pugnus” (“fist"). Plautus has the forms dispenno, dispessus (Mil. 360, 1406); Lucretius uses both dispansus (i 306) and dispessus (ii 1126, Munro; iii 988).

: this, not derexit, is the reading of the better MSS. (Q has derexerit); M has dirigerent in Claud. 20, 3, but derecta in Calig. 46 and derecto in Calig. 19, 1. In all four passages Ihm adopts the spelling der-, in accordance with the commonly accepted view that derigo (which is found in inscriptions and in the oldest Lat. MSS.) is probably the only genuine ancient form; see Ribbeck Proleg. ad Verg. 401 sqq., Munro on Lucr. vi 823, the Lexica of Caesar by Meusel and by Menge and Preuss, and the Thes. Ling. Lat.

: cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, Sagittarum tam doctus fuit ut inter patentes digitos extentae manus viri procul positi spicula eius transvolarent. Stahr gives a modern parallel to Domitian's feat:-"Man erzählt Ähnliches von dem bekannten preussischen Prinzen Louis Ferdinand (der bei Saalfeld blieb), der vielleicht nicht ahnte wer sein Vorgänger in dieser Art barbarischer Virtuosität war."

: see on "liberales disciplinas,” Galb. 5, 1. Suetonius has already mentioned (in c. 2, 2) the interest which Domitian pretended to take in literature, especially poetry, before he became emperor; for his essays in poetry and the estimate of his poetic talent by other writers see the note on that passage.
: see on Galb. 14, 1.

: the fire referred to is that which devastated part of Rome in the reign of Titus (see Tit. 8, 3 and notes). Among the buildings which Dio mentions as destroyed then was the Porticus Octaviae and the library contained there (τὰ Ὀκταουίεια οἰκήματα μετὰ τῶν βιβλίων). Macé (op. cit. p. 222) points out that when Suetonius is speaking of the Palatine library he uses the sing. bibliotheca, but the pl. when he is speaking of the library in the Porticus Octaviae (this library probably occupying more than one wing of the rectangular colonnade), and Macé concludes that it was only the latter library which was restored by Domitian. Julius Caesar had planned a library at Rome and had commissioned Varro to procure the books, but the project was cut short by Caesar's death. Asinius Pollio, out of the spoils of his Illyrian campaigns, founded the first public library in the Atrium Libertatis on the Aventine, and Augustus established two others: (1) the bibliothecae Octavianae in the Porticus Octaviae (named after the sister of Augustus); (2) that in the colonnade of the temple of Apollo on the Palatine. There was a library in the Palace of Tiberius (bibliotheca domus Tiberianae), and Tiberius also built a library, dedicated to the Muses, in connexion with the temple to the deified Augustus on the slope of the Palatine facing the Capitol. Vespasian established a library in his temple to Peace (Vesp. 9, 1; cf. Gell. v 21, xvi 8). These are the only libraries at Rome which we know of as earlier than the reign of Domitian.

: this superlative of impense is not found earlier, nor is impensissimus which Suetonius uses in Tib. 13, 2, impensissimis precibus. Other superlative adjs., ptcples., or advs. which appear first (if not exclusively) in Suet. are enixissime (cf. enixius, Galb. 3, 3), animosissime, criminosissimus (and -e), inaequalissimus, remississimus, diversissime (diversissimus is common), excogitatissimus, immoderatissimus. Some are only found in isolated instances outside Suet., e.g. evidentissime, minacissimus, assiduissimus, sollicitissime, persuasissimum, amarissime, reverentissime, notatissimus. See Freund, De Suetonii usu atque genere dicendi 49 sq.

: Duker proposed reparari, but when Suetonius uses curare in the sense of getting something done by the agency of others, he regularly joins with it the gerundive and not the acc. and inf. pass. Here he is emphasizing the personal interest and trouble which Domitian took in restoring the library or libraries.

: the same means as were adopted by Vespasian in restoring the bronze records destroyed by the burning of the Capitol; Vesp. 8, 5, aerearumque tabularum tria milia, quae simul conflagraverant, restituenda suscepit undique investigatis exemplaribus.

: Ptolemy Philadelphus (king of Egypt, 285-247 в.с.) collected throughout Greece and Asia a multitude of volumes which he deposited at Alexandria, the greater number in the library in the Museum, and the remainder in the library in the Serapeum or temple of Serapis (Vesp. 7, 1). The Museum library was burnt during the blockade of Julius Caesar at Alexandria in 47 B.C., and 400,000 volumes are said to have perished. This loss was partly made good by the transfer to Alexandria of the 200,000 volumes from the library of the kings of Pergamum which Antony presented to Cleopatra (Plut. Ant. 58). The Serapeum library was destroyed under the emperor Theodosius in 389 A.D. It is uncertain whether Suetonius used the form Alexandrea or Alexandria for ᾿Αλεξάνδρεια. In 11 places -ia is the better attested; in 6 (including this) -ea. Here Roth, Preud'homme, and Ihm read eam, but -iam in Vesp. 7, 1: Tit. 5, 3.

: explained by the following sentence; Domitian would not take the trouble to learn to compose the ordinary epistulae orationesque et edicta which the emperor usually drafted. Baumg.-Cr. takes necessario as the adv., but it seems clearly to be the adj.

: commentarii (ὑπομνήματα) here means the private memoirs written by Tiberius, which are mentioned in Tib. 61, 1, commentario quem de vita sua summatim breviterque composuit. Similar memoirs were written by Augustus (Aug. 85, 1), and by Agrippina, mother of Nero (Tac. A. iv 53). The expression “commentarii principis (principales)" is often used (e.g. in Tac. H. iv 40) in another sense for the record or register of the acta of the emperor, these including the official decisions which he gave in matters referred to him (C.I.L. iii 411), privileges granted by him (Plin. Ep. x 95, 105), and the accusations ordered by him or brought before him (Suet. Calig. 15, 4: Tac. A. xiii 43). See Introd. c. iii; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 906. orationes et edicta: see note on c. 2, 3. For alieno ingenio cf. Tac. A. xiii 3 on Nero's aliena facundia supplied by Seneca. =

: nec is generally explained as non, but this seems quite unsound. In old Lat. there are instances of nec so used (see Kühner-Stegmann, i 817), but in no other passage of Suetonius has it this meaning. Alexander (op. cit. p. 13), taking nec here as = non, cites various passages (e.g. Iul. 78, 2; Calig. 6, 2; Claud. 43; Ner. 26, 1; 34, 4; Oth. 9,3; 12, 2; Dom. 15, 2) in which he says nec carries the value of non, possibly in all, indubitably in some; but an examination of these passages shows that in all of them nec is to be taken in the sense of et non or ne quidem. In our passage some words must have fallen out before nec inelegantis. Bücheler suggested <nec indiligentis > nec inelegantis, but more probably the original reading was <nec neglegentis > nec inelegantis. For neglegens (neclegens) as an epithet of sermo cf. Quintil. x 7, 28, ne id quidem tacendum nullum nostrum usquam neglegentem esse sermonem. What is probably a similar corruption occurs in Vesp. 15, neque caede laetatus, where see note. ..

: “clever sayings” “mots”; cf. Suet. Gramm. 23, dicto non infaceto notatum (Palaemonem) ferunt: Hor. A.P. 273, inurbanum lepido seponere dicto: Macrob. Sat. ii 1, 14, Cicero in libro epistolarum ad Cornelium Nepotem secundo sic ait: Itaque nostri, cum omnia, quae dixissemus, dicta essent, quae facete et breviter et acute locuti essemus, ea proprio nomine appellari dicta voluerunt. One of the works of Julius Caesar was entitled Dicta Collectanea, a collection of apophthegms (Iul. 56), referred to in Cic. Fam. ix 16 as volumina ἀποφθεγμάτων. See also note on diceret in Vesp. 20. ..

div.p: "Vellem videtur'': practically the same jeu d'esprit is attributed to Aristotle, who said to an unprincipled youth who prided himself on his good looks: “Νεανίσκε, οἷός δοκεῖς αὐτὸς εἶναι, ἐγὼ γενοίμην· οἷος δὲ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ ὑπάρχεις, τοιοῦτοι μοι οἱ ἐχθροὶ γένοιντο ” (Stob. Serm. 45.) τι دو

p.note: : quite unknown, and the MSS. vary in the spelling: M has maetius (“corr. ex maecius ut vid.," Ihm), and this is read by Preud'homme; G has mecius; the others metius. We find mention of three men who bore the name of "Maecius" under the Flavian emperors: M. Maecius Celer, sent out by Domitian as legatus of a legion in Syria (cf. Stat. S. iii 2); L. Maecius Postumus, one of the Fratres Arvales under Vespasian, Titus, and Domitian; M. Maecius Rufus, proconsul of Bithynia in 79 A.D. See Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii 319 sq. The editors who read "Metius" or "Mettius" suppose this to be Mettius Pompusianus (see c. 10, 3: Vesp. 14); a Mettius Rufus was appointed prefect of Egypt by Domitian (see c. 4, 2). Other

: “reddish,” ὑπόπυρρον; cf. Plin. N.H. x 8, etc. similar compounds with the same meaning are subrufus, subrubicundus, subruber, subrubeus. Suetonius also uses subflavus (Aug. 79, 2: Ner. 51); subdebilis (Vitell. 17, 2).
: ''with a sprinkling of white hairs"; cf. Gloss. Cyrill. “incanus. σπαρτοπόλιος.” This adj. is only used in poetry and in post-Aug. prose. or

: mulsum (sc. vinum), “honey-wine" "mead," was best made by mixing some old rough wine, such as Massic or Falernian, with new Attic honey; cf. Macrob. Sat. vii 12, 9, illud proverbium quo utuntur gulones: Mulsum quod probe temperes miscendum esse novo Hymettio et vetulo Falerno. The blend of snow and mead was suggested to Domitian's mind by the practice of cooling mead and wine with snow; cf. Plin. Ep. i 15, where Pliny playfully tells a friend who had disappointed at dinner that he will have to pay for the fare provided, and among other items for the "mulsum et nix, nam hanc quoque computabis, immo hanc in primis, quae perit in ferculo." To clarify, as well as to cool, wine it was strained through a cloth covered with snow; cf. Mart. viii 45, 3: ix 22, 8, Et faciant nigras nostra Falerna nives. condicionem principum miserrimam: a saying of Hadrian's also; cf. Vulc. Gall. Αvid. Cass. 2, where Marcus Aurelius, replying to a letter of Verus warning him against the treasonable designs of Avidius Cassius, points out that in cases of treason it is inevitable that even those who have been proved guilty seem to suffer injustice, and then adds: Scis enim ipse quid avus tuus Hadrianus dixerit: “misera condicio imperatorum, quibus de adfectata tyrannide nisi occisis non potest credi.” Eius autem exemplum ponere malui quam Domitiani, qui hoc primus dixisse fertur. Tyrannorum enim etiam bona dicta non habent tantum auctoritatis quantum debent. Dio (liv 15), when mentioning those charged with conspiracy against Augustus, has a similar reflection on the difficulty of knowing whether such charges are just or unjust: οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ἀκριβῶς τὰ τοιαῦτα τοῖς ἔξω αὐτῶν οὖσιν εἰδέναι. πολλὰ γὰρ ὧν ἂν ὁ κρατῶν πρὸς τιμωρίαν, ὡς καὶ ἐπιβεβουλευμένος, ἤτοι δι᾽ ἑαυτοῦ ἢ καὶ διὰ τῆς γερουσίας (senatus) πράξῃ, ὑποπτεύεται κατ᾿ ἐπήρειαν, κἂν ὅτι μάλιστα δικαιότατα συμβῇ, γεγονέναι.
: see on Galb. 10, 2.

: Pliny (Pan. 82) contrasts the employment of leisure by Trajan and by emperors like Domitian: Otio prodimur. An non plerique principes hoc idem tempus in aleam, stupra, luxum conferebant, cum seriarum laxamenta curarum vitiorum contentione supplerent? Diceplaying and gambling were forbidden by law at Rome both under the Republic and under the Empire, an exception being allowed, by law or by custom, at the Saturnalia. Repressive laws were quite ineffective, and Juvenal (i 88) describes the intensity of the gambling fever in his day: Alea quando | hos animos? neque enim loculis ("purse") comitantibus itur | ad casum tabulae, posita sed luditur arca (“money-chest'"). The emperors were notorious gamesters; cf. Aug. 70, 2, (Augustus) notatus est ut aleae indulgens: 71, 1, aleae rumorem (‘ill-repute'") nullo modo expavit, lusitque simpliciter et palam oblectamenti causa: Calig. 41, 2, ne ex lusu quidem aleae compendium spernens (Caligula played at dice in his Alban villa during his sister Drusilla's funeral, Sen. Cons. ad Polyb. 17, 4): Claud. 5, ex contubernio sordidissimorum hominum super veterem segnitiae notam ebrietatis quoque et aleae infamiam subiit; Claud. 33, 2 (quoted along with Ner. 30, 3 in the notes on Vitell. 4, where Suetonius says that Vitellius won the intimacy of Claudius and of Nero per aleae studium).

: so too Augustus; cf. Aug. 71, 1, lusit praeterquam Decembri mense (i.e. during the Saturnalia, Dec. 17-23) aliis quoque festis et profestis diebus. For profesti dies cf. Macrob. Sat. i 16, 2, Numa ut in menses annum ita in dies mensem quemque distribuit, diesque omnes aut festos, aut profestos, aut intercisos vocavit: festi dis dicati sunt, profesti hominibus ob administrandam rem privatam publicamque concessi, intercisi deorum hominumque communes sunt.

: for de die see on de nocte in Vesp. 21; it means "in full day," before the afternoon has begun. The normal time for the bath was the 8th-9th hour, i.e. about 2-3 p.m.; cf. Cic. Att. xiii 52, Inde ambulavit (Caesar) in litore. Post horam viii in balneum: Mart. xi 52, 3, octavam (horam) poteris servare; lavabimur una. But we often read of bathing about the 5th hour, before the prandium; e.g. Plin. Ep. iii 5, 10 (of the elder Pliny), Post solem (i.e. the apricatio) plerumque frigida lavabatur, deinde gustabat (i.e. took the prandium) dormiebatque minimum: Epictet. Diss. i 1, 29, ᾿Αλλὰ ἦλθεν ἡ πεμπτή· ταύτῃ δ' εἰώθει γυμνασάμενος ψυχρολουτρεῖν : Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 30, Egressus balneas multum lactis et panis sumebat, ova, deinde mulsum; atque his refectus aliquando prandium inibat, aliquando cibum usque ad cenam differebat: Juv. xi 204, Iam nunc in balnea salva | fronte licet vadas, quanquam solida hora supersit | ad sextam. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 269 sqq. prandebat ad satietatem: the prandium, the meal between the iantaculum (Vitell. 13, 1, n.) and the cena, was usually taken about the sixth hour; cf. Aug. 78, 1, post cibum meridianum: Claud. 34, 2, meridie dimisso ad prandium populo. This midday meal or lunch might be of a very light nature, as in the case of Augustus, Aug. 76, 1, nos in essedo panem et palmulas ('dates") gustavimus; cf. Sen. Ep. 83, 6, panis siccus et sine mensa prandium, post quod non sunt lavandae manus: Hor. S. i 6, 127, pransus non avide quantum interpellet inani | ventre diem durare. Generally, however, it was of a more substantial kind with cold or hot meats, fish, vegetables, fruit, and wine; see the passages quoted by Marquardt, op. cit. 267. Nero, like Domitian, indulged freely at the prandium; cf. Tac. A. xiv 2, medio die cum id temporis per vinum et epulas incalesceret; so too Vitellius (Vitell. 13, 1).
: see on Tit. 6, 2.

: see on Tit. 8, 1. Pliny (Pan. 49), addressing Trajan, says that Domitian by his gorging at his lonely lunch had turned this prandium into a solitaria cena; and so when the regular cena was being served, the sated tyrant was free to spy on and insult his guests: Non enim ante medium diem distentus solitaria cena spectator adnotatorque convivis tuis immines nec ieiunis et inanibus plenus ipse et ructans non tam adponis quam obicis cibos, quos dedigneris attingere, aegreque perpessus superbam illam convictus simulationem rursus te ad clandestinam ganeam occultumque luxum refers.

: the Matian apple is mentioned in Plin. N.H. xv 49 as one of those deriving their names from persons; it was probably called after C. Matius Calvena, whom Pliny (N.H. xii 13) names as the inventor of the art of clipping arbours: primus C. Matius ex equestri ordine, divi Augusti amicus, invenit nemora tonsilia intra hos lxxx annos. This C. Matius was a friend of Julius Caesar (Iul. 52, 2) and of Cicero (Cic. Fam. xi 27, 28, etc.); he translated the Iliad into Latin verse, and wrote a complete account of the art and science of cookery in three books (Colum. xii 4, 44). Palmer (Introd. to Hor. S. ii 4) argues strongly that the Catius whose precepts on cookery are given by Horace is C. Matius. The Matianum malum is also mentioned in Colum. v 10, 19: Macrob. Sat. iii 19, 2 (where the form used is Mattianum): Athen. iii 82 c, ἐγὼ . . μάλιστα τεθαύμακα τὰ κατὰ τὴν ῾Ρώμην πιπρασκόμενα μῆλα, τὰ Ματτιανὰ καλούμενα, ἅπερ κομίζεσθαι λέγεται ἀπό τινος κώμης ἱδρυμένης ἐπὶ τῶν πρὸς ᾿Ακυληίᾳ (Aquileia) ῎Αλπεων. For the use of apples at dessert (mensae secundae) cf. Hor. S. i 3, 6; Mart. x 48, 18.

: Statius (S. v 1, 121 sqq.) flatteringly alludes to the abstemiousness of Domitian as a model which Priscilla commended to her husband Abascantus for imitation: fovet anxia curas | coniugis hortaturque simul flectitque labores, ipsa dapes modicas et sobria pocula tradit | exemplumque ad erile (i.e. of Domitian, their lord) monet.

: the ampulla (λήκυθος) was a narrow-necked vessel with globular body, principally used for holding oil, but also for vinegar, wine, and drink of any kind. At times the Romans used to drink out of the ampulla itself; such a drinking-flask is called ampulla potoria in Mart. xiv 110, and glass ampullae for this purpose are mentioned in Mart. vi 35, 3, At tu multa diu dicis vitreisque tepentem | ampullis potas semisupinus aquam.
: see on Vesp. 19, 1.
: contrast Nero, Ner. 27, 2, epulas a medio die ad mediam noctem protrahebat.

: the comissatio (κῶμος, κωμάζειν) or drinking revel took place after the cena, sometimes in the same room, sometimes the diners went on to another house (e.g. Liv. xl 7, 5: Petron. Satyr. 65). With their anointed locks wreathed with roses the comissatores drank more Graeco under the presidency of a magister or arbiter bibendi (Cic. Sen. 14, 46: Hor. C. ii 7, 25), and were entertained by the performances of artistes of various kinds, the revel being often protracted till midnight or later (cf. Tit. 7, 1). Vitellius was peculiar in making the comissatio his fourth great meal for the day (Vitell. 13, 1). See Marquardt, op. cit. 331 sqq.

: this elliptical mode of expression, in which a verb of general signification like facere must be supplied out of a verb of special signification, is found in Nepos (Ages. 4, Tissaphernes nihil aliud quam bellum comparavit), and is frequent from Livy on. Suetonius is fond of it; e.g. Aug. 83, nihil aliud quam vectabatur et

: Vesp. 5, 2, nec illam quicquam aliud quam cachinasse. Sometimes nihil aliud quam is used quite adverbially ("only” “merely”), e.g. Liv. ii 63, hostes, nihil aliud quam perfusis vano timore Romanis, citato agmine abeunt. Similarly nihil (nec quicquam) amplius quam is found at times with an ellipse of facere, at times = tantum, tantum modo; e.g. Tit. 9, 1, nihil amplius quam monuit: Aug. 2, 3, ipse Augustus nihil amplius quam equestri familia ortum se scribit. Such usages are very rare in Tacitus (A. iv 34, xiii 40, xv 13, H. ii 91). Cicero in a few instances uses nihil aliud nisi in this way, e.g. Sest. 14, nihil aliud nisi meum nomen causamque sustinuit; usually he has the fuller form of expression, e.g. Rosc. Am. 108, nihil aliud fecerunt nisi rem detulerunt. See Kühner-Stegmann, ii 564.

: cf. Dio lxvii 6, ἀσωτότατος καὶ ἀσελγέστατος καὶ πρὸς γυναῖκας καὶ πρὸς μειράκια ἦν: Oros. vii 10, 2, libidinis intemperantia quidquid cogitari potest fecit. Suidas describes Domitian as “ἀκρατὴς καὶ ἀκόλαστος τὰ περὶ τὸ σῶμα, γυναικομανίας καὶ ἀνδρομανίας ἀνάπλεως." For the genitive of quality cf. Claud. 33, 2, libidinis in feminas profusissimae.

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 11, 7, furens libidine, cuius foedum exercitium Graecorum lingua κλινοπάλην vocabat. Martial is probably referring to Domitian's use of the word κλινοπάλη (lectilucta) when in an ambiguous epigram (xiv 201) he says of a palaestrita or wrestler: Non amo quod vincat, sed quod succumbere novit | et didicit melius τὴν ἐπικλινοπάλην.
: see on Tit. 5, 3.
: cf. Galb. 22. Marquardt, Privatl.2 787.
: Elagabalus indulged in similar practices: Lamprid. Heliog. 31, in balneis semper cum mulieribus fuit, ita ut eas ipse psilothro curaret, etc.

: Domitia Longina, whom Domitian married after taking her away from her husband Aelius Lamia (Dom. 1, 3; 10, 2). palam dilexit: Philostratus (vit. Apollon. vii 7, quoted on c. 10, 4) says that Domitian married (ἤγετο) Julia after he had put her husband Sabinus to death, but there is no other evidence of this. Dio (lxvii 3) states that after Domitian had sent away his wife Domitia for intriguing with the actor Paris (see c. 3, 1) he cohabited more openly with Julia as if she were a wife (τῇ Ἰουλίᾳ ἀπαρακαλυπτότερον ὡς γαμετῇ συνῴκει), and when he took back Domitia at the request of the people, he none the less kept up his illicit relations with Julia (ἐχρῆτο δ᾽ οὐδὲν ἧττον τῇ ᾿Ἰουλίᾳ).

: cf. Plin. Ep. iv 11, cum ipse (Domitianus) fratris filiam incesto non polluisset solum, verum etiam occidisset: nam vidua abortu periit (the use of vidua, "in her widowhood," shows that she was not married to Domitian). For the date of her death see on Tit. 4, 2. =

: conceptum may be either from the subst. conceptus (coner. fetus, cf. Stat. Th. x 805, quosve ego conceptus aut quae mala pignora fudi?) or the neut. ptc. used substantivally (cf. Scrib. Larg. Ep. ad Callist. p. 3, ne praegnanti medicamentum, quo conceptum excutitur, detur). The Thes. Ling. Lat. (iv 23 and 62) is inconsistent on the point.
