The words a se (i.e. Domitian) are to be taken with conceptum; cf. Colum. vi 37, 10, quae (equa) cum ex asino conceptum edidit. The usual phrase for forcing birth or procuring abortion is partum abigere; e.g. Cic. Cluent. 32, partum sibi ipsa. medicamentis abegisset. Juvenal (ii 29 sqq.) denounces Domitian, who had revived the lex Iulia de adulteriis et stupro, for his treatment of Julia: Qualis erat nuper tragico pollutus adulter | concubitu (i.e. Domitian's incest was like that of Oedipus in Greek tragedy), qui tunc leges revocabat amaras | omnibus atque ipsis Veneri Martique timendas, | cum tot abortivis fecundam Iulia vulvam | solveret et patruo (i.e. Domitian) similes effunderet offas. Pliny (Pan. 63) accuses Domitian of stupra and incestae noctes. Claudius, in order to wed Agrippina, got a decree passed by the senate legitimizing marriage with a brother's daughter (Claud. 26, Tac. A. xii 7). Gaius (Inst. i 62) mentions that this was still in force, though marriage with a sister's daughter was illegal. Constantine restored the ancient law and prohibited marriage with a brother's daughter as incestuous.

: the ordinary people at Rome had not been affected by the tyranny of Domitian in the same way as those of higher rank, and moreover the populus under the Empire had come to be absolutely indifferent to affairs of state; cf. Juv. x 77, populus iam pridem ex quo suffragia nulli | vendimus, effudit curas; nam qui dabat olim | imperium fasces legiones omnia, nunc se | continet atque duas tantum res anxius optat, | panem et circenses.

: this post-Aug. adv. is used in the sense of "indiscriminately, by Quintilian (e.g. xi 3, 1, utraque appellatione indifferenter uti licet) and Gellius (x 24, 8). Suetonius is peculiar in using indifferens of men in the sense of "careless” “indifferent,” Iul. 53, circa victum ("food") C. Oppius adeo indifferentem (Caesarem) docet; the adj. was introduced by Cicero (Fin. iii 16) to express the Stoic ἀδιάφορον, i.e. neutrum, nequè bonum, neque malum.

: for reasons given in Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, 9, Quo moti milites, quibus privatae commoditates dispendio publico largius procedunt, auctores necis ad supplicium poscere, more suo, seditiosius coeperunt. Qui vix aegreque per prudentes cohibiti, tandem in gratiam optimatum convenere. Neque minus per se moliebantur bellum, quod iis conversum imperium maestitiae erat, ob omissionem praedarum per dona munifica. Domitian had lavishly increased the soldiers' pay (c. 7, 3). According to Philostratus (vit. Soph. i 7) the legions on the Danube were dissuaded from revolting on Domitian's death by the famous Dio Chrysostom, who had been forced to flee from Italy by Domitian's decree expelling the philosophers. He used his great eloquence in inveighing against the dead tyrant, and persuaded the soldiers that they would do better to obey the senate.
: Domitian was one of the emperors not deified after death; for such deification see on Vesp. 23, 4.
: the prefects of the praetorians were themselves involved in the conspiracy against Domitian; see on c. 14, 1.

: under Nerva in 97 A.D. the praetorians, led by their prefect Casperius Aelianus, wreaked vengeance on the assassins, as is described in [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 12, 7, Cum interfectores Domitiani ad exitium poscerentur, tantum est consternatus (Nerva) ut neque vomitum, neque impetum ventris valuerit differre: et tamen vehementer obstitit, dictitans aequius esse mori quam auctoritatem imperii foedare, proditis potentiae sumendae auctoribus. Sed milites, neglecto principe, requisitos, Petronium uno ictu, Parthenium vero, demptis prius genitalibus et in os coniectis, iugulavere. They even coerced Nerva into publicly returning thanks to them for slaying “nefandos pessimosque omnium mortalium.” Dio (lxviii 3) says that Nerva presented his own throat to their swords in a vain attempt to save Domitian's assassins who had secured the throne for him. The soldiers similarly avenged the murder of Alexander Severus; cf. Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 63, mortem eius milites gravissime tulerunt atque auctores caedis trucidarunt (one of the many passages in which the Scriptores Historiae Augustae imitate Suetonius; see Introd. p. 26).

: the senate in the later years of Domitian had been mere slaves of the despot. Marcellus Eprius, the informer against Thrasea (c. 10, 3), defended himself on the ground that he was but one member of a senate who had all been slaves together (se unum esse ex illo senatu qui simul servierit, Tac. H. iv 8). Tacitus (Agr. 45) vividly describes the dragooning of the senate by the display of armed force (obsessam curiam et clausum armis senatum), and the way in which he and his fellow-senators passed servile decrees of condemnation and even laid violent hands upon members of their own order; see on c. 11, 3. Hence the frantic exultation at Domitian's death, which Pliny (Pan. 52) depicts: Iuvabat illidere solo superbissimos vultus, instare ferro, saevire securibus, ut si singulos ictus sanguis dolorque sequeretur. Nemo tam temperans gaudii seraeque laetitiae, quin instar ultionis videretur cernere laceros artus, truncata membra, postremo truces horrendasque imagines abiectas excoctasque flammis, ut ex illo terrore et minis in usum hominum ac voluptates ignibus mutarentur.
: as on the death of Titus, but for a very different purpose; see Tit. 11.

: see on adclamari, c. 13, 1. Cf. Lamprid. Comm. 18, adclamationes senatus post mortem Commodi graves fuerunt. Lampridius fills two chapters with what purport to be the actual outcries of the senate on that occasion, the following being a portion: "Hosti patriae honores detrahantur. Parricida trahatur. Hostis patriae, parricida, gladiator in spoliario lanietur. Hostis deorum, carnifex senatus, qui senatum occidit, unco trahatur; qui innocentes occidit, unco trahatur; ... qui sanguini suo non pepercit, unco trahatur; Gladiatoris et parricidae statuae detrahantur." (More of these adclamationes of the senate against the delatores who flourished under Commodus are quoted on Tit. 8, 4.) clipeos: shields emblazoned with portraits, medallion busts. Pliny (N.H. xxxv 3) says that Appius Claudius, consul in 495 B.C., was the first to hang such shields with portraits of his ancestors in the temple of Bellona. Macrobius (Sat. ii 3) tells a story about Cicero's witty remark on a shieldbust of his brother Quintus: Cum in ea provincia quam ille rexerat vidisset clipeatam imaginem eius ingentibus lineamentis usque ad pectus ex more pictam (erat autem Quintus ipse staturae parvae), ait: Frater meus dimidius maior est quam totus. We find constant references to such clipei with portraits of the emperors which were placed in temples or (as here) in the senate-house (e.g. Mon. Ancyr. 34: Capitol. Anton. Pius 5: Treb. Poll. Claud. 3). In Calig. 16, 4 Suetonius mentions that the senate decreed to Caligula an aureus clipeus which was borne in solemn state to the Capitol every year by priests attended by senators, with high-born youths and maidens chanting his praises. For the clipeus decreed to Germanicus after his death see Tac. A. ii 83.

: those in the senate-house first of all, and then the other busts and statues were pulled down, and the statues of gold and silver (c. 13, 2) were melted; cf. Dio lxviii 1, μίσει δὲ τοῦ Δομιτιανοῦ αἱ εἰκόνες αὐτοῦ, πολλαὶ μὲν ἀργυραῖ, πολλαὶ δὲ καὶ χρυσαῖ οὖσαι, συνεχωνεύθησαν: Plin. Pan. 52, illae aureae et innumerabiles (statuae) strage et ruina publico gaudio litaverunt. The colossal equestrian statue of Domitian, the theme of Stat. S. i 1, was probably destroyed among the rest (see Vollmer ad loc.). Procopius (6th cent. A.D.) in his Hist. arcana, 8 p. 55 Dind., has a curious story that the body of Domitian was hewn in pieces, which were collected and put together by his wife as a model for a bronze statue. This was set up on the right of the ascent from the Forum to the Capitol and was the sole existing statue of Domitian in the time of Procopius, who says that it bore a strange resemblance to Justinian (Friedl., Sitteng. iii¹º 60). For the destruction of the statues of the fallen great cf. Juv. x 58, descendunt statuae restemque sequuntur | iam strident ignes, iam follibus atque caminis | ardet adoratum populo caput, et crepat ingens | Seianus. Mayor, in his note there, cites many parallels; among the emperors whose statues were so treated were Caligula, Nero, Vitellius, Commodus, Maximinus, and Theodosius. In 1878 a mutilated statue, probably of Domitian, was found in the Tiber. =

: used by Suetonius as adv. (13 times) and prep. (6 times). As adv., (a) = in conspectu suo, as here and in Vitell. 14, 2, quendam coram interfici iussit; (b) in conspectu aliorum vel omnium, e.g. Ner. 7, 1, amitam Lepidam ream testimonio coram afflixit; (c) = in os "to one's face," e.g. Aug. 13, 2, hunc foedissimo convicio coram prosciderunt. As a prep. it either precedes or follows its case; e.g. Tib. 62, 2, coram se: Oth. 1, 2, se coram: Aug. 56, 4, coram iudicibus: Tit. 10, 1, populo coram. The postposition of coram is not found in class. prose; it occurs most frequently in Tacitus.

: cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 11, 8, senatus radendum nomen decrevit: Macrob. Sat. i 12, 37, sed ubi infaustum vocabulum (Domitiani) ex omni aere vel saxo placuit eradi, menses quoque usurpatione tyrannicae appellationis (see Dom. 13, 3) exuti sunt: Procop. 1.C., δόγμα ἐγεγόνει τῆς συγκλήτου βουλῆς μηδ' ὄνομα τοῦ βασιλέως τούτου ἐν γράμμασιν εἶναι, μηδ' εἰκόνα ἡντιναοῦν αὐτοῦ διασώζεσθαι: Euseb. Hist. Eccl. iii 20, μετὰ δὲ τὸν Δομετιανὸν πεντεκαίδεκα ἔτεσιν ἐπικρατήσαντα, Νέρουα τὴν ἀρχὴν διαδεξαμένου, καθαιρεθῆναι μὲν τὰς Δομετιανοῦ τιμὰς . . ἡ ῾Ῥωμαίων σύγκλητος βουλὴ ψηφίζεται. Domitian's name has been erased on extant inscriptions; see the list in Dessau, Inscr. Lat. Sel. iii 1, 273. Commodus (ob. 192) and Maximinus (ob. 238) were similarly dishonoured; cf. Lamprid. Comm. 20, Censeo quae is ob honorem suum decerni coegit abolenda: statuas abolendas, nomenque ex omnibus privatis publicisque monumentis eradendum: Capitol. Gord. 9, Appellato igitur Gordiano imperatore, iuvenes, qui auctores huius facinoris erant, statuas Maximini deiecerunt, imagines perfregerunt, nomen publicitus eraserunt. Mommsen (Staatsr. iii³ 1190) shows that while the statues of the enemies of the people were overthrown under the Republic, the first instance of a name being expunged from the list of magistrates was that of M. Antonius after the battle of Actium. A proposal in the senate that the name of Piso (see Vitell. 2, 3) should be removed from the consular records (nomen Pisonis radendum fastis) was vetoed by Tiberius (Tac. A. iii 17, 18). abolendam memoriam: cf. Calig. 60 (after the murder of Caligula), senatus in asserenda libertate adeo consensit, ut quidam abolendam Caesarum memoriam ac diruenda templa censuerint: Lamprid. Comm. 19, parricidae gladiatoris (Commodi) memoria aboleatur: Val. Max. viii 14, 5, bene consuluerant Ephesii decreto memoriam taeterrimi hominis abolendo. For the senate's damnatio memoriae and rescissio actorum in the case of a dead emperor see Mommsen, Staatsr. ii 1134. One result of the damnatio memoriae of Domitian is that comparatively few inscriptions of his reign have survived. In Rome itself only one has been found (C.I.L. vi 932, Dessau 246), but a certain number have been preserved in Italy and the provinces (see Weynand in Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2542; Gsell, op. cit. 331, n. 3; Imhof, op. cit. 124). From the very considerable number of Domitian's coins still extant Gsell (330, n. 2) concludes that it is improbable that the senate ordered the coins with his name to be melted down, as was done later with those of Geta (Dio lxxvii 12). ..

div.p: § 2. cornix elocuta est: the crow was reputed to possess the gift of imitating human speech; cf. Varr. L.L. vi 56: Plin. N.H. x 124, cornix plura contexta verba exprimens et alia atque alia crebro addiscens (from which it has been proposed to read cornix for perdix in Stat. S. ii 4, 20, refert iungens iterata vocabula perdix): Ov. M. ii 547, quem garrula motis | consequitur pennis, scitetur ut omnia, cornix | auditaque viae causa 'non utile carpis," | inquit, "iter: ne sperne meae praesagia linguae!” Crows were among the birds which gave omens by their note (oscines); cf. Paulus (Fest. p. 197), oscinum tripudium est, quod oris cantu significat quid portendi; cum cecinit corvus, cornix, noctua, parra, picus: Cic. Ac. ii 128, cum cornix cecinerit, tum aliquid eam aut iubere aut vetare: Cic. Div. ii 78, nec (Deiotaro) cornix canere potuit recte eum facere. ἔσται πάντα καλῶς : cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 13, 10 (praising the virtues of Trajan), Quae omnia eo maiora visebantur, quo per multos atque atroces tyrannos perdito atque prostrato statu Romano, in remedium tantorum malorum divinitus credebatur opportune datus; usque eo, ut adveniens imperium eius pleraque mirifica denuntiaverint, in quis praecipuum, cornicem e fastigio Capitolii Atticis sermonibus effatam esse “καλῶς ἔσται.” ..

p.note: : cf. Galb. 8, 2: Vesp. 5, 3: Tit. 5, 3.

: cf. Calp. Ecl. 7, 24, spectacula Tarpeium prope despectantia culmen: Sil. Ital. iii 609, Tarpei culminis ignes: vi 102, culmina Tarpeia exosus: x 360, ipse refulgebat Tarpeiae culmine rupis. On the N. summit of the Mons Capitolinus was the Arx; on the S. summit the Capitolium or temple of Jupiter. The "Tarpeia rupes" was on the S.W. slope of the S. summit, and that summit was called the Mons Tarpeius, though Mons Tarpeius, Arx Tarpeia, and Capitolium are sometimes used to designate the whole hill, which was more correctly described as “Arx Capitoliumque."

: "hunch,” “hump"; the fem. form also in Amm. Marc. xxiii 4; gibbus in Juvenal (vi 109: x 294,309). Suetonius uses the adj. gibber (Galb. 3, 3) and also has gibberosus in a specimen which he cites of the caustic utterances of Orbilius ("plagosus''): Gramm. 9, 2, Ac ne principum quidem virorum insectatione abstinuit; siquidem ignotus adhuc cum iudicio frequenti testimonium diceret, interrogatus a Varrone Murena diversae partis advocato, quidnam ageret et quo artificio ("profession'') uteretur, gibberosos se de sole in umbram transferre respondit; quod Murena gibber erat (see note on Galb. 3, 3).

: as a prep. also in Tib. 68, 2 (p. occipitium) and Ner. 51 (p. verticem); as an adv. in Iul. 20, 1 (lictores p. sequerentur). It is most frequent in Plautus; only twice in Cicero (Tim. 37 and 48); not in Caesar; twice in Livy; six times in Tacitus. Quintilian (viii 3, 25) mentions it among the words by which Virgil gave to his work an air of antiquity.
: Suetonius uses the sing. in 8 passages, the pl. in 4 (e.g. Vitell. 17, 1, iniecto cervicibus laqueo). Down to the time of Livy the sing. is limited to poetry. See Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 248 sq.
: 'somnium hoc Domitiani significabat, a tergo eius, hoc est, post ipsius obitum, futuros principes optimos, qui aetatem auream orbi terrarum reducerent” (Beroaldus).
: cf. c. 9, 1: 10, 1; see on “abstinuit,” Tit. 7, 3.

: the mild and beneficent rule of Domitian's successors, Nerva (96-98) and Trajan (98-116), is attested by various writers; e.g. Philostr. vit. Apollon. vii 8, ἀρχῇ πρέπειν ἐδόκει Νέρουας, ἧς μετὰ Δομετιανὸν σωφρόνως ἥψατο : Aur. Vict. Caes. 12, 1, Quid enim Nerva prudentius magisque moderatum? (Epit. 11, 15, quid enim Nerva prudentius aut moderatius? quid Traiano divinius? quid praestantius Hadriano?): Eutrop. viii 1, respublica ad prosperrimum statum rediit bonis principibus ingenti felicitate commissa; Domitiano enim, exitiabili tyranno, Nerva successit: Tac. H. i 1, rara temporum (i.e. under Nerva and Trajan) felicitate, ubi sentire quae velis et quae sentias dicere licet: Tac. Agr. 3, nunc tandem redit animus; et quamquam primo statim beatissimi saeculi ortu Nerva Caesar res olim dissociabiles miscuerit, principatum ac libertatem, augeatque cotidie felicitatem Nerva Traianus, nec spem modo ac votum securitas publica, sed ipsius voti fiduciam ac robur adsumpserit, natura tamen infirmitatis humanae tardiora sunt remedia quam mala: Florus, praef. 8, sub Traiano principe movet lacertos (populus Romanus), et praeter spem omnium senectus imperii, quasi reddita iuventute, revirescit. Gibbon, Decline and Fall c. 3, says: “If a man were called to fix the period in the history of the world during which the condition of the human race was most happy and prosperous, he would, without hesitation, name that which elapsed from the death of Domitian to the accession of Commodus. The vast extent of the Roman empire was governed by absolute power, under the guidance of virtue and wisdom. The armies were restrained by the firm but gentle hand of four successive emperors, whose characters and authority commanded involuntary respect. The forms of the civil administration were carefully preserved by Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, and the Antonines, who delighted in the image of liberty, and were pleased with considering themselves as the accountable ministers of the laws. Such princes deserved the honour of restoring the republic, had the Romans of their days been capable of enjoying a rational freedom." APPENDICES. 2R
